assessments.operationalization: Measure fundamental frequency of cow, bull and calf calls under the same recording protocol. The claim is confirmed if cows are lower than bulls and calves lower than adults, and refuted if bulls are lower than cows or adults lower than calves.
obstacles: Cattle-call spectra exist in a few bioacoustic papers and are not compiled as paired sex and age samples.
Call type (contact, distress, roar) changes pitch and has to be matched before sexes are compared.
assessments.rationale: The comparison is a simple acoustic contrast and would cleanly support or refute the exception Aristotle states for cattle. Existing recordings are few, unmatched across call types, and not deposited as an analysis-ready table. They allow a preliminary look and do not yet decide the claim.

assessments.operationalization: Compare voice pitch and other sex characters before and after castration in males, against intact males and females. The claim is supported if gelded males shift toward female values, and refuted if castration leaves those characters unchanged.
obstacles: Castration effects on voice and plumage or antlers are in veterinary and endocrine papers, not a comparative dataset.
The species he has in mind (man, deer, birds) need to be analyzed separately because the traits differ.
assessments.rationale: The effect of removing the testes on voice and secondary characters is experimentally tractable and has been measured in humans, deer, capons and other domestic animals. Those results can test the mechanism for several species. They are not in one open table, so the cross-species claim is only partly assembled.

assessments.operationalization: Compare published gestation lengths for the domestic dog with the interval 60 to 63 days, and, where litter-level data exist, test whether gestations under 60 days fail. The duration claim fails if the typical range lies outside that window.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for Canis lupus familiaris

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: an independent gestation-length value for the dog or wolf

obstacles: Both databases report a species-level duration, not the claim that litters born before 60 days die.
assessments.rationale: Gestation length of the dog is a standard field in AnAge and PanTHERIA, and the stated window of 60 to 63 days can be compared with those values directly. The further claim about non-survival of shorter litters is not in the tables and remains a veterinary detail. The central duration is resolvable with the life-history databases now.

assessments.operationalization: Compare typical adult lifespan of stallions and mares with 35 and a little over 40 years, keeping maximum records separate. The claim is confirmed if typical male and female longevities fall near those figures, with mares living longer, and refuted if typical lifespans or the sex order differ.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and, where recorded, sex of the record for Equus caballus

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity for the horse as a second compiled estimate

obstacles: The open fields are maximum longevity, while the claim is a typical lifespan.
Sex-specific typical ages are not separate columns, and record ages exceed both stated figures.
assessments.rationale: AnAge and PanTHERIA give horse longevity, so a numerical comparison is immediate. They record maxima and exceptional ages, whereas Aristotle states a usual life of about 35 years for stallions and a little over 40 for mares. The sex difference in typical lifespan is therefore only partly addressed by the same sources, and a maximum above 40 does not by itself refute a statement about the usual life.

assessments.operationalization: Use age-specific fertility to find the ages at which male and female fertility become rare, and compare them with about 65 and about 45, and with the outer limits of 70 and 50. The claim fails if the ages at which fertility effectively ends lie well away from those figures.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility rates that show until what age women bear children

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive lifespan context for Homo sapiens, complementary to the fertility schedule

obstacles: The Human Fertility Database measures births by maternal age; paternal age is much less complete.
Modern fertility is shaped by contraception and is a biased proxy for biological capacity.
assessments.rationale: Female age-specific fertility is a public, analysis-ready series and can test the claim that conception becomes rare around forty-five and exceptional by fifty. Male fertility to sixty-five or seventy is not in the same table at comparable coverage. Social control of fertility also separates observed births from biological capacity, so the female half is testable and the male half and the biological reading remain partial.

assessments.operationalization: Compare gestation length and litter size of Camelus dromedarius with twelve months and one young. The claim is confirmed if gestation is about twelve months and twinning is absent or exceptional, and refuted if either value is substantially different.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and litter size for the dromedary

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: independent gestation length and litter size for camels

obstacles: Published gestations cluster near twelve to thirteen months, so 'twelve' is a rounded target rather than an exact day count.
assessments.rationale: Gestation length and litter size of the dromedary are both fields in AnAge and PanTHERIA. Either database can confirm or refute a twelve-month pregnancy and single young. The analysis is a direct lookup, with the only subtlety being that reported means sit slightly above twelve months.

assessments.operationalization: Compare gestation and litter size of Elephas maximus and Loxodonta africana with two years and one calf. The claim is confirmed if gestation is about twenty-four months and twin births are absent or rare, and refuted if gestation or the usual litter size differs.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and litter size for both living elephant species

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: a second compiled gestation and litter size for elephants

obstacles: The two living species differ by weeks, and 'two years' has to be scored against means near twenty-two months.
Rare twin births mean 'only one' is a rule about the usual litter, not a strict impossibility.
assessments.rationale: Elephant gestation and litter size are standard entries in the mammal life-history databases. Those values can confirm a single calf and can show whether 'two years' matches the measured pregnancy or overshoots it. The comparison is immediate and decides the claim as a quantitative generalization, with species differences and rare twins as stated caveats rather than missing data.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate lifespan of Bolinus brandaris and Hexaplex trunculus and test whether spiral checks are annual. The claim is confirmed if typical life is about six years and each check matches one year, and refuted if lifespan or the check interval differs.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: longevity and growth notes for the purple murex species, where a value has been entered

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic identity of the Mediterranean purple murex so growth studies can be matched to species

obstacles: Longevity entries are sparse, and annual shell checks are a sclerochronology result in papers.
Bolinus and Hexaplex need not share one lifespan.
assessments.rationale: Lifespan and the meaning of shell increments are measurable, and growth studies exist for the Mediterranean muricids. SeaLifeBase may carry a longevity figure and does not encode whether each spiral interval is one year. Both halves of the sentence can be pursued in the primary literature for these species and are not in a ready comparative file.

assessments.operationalization: Record whether Pinna nobilis houses a shrimp or pea crab, and whether experimental removal raises mortality. The association is confirmed by co-occurrence; the claim that the mussel soon dies without the guest requires a removal result.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: commensal and host records linking Pinna with pontoniine shrimps and pea crabs

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species account of Pinna nobilis and notes on its associated crustaceans

obstacles: Interaction records show co-occurrence, not death after removal.
The guest is sometimes a shrimp and sometimes a crab, so 'the' pinna-guard is not one species.
assessments.rationale: The housing of a small crustacean in Pinna is a documented association and can be read from interaction compilations. The further claim that the mussel dies soon after losing that companion is a causal mortality statement and is not what those records contain. Existing data can test the partnership and leave the death clause weakly constrained.

assessments.operationalization: Test two predictions: that bivalves, gastropods, barnacles and ascidians arise without parents from mud, and that oysters, cockles and limpets sort onto slime, sand and rock. Life cycles with larvae or eggs refute spontaneous generation; habitat frequencies test the substrate sorting.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: larval development and habitat notes for oysters, cockles, mussels, limpets and barnacles

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences with substrate or habitat context for the same groups

obstacles: Habitat fields are coarse, so slime versus sand versus rock hollows is only partly captured.
Spontaneous generation is refuted by life cycles that are described species by species.
assessments.rationale: Larval life cycles of oysters, cockles and limpets are on record and contradict an origin from mud without parents. Substrate preferences are a separate, genuine pattern and can be compared with occurrence data where habitat was recorded. The mechanistic half is decidable from existing life histories, and the habitat half is only as sharp as the substrate fields.

assessments.operationalization: Measure egg diameter at laying and during incubation for a lobster or crayfish, a cephalopod and an oviparous fish. The claim is confirmed if diameter increases after laying in each group and refuted if size is fixed at deposition.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg-size records for oviparous fishes, a baseline rather than a swelling time series

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg and early-development notes for crustaceans and cephalopods

obstacles: Post-laying swelling is measured in species studies and is not a comparative field.
Water uptake at fertilization has to be separated from later embryonic growth.
assessments.rationale: An increase in egg size after laying is a simple measurement, and it has been reported for fish eggs that harden by water uptake and for some cephalopod and crustacean eggs. The life-history databases store a single egg size, not the before-and-after contrast. The claim is testable from those studies for particular species and is not a column one can average across the three groups.

assessments.operationalization: Compare maximum or typical lifespan of squid, cuttlefish and octopus with one year. The claim is confirmed if almost all species die within a year and refuted if a substantial set lives longer.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: longevity entries for squids, cuttlefishes and octopuses

obstacles: Lifespan is filled for a minority of species.
Some octopuses, and nautiluses if they are admitted, live well beyond a year, so scope decisions matter.
assessments.rationale: SeaLifeBase contains longevity for a number of cephalopods, which is the right variable for a one-year limit. Many common octopuses and squids are short-lived, and several documented lifespans exceed a year, so the 'few exceptions' clause can be inspected where a number exists. Missing entries for most species keep the test partial.

assessments.operationalization: Ask whether the adult insect is formed from the whole larval body or from imaginal discs while most larval tissue is broken down, and whether any butterflies lay a hard egg rather than a grub-producing egg. The 'whole grub' clause fails if the adult arises from discrete primordia.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: developmental records of imaginal discs in Drosophila, the best-tabulated case of adult tissue arising from parts of the larva

obstacles: The detailed map of imaginal discs is for Drosophila, not for insects generally.
What counts as 'a portion' of the grub versus the whole grub is a histological judgment.
assessments.rationale: FlyBase documents that the adult fly is assembled from imaginal discs while much of the larva is histolyzed, which is a direct contrast with 'the grub entire becomes the animal'. That is one model species. The exception for a butterfly that lays a hard egg, and the same contrast in bees and beetles, remain in the broader developmental literature rather than in that database.

assessments.operationalization: Map the three worms to tapeworm, Ascaris and pinworm and score whether adults produce eggs or larvae that become the next generation. The claim is refuted if any of them reproduces, and the melon-seed clause can be compared with tapeworm proglottids.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: host records for these worms in humans, consistent with transmission between hosts

obstacles: The three Greek kinds are approximate matches to tapeworm, roundworm and pinworm.
Lifecycle stages in a genome resource are not a demographic demonstration of fertility, though they record the successive generations.
assessments.rationale: Whether intestinal worms produce offspring is decided by their life cycles, which include eggs and larvae for all three modern counterparts. WormBase ParaSite organizes those stages, and interaction records place the worms in human hosts across generations. The name match is approximate and the databases are not fertility trials, so the refutation is strong in substance and still one step removed from a purpose-built table.

assessments.operationalization: Score feeding and defecation in larvae and in pupae of butterflies, bees and wasps. The claim is confirmed if caterpillars and grubs do both and pupae do neither, and refuted if pupae feed or regularly void gut contents.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle accounts of feeding larvae and non-feeding pupae in Lepidoptera and Hymenoptera

obstacles: The pattern is in natural-history accounts rather than a trait matrix of gut activity.
Meconium voided at eclosion can be mistaken for pupal excretion if the stage is not timed carefully.
assessments.rationale: Feeding and defecation by stage are observable, and accounts of butterflies, bees and wasps describe feeding larvae and quiescent pupae. That literature can test the claim for the main holometabolous groups he names. It is not a downloaded character, and a few edge cases around emergence have to be kept separate from pupal life.

assessments.operationalization: Separate two readings: development rate depends on heat, and generation is caused by the sun or the wind rather than by parents. Degree-day series test the first; a life cycle from eggs tests the second. Only the second discriminates the claim from ordinary reproduction in warm weather.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: parental life cycles of insects that pass through a grub, the observation that distinguishes parental generation from sun or wind

obstacles: Temperature speeds development and does not show that the sun or the wind is the cause of generation.
Wind as a generative cause has no separate measurement.
assessments.rationale: Insect development is temperature-dependent, and that fact is compatible with ordinary egg-laying in warm weather. The sentence says generation is due primarily to the sun or the wind. Life-cycle accounts that derive grubs from eggs refute that causal claim for the species they cover, while no dataset isolates wind as a cause. The test works only on the parental-origin reading and only for compiled life cycles.

assessments.operationalization: Search copper-smelting fires for a winged insect, larger than a bluebottle, that lives in the fire and dies when removed. The claim is confirmed by a sustained population in the fire and refuted by monitored furnaces in which no such animal occurs.
obstacles: Faunal lists of Cyprus do not encode a habitat of 'inside the fire', so absence from those lists is not the test.
Ancient smelting heaps are not a sampled environment in any open occurrence dataset.
assessments.rationale: The report is a concrete natural-history claim: a winged animal is generated in Cypriot copper fires and depends on the fire. No public dataset records animals living in smelting furnaces, and species catalogues cannot substitute for that microhabitat. A test would require new observation at operating or reconstructed furnaces. Until then the claim is unresolvable with existing data.

assessments.operationalization: Identify the wasp, then score whether females kill spiders, seal them in a mud-closed hole, and develop their young there. The claim is confirmed for pompilids or mud-daubers if that sequence holds and weakened if the animals are ichneumonid parasitoids with a different habit.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: wasp-spider predation and provisioning records

candidate_datasets.name: WaspWeb
candidate_datasets.role: biology pages for spider-hunting wasps and mud-daubers, used to fix the Greek name

obstacles: 'Ichneumon' in modern taxonomy is a parasitoid family, while the described habit matches pompilids or mud-daubers.
Mud-sealing and the kill are behavioral details only partly captured by interaction records.
assessments.rationale: Spider-provisioning and mud closures are well described for pompilid wasps and for Sceliphron mud-daubers, and interaction databases record wasp-spider links. Aristotle's name points at ichneumons, whose modern members mostly parasitize other hosts. Once the animal is identified from the behavior, the sequence can be checked; the name itself makes the test ambiguous.

assessments.operationalization: Trace the carbon source of beeswax and of honey in Apis mellifera, and test whether honey matches floral nectar or atmospheric dew. Wax synthesized from metabolized sugars, and honey made from nectar, refute the split he states; honey chemically identical to dew would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: flower-visitation records for Apis, a proxy for a floral source of nectar and not a chemical assay of honey

obstacles: Nectar-to-honey conversion and wax-gland synthesis are in apicultural chemistry papers, not one open table.
Visitation records cannot by themselves show that honey is collected dew.
assessments.rationale: The two clauses make opposite claims about origins: wax is made from flowers, honey is gathered from the air. Chemical and behavioral studies of Apis mellifera identify nectar as the honey source and wax as a glandular secretion fed by that sugar. Those results are published in detail and are not deposited as a single analysis-ready dataset, so a team synthesizes them rather than downloading a column. The discriminating evidence exists and still has to be compiled.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate lifespan separately for workers, queens and colonies and compare each with six years, or seven at most. The claim is confirmed for whichever bearer is intended if that lifespan is usually six and at most seven, and the test is blocked while the bearer is unspecified.
obstacles: Worker, queen and colony lifespans differ by orders of magnitude, and the text does not say which is meant.
Queen and colony survival figures are in apicultural reports rather than a life-history database of the AnAge kind.
assessments.rationale: A numerical lifespan is easy to test once the individual is fixed. Workers live weeks to months, queens often a few years, and colonies can persist longer, so the same figure of six or seven years is plausible for one reading and false for another. No open longevity table removes that ambiguity. The data can test each reading and cannot decide which reading the sentence asserts.

assessments.operationalization: Record whether scorpion young kill the mother after leaving her back, and whether spiderlings kill the mother, by species. The claim is confirmed if matriphagy or matricide follows hatching in scorpions and in spiders generally, and refuted if the young disperse without killing the parent.

candidate_datasets.name: World Spider Catalog
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for the spider species in which offspring consume the mother

obstacles: Matriphagy is known in some spiders and is not the spider life cycle.
Scorpion broods ride on the mother; killing her is not a tabulated outcome and is not the usual account.
assessments.rationale: Offspring killing the parent is a behavioral event, and it is documented for particular spiders such as Stegodyphus. Spider trait compilations can hold that behavior when it has been entered, and they do not show it as general. Scorpion maternal care is described in the opposite direction, from papers rather than from the spider databases. The spider half is partly testable and the scorpion half is a separate, thinly tabulated claim.

assessments.operationalization: For Mediterranean acridids, record oviposition date and whether adults die after laying, males included. The claim is confirmed if eggs are laid at the end of summer and both sexes then die, and refuted if adults overwinter or lay earlier and survive.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle summaries for grasshoppers, including season of oviposition and annual adult death where described

obstacles: 'Grasshopper' covers many species, only some of which are strictly semelparous annuals.
Phenology is regional, and a northern European calendar need not match Greece.
assessments.rationale: End-of-summer oviposition followed by adult death is a recognizable annual life cycle and is described for many temperate grasshoppers. The accounts are species-level natural history, not a phenology table for the Greek fauna, and some species overwinter as adults or lay over a longer season. The pattern can be checked for familiar species and not confirmed as the grasshopper life cycle.

assessments.operationalization: Score tymbal presence and calling by sex in cicadas. The claim is confirmed if only males call and females are silent, and refuted if females produce the song or males of a singing species are silent.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: cicada accounts stating that males sing and females do not

obstacles: Sex of the singer is in morphological accounts and is not a downloaded character for every cicada species.
Some females produce soft sounds that have to be distinguished from the male song.
assessments.rationale: Male-only song, produced by timbals, is a standard sex character in cicadas and is stated in open family accounts. That is enough to test the claim for the well-known species and for the family-level generalization. There is no species-by-sex song matrix, so confirming it for both of Aristotle's size classes still means reading the morphological literature.

assessments.operationalization: Follow eggs ('nits') of lice, fleas and bedbugs to the next stage. The claim is refuted if nits hatch into nymphs that become reproductive adults, and it would stand if the eggs produced nothing further.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life cycles of Pediculus, Pulex and Cimex from egg through nymph to adult

obstacles: Life cycles are narrative species accounts rather than a stage-structured dataset.
Bedbug, flea and louse eggs are all called nits in the claim and have to be matched separately.
assessments.rationale: The life cycles of human lice, fleas and bedbugs are standard and state that the egg hatches into a nymph which becomes an adult. Open species accounts carry that sequence. They are not a single demographic table, but they are sufficient to confirm or refute the claim that the nit generates nothing, for these three parasites, without new rearing.

assessments.operationalization: Search host-parasite records for lice and ticks on Equus asinus, and compare with records on other mammals and birds. The donkey exception is refuted by a credible louse or tick record; the universal infestation of all other hairy and feathered animals needs a much wider host survey.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: host-parasite records for lice and ticks on donkeys and other mammals and birds

obstacles: A positive record can refute the donkey exception, while 'all other animals are infested' is far broader than the interaction tables.
Veterinary records and wildlife records are unevenly digitized, so absence is weak evidence.
assessments.rationale: GloBI aggregates parasite-host interactions, which is the right structure for lice and ticks on Equus asinus. A documented infestation refutes the claimed exemption. The same tables cannot show that every other bird and mammal is infested, because most hosts have never been surveyed into the database. The exception is testable and the universal is not.

assessments.operationalization: Follow Blastophaga psenes from caprifigs into the ostiole of cultivated Ficus carica and test whether fruit drop increases when wasps are excluded. The claim is confirmed if wasps reared in wild figs enter edible figs and retention depends on that entry, and refuted if exclusion does not increase drop.

candidate_datasets.name: FigWeb
candidate_datasets.role: biology of the fig-wasp mutualism, including Blastophaga psenes, caprifigs and the cultivated fig

obstacles: Fruit retention is an agricultural outcome of pollination, and the trials that measure drop are summarized rather than stored as a raw table on the site.
assessments.rationale: FigWeb documents the caprifig cycle of Blastophaga psenes and the entry of the wasps into edible figs, which is the natural-history core of the claim. Exclusion experiments showing that unpollinated figs drop are part of the same published system the site organizes. A team can compare the sentence with that body of evidence in a short review; the only gap is that the drop counts themselves are in the agronomic papers rather than in a fresh download.

assessments.operationalization: Code reproductive mode and litter size for vipers and for other snakes. Viviparity with retained eggs confirms the viper clause; oviparity in vipers, or viviparity widespread in other snakes, challenges the contrast. Litter size near twenty and birth within one day are separate numeric checks.

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and litter or clutch size for vipers and other snakes

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and related reproductive traits for snakes, as a numeric check on 'about twenty'

obstacles: 'The viper' covers several species whose litter sizes are not all near twenty.
Many boas, sea snakes and some colubrids are also viviparous, so 'other serpents lay eggs' is a separate clause.
assessments.rationale: Reproductive mode and litter size are recorded for snakes in the Reptile Database and in the amniote life-history compilation. Those fields can confirm internal egg retention with live birth in Vipera and can show that live birth is not confined to vipers. The 'about twenty' and 'all in one day' details are only as complete as the species-level litter data, which is enough to test the claim and not enough to make every clause equally sharp.

assessments.operationalization: Map crooked-talon birds to living raptors and owls, then compare clutch-size distributions with the kestrel. The claim stands if kestrels have the highest clutch sizes in that set and commonly reach four or more eggs, and fails if several other raptors match or exceed them or if kestrels rarely reach four.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: species-level clutch size for raptors, owls and the common kestrel

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size and related reproductive traits for the same species

obstacles: Crooked talons need an explicit taxon list, including whether owls belong.
Unprolific needs a numeric clutch-size cutoff.
assessments.rationale: Clutch size is a standard field in open avian life-history tables, with broad coverage of hawks, falcons and owls. A ranking of those clutch sizes directly tests both the general scarcity of eggs and the kestrel exception. Species limits and the word unprolific are the main judgments a pre-registered cutoff has to fix.

assessments.operationalization: Compare yolk mass as a fraction of egg contents, and albumen fraction, between birds that nest or feed in marshes and rivers and birds that do not, within developmental mode. A higher yolk fraction and lower albumen fraction in the waterbirds would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad: bird egg composition and shape
candidate_datasets.role: shell, yolk and albumen proportions linked to egg shape for a comparative bird sample

candidate_datasets.name: Deeming egg-composition compilation
candidate_datasets.role: yolk and albumen masses for 279 bird species across 21 orders

obstacles: Waterbirds are mostly precocial, so habitat is confounded with hatchling maturity.
Marsh and river species are a subset of the published composition tables.
assessments.rationale: Published compilations record yolk and albumen masses for hundreds of species, so the proportion itself is measurable. Habitat and developmental mode move together, and a test that does not separate them cannot tell a waterbird effect from the known precocial-yolk pattern. The comparison is feasible for the species already measured and thin outside that sample.

assessments.operationalization: On domestic-hen eggs, relate a shape index (length-to-breadth and bluntness of the narrow end), measured before incubation, to hatchling sex, with hen and egg mass as covariates. A repeatable excess of females from long pointed eggs and males from rounder eggs would support the claim.
obstacles: Paired egg-shape and sex-at-hatch records are scattered in small poultry trials.
No open multi-flock table covers the rule as stated.
assessments.rationale: Egg shape and hatchling sex are both measurable, and a pre-registered regression would discriminate the rule from chance. The trials that exist are small, dispersed and mostly limited to the domestic hen, so they can probe the claim without covering it at the scale of a life-history database. A decisive test needs those records compiled or collected again.

assessments.operationalization: In flocks of hens and geese known never to have been with a male, record whether they lay eggs and whether those eggs are infertile. Laying by never-mated females would refute the view that wind-eggs are leftovers of earlier copulation.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of domestic fowl and goose reproduction, including unfertilized laying

obstacles: Quantitative virgin-flock trials sit in poultry papers rather than a trait table.
Coverage is much stronger for the hen than for the goose, partridge or pigeon.
assessments.rationale: The decision criterion is direct: females with no mating history either lay infertile eggs or they do not. Poultry husbandry and anatomical accounts document that outcome for the domestic hen, with thinner published coverage for geese and the other birds named alongside them. The rival residue-of-copulation account is what those virgin layings discriminate.

assessments.operationalization: Regress incubation length, and where recorded the interval from ovulation or mating to laying, on adult body mass across birds, with phylogeny controlled. A positive size relationship for both intervals would support the claim; a flat incubation relationship would refute that half.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and incubation duration across birds

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: incubation and body-mass records for the same comparison

obstacles: Time to form the egg after copulation is sparsely recorded.
Body size is confounded with developmental mode and clutch size.
assessments.rationale: Incubation duration and adult mass are standard open variables, so the hatching half of the claim can be fit directly. The time required to form the egg is a different interval and is mostly in species studies, so the compound claim is only partly covered. Phylogenetic controls are routine and do not remove that gap.

assessments.operationalization: Using staged chick embryos, record when a beating heart and paired vitelline vessels first appear relative to other organs. The claim stands if that stage is a small blood-red beating heart with two blood-filled vessels leaving it, and fails if the heart is not yet beating when it becomes visible or the vessel pattern differs.

candidate_datasets.name: eChickAtlas
candidate_datasets.role: staged chick anatomy through the period of heart-tube and vessel formation

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA chicken-embryo gene-expression atlas
candidate_datasets.role: stage and anatomical location of early heart development in the chick

obstacles: Open atlases are built on the domestic chick, with other birds inferred.
Which structure counts as first is a staging judgment.
assessments.rationale: Hamburger-Hamilton staging and public chick atlases show the heart tube and the early vessels at known stages. A small team can score those images against the beating speck and the two vessels without new experiments. Coverage is excellent for the hen's egg, which is the observation Aristotle reports.

assessments.operationalization: In staged bird embryos, locate the embryo relative to yolk and albumen and trace whether nutrients reach it through the yolk-sac stalk. Yolk-sac nutrition would support the nourishment clause; a blastoderm seated on the yolk would undermine the claim that the life of the chick lies in the white.

candidate_datasets.name: eChickAtlas
candidate_datasets.role: position of the chick embryo relative to yolk and extraembryonic membranes

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA chicken-embryo gene-expression atlas
candidate_datasets.role: early embryonic tissues at the yolk surface and in the yolk sac

obstacles: Life-element is not a measured variable.
Albumen and yolk are both nutritive, so the exclusive wording needs a pre-set criterion.
assessments.rationale: Atlases can show where the embryo sits and that a yolk-sac circulation supplies it, which is the observable nutrition clause. The further claim that the principle of life lies in the white is only partly fixed by that anatomy, because both egg fractions contribute water, protein or lipid. The nutrition path is testable now; the life-element wording stays interpretive.

assessments.operationalization: Take age at first reproduction for birds and compute the share with that age under one year. The claim stands if that share is very small under a pre-registered cutoff, and fails if a large fraction of species, especially small passerines, breed in year one.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: age at first reproduction across birds

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: female and male age at sexual maturity for birds

obstacles: Very few needs a numeric threshold.
Age at maturity is an imperfect stand-in for age at first successful breeding.
assessments.rationale: Age at first reproduction is tabulated for thousands of bird species. The distribution either concentrates above one year or it does not, which is enough to confirm or refute a claim that very few birds breed in their first year. Missing species and the maturity proxy limit precision, and they leave the direction of the result readable.

assessments.operationalization: After a defined injury that destroys the eye of nestling barn swallows, follow whether the eye regenerates and whether vision returns. Recovery of sight would support the claim; permanent blindness in a pre-registered sample would refute it.
obstacles: No public experimental series records this injury in Hirundo rustica.
General reviews of vertebrate regeneration do not replace a swallow outcome.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is a clear recovery-or-not endpoint. Published regeneration summaries do not contain a swallow puncture series with sample size, follow-up and a vision measure. Resolving the claim requires that experiment or an equivalent unpublished record brought into the open.

assessments.operationalization: For Aquila species, summarize clutch size, number hatched, incubation length and the cause of brood reduction. Support requires modal clutch near three, usual brood of two, incubation near 30 days, and the parent actively expelling a chick; siblicide or starvation without expulsion would fail that clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size and incubation duration for eagle species

candidate_datasets.name: British Trust for Ornithology
candidate_datasets.role: nest records for clutch, hatch and incubation in monitored raptors

obstacles: Aquila species differ in clutch size and incubation.
Parental expulsion is rarely separated from siblicide in nest records.
assessments.rationale: Clutch size and incubation length for eagles are in open life-history tables and nest schemes, so those numbers can be checked now. Active expulsion by the mother is a behavioral detail that standard tables do not code, and brood reduction in eagles is often sibling aggression. The numerical clauses are testable; the expulsion clause needs case narratives.

assessments.operationalization: Compare foot and beak measurements and phylogenetic placement of Cuculus canorus with Accipiter hawks, and compile records of hawks killing cuckoos. Separate ancestry plus hawk-like talons absent in the cuckoo, or predation of cuckoos by hawks, would refute the transformed-hawk account.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic separation of cuckoos and hawks

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak, tarsus and body-size measurements for cuckoos and hawks

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: diet and foraging records bearing on hawk predation

obstacles: Talon curvature is only partly captured by tarsus length.
Predation events are rarer in trait tables than in species monographs.
assessments.rationale: Aristotle's criteria are anatomical difference and cross-species predation, both of which public phylogenies and morphological tables address. Cuckoos and hawks are not close relatives, and foot and bill measurements quantify the talon and head contrast he uses. Predation records add a behavioral check and are less complete than the tree.

assessments.operationalization: For the common cuckoo, score nest-building, eggs per host nest, removal or eating of host eggs, and whether the host incubates and feeds the young. The claim fails if common cuckoos regularly build and incubate, lay large clutches in their own nests, or leave the host's eggs intact as the usual pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Field Museum brood-parasite host lists
candidate_datasets.role: compiled host records for Old World cuckoos, including the common cuckoo

candidate_datasets.name: British Trust for Ornithology
candidate_datasets.role: nest records of cuckoo eggs in host nests in Britain

obstacles: Host lists record the foster species more often than whether the female ate the host eggs.
Some other cuckoo species are not parasitic, so the species map must stay on Cuculus canorus.
assessments.rationale: Brood parasitism of the common cuckoo is documented in an open host list and in long-running nest records. Those sources show laying in other birds' nests and rearing by the host. Whether the adult eats the host clutch, rather than removing an egg while the chick later ejects the rest, is a finer point inside species studies.

assessments.operationalization: Compare testis mass, scaled by body mass, in and out of the breeding season for male birds, with the domestic cock and male partridge included. Seasonal enlargement, largest in those two, would support the claim; no seasonal change would refute it.
obstacles: Seasonal testis size is in endocrinology papers, not a life-history column.
Salacious is not an independent measured trait.
assessments.rationale: Testis mass by season is a standard measurement, and published series exist for poultry, galliforms and many passerines. They are not gathered into one open table, so a test means compiling those series for a pre-chosen species list. The within-male seasonal contrast is clean once the numbers are in hand; ranking salaciousness is the softer clause.

assessments.operationalization: Code reproductive mode for cartilaginous fishes and for bony fishes, and check Lophius separately. The claim stands only if cartilaginous fishes are viviparous after internal eggs, other fishes are oviparous, and the fishing-frog is the stated exception.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for bony fishes and for Lophius

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of sharks, rays and chimaeras, including egg-laying and live-bearing

obstacles: Aristotle's cartilaginous group includes the fishing-frog, which is a bony fish.
Skates are cartilaginous and many lay eggs, so the universal needs that exception counted.
assessments.rationale: Reproductive mode is a core field in FishBase and Sharkipedia, covering thousands of fishes and the living sharks and rays. Those tables can confirm or refute universal viviparity of cartilaginous fishes, universal oviparity of the rest, and the status of Lophius. The remaining care is mapping his group names onto those taxa.

assessments.operationalization: For Mustelus mustelus, record whether embryos attach to the uterine wall by a cord after yolk stores decline, and whether a chorion and extraembryonic membranes are present. A yolk-sac placenta with those membranes would support the claim; yolk dependence until birth without a uterine cord would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode, including placental viviparity, for smooth-hounds

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and embryo notes for Mustelus

obstacles: Several Mustelus species differ in placental detail.
Chorion and membrane histology sit in anatomical papers more than in the trait table.
assessments.rationale: Smooth-hound reproductive mode, including placental attachment, is recorded in open elasmobranch trait data and species accounts. That is enough to test the cord-to-the-womb claim for the species usually identified with Aristotle's smooth shark. Fine structure of the chorion still has to be read from the anatomical descriptions those databases cite.

assessments.operationalization: Compare parturition locations with offshore habitat for sharks and rays, and test whether nursery sites are warmer and have fewer predators than adjacent adult habitat. Inshore pupping would support the movement clause; no temperature or predator difference would leave the stated purpose unsupported.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: parturition and nursery-related life-history traits for sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: coastal versus offshore occurrence of sharks and rays

obstacles: For the sake of warmth and protection is not fixed by location alone.
Many pelagic species pup far from shore.
assessments.rationale: Nursery use and coastal occurrence can be scored for a substantial set of sharks and rays. The purpose clause needs a contrast of temperature and predation that existing occurrence tables only partly supply, and food or current cues fit the same inshore pattern. The movement is partly testable; the final cause is weakly separated from rivals.

assessments.operationalization: Tally documented hybrid pairings among fishes against the number of species pairs with intensive breeding studies. The general rule stands if hybrids are rare relative to opportunity, and fails if interspecific pairing is common in well-studied groups.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts and reproductive notes that record fish hybrids

obstacles: Kind can mean species or a broader sort of fish.
Hybrid lists are biased toward freshwater fishes that people breed.
assessments.rationale: FishBase and the papers behind it record many hybrids, which is enough to test a general ban on cross-kind pairing in well-studied families. Absence of a hybrid record is weak evidence that pairing never occurs, and marine species are poorly covered. The rule can be assessed as a frequency in the compiled subset, not as a universal negative.

assessments.operationalization: For every living cetacean, record reproductive mode and whether an egg stage is carried. Universal live birth with no egg-laying would support the claim; any egg-laying cetacean would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and gestation for cetacean species

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of cetacean reproduction

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for dolphins, porpoises and whales

obstacles: Fossil stem cetaceans are outside the living animals the claim describes.
assessments.rationale: Live birth versus eggs is recorded for the living whales, dolphins and porpoises in mammal trait tables and species accounts. The set is small enough to check species by species. A single egg-laying cetacean would refute the universal claim, and the open accounts agree on the variable that would show it.

assessments.operationalization: For dolphins and porpoises, record presence of mammary glands, milk and a nursing period. Nursing of the young would support the claim; absence of lactation would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: weaning age as evidence of lactation in dolphins and porpoises

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of nursing in dolphin and porpoise species

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: lactation and parental care for Delphinidae and Phocoenidae

obstacles: Weaning age is a proxy for milk transfer when milk composition itself is untabulated.
assessments.rationale: Lactation and a weaning period are standard entries for dolphins and porpoises. Species accounts describe nursing directly, and trait tables record weaning age across the groups. The claim is a presence statement with a small, well-covered taxon list.

assessments.operationalization: Code reproductive mode for scaled teleosts, for eel-like slippery fishes, and for Anguilla. The claim stands if the scaled and slippery species are oviparous and eels are not; live-bearing scaled fishes, or oviparous eels, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for bony fishes, including eels and mullets

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: modern names for the basse, mullet, etelis and eel

obstacles: Scaly and smooth are ancient groupings, not taxa.
The eel exception is itself an empirical clause that the life cycle can fail.
assessments.rationale: FishBase codes oviparity and live-bearing across bony fishes, including the named mullets, basses and the European eel. That is enough to test the universals once a taxon map is fixed. The map from scaly and smooth to modern groups is the main limit, because different maps change which exceptions count.

assessments.operationalization: For each candidate identification of erythrinus and channa, tally the sex ratio and the fraction of adults carrying eggs. The claim stands if samples contain only egg-bearing fish; a regular class of fish without eggs would refute it for that identification.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex strategy and reproductive state for candidate serranids and seabreams

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: candidate scientific names for channa and erythrinus

obstacles: Channa and erythrinus have competing modern identifications.
Hermaphrodite labels are not the same as a catch composition of all-pregnant fish.
assessments.rationale: If the names are serranids or a protogynous seabream, FishBase records sex strategy and spawning biology for those candidates. Simultaneous hermaphroditism would explain catches that all contain eggs, and it is not the same measurement as Aristotle's never caught except pregnant. Because the Greek names map in more than one way, the result can differ by identification.

assessments.operationalization: For externally fertilizing fishes, compare development of eggs with and without sperm exposure. Development restricted to sperm-exposed eggs would support the claim; regular development of unexposed eggs, or an internal-fertilization life cycle, would limit or refute the universal wording.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fertilization mode and reproductive mode across oviparous fishes

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish fertilization assays in which eggs develop only after sperm exposure

obstacles: Many oviparous fishes fertilize internally, outside the milt-over-eggs picture.
Trial data are dense for aquaculture and model species and thin elsewhere.
assessments.rationale: Fertilization mode is coded broadly, and experimental systems such as zebrafish measure development with and without sperm. Those data test the mechanism for external fertilizers. They do not cover every oviparous fish, and internal fertilizers are a different procedure, so the universal scope stays partly open.

assessments.operationalization: Compare spawning and larval locations of marine fishes with offshore waters, and test whether inshore sites are warmer, richer in food and lower in large predators. A majority of species spawning offshore, or no inshore advantage on those three measures, would undermine the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: spawning habitat and fecundity for marine fishes

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence of fish eggs and larvae inshore and offshore

obstacles: Eels, tunas and many others spawn in the open sea.
Warmth, food and protection are confounded reasons for the same coastal pattern.
assessments.rationale: Spawning habitat and larval occurrences can show how often marine fishes use the shore. The three benefits Aristotle names are only partly measured in those tables, and several rival reasons predict the same shift inshore. The location claim is testable for well-known species; the purpose claim is not cleanly separated.

assessments.operationalization: In normal tables for oviparous fishes, order the first visible appearance of eyes against other organs, and compare that sequence with insect larvae that differentiate the posterior end first. Eyes among the first large external organs would support the fish clause; an earlier non-eye organ as the rule would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish staging series with the timing of optic vesicle and eye formation

obstacles: Staging coverage is deep for zebrafish and a few other models, not for fishes generally.
First visible organ depends on the imaging method.
assessments.rationale: Zebrafish and a handful of other fishes have public stage series in which eye formation can be ordered against somites, brain and heart. That tests the claim for those species and against grub-like posterior-first development. It does not yet cover oviparous fishes as a whole.

assessments.operationalization: For Silurus aristotelis, measure days of male attendance at the egg mass, whether the female leaves after spawning, and egg developmental time relative to other freshwater fishes. A male guard period of about 40 to 50 days with female departure would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: parental care and reproductive notes for Silurus aristotelis and related catfishes

obstacles: Guard duration is rarely a database field and rests on a few field studies.
Developmental time depends on temperature.
assessments.rationale: FishBase records parental care for Aristotle's catfish and its relatives, which tests male guarding and female departure at a coarse level. The specific 40-to-50-day watch and the claim of exceptionally slow development sit in a small field literature, not in a multi-population table. The species identification itself is unusually secure.

assessments.operationalization: Code migration direction for Mugilidae and for Anguilla anguilla between sea and rivers or marshes. The claim stands if mullets move from the sea into brackish or fresh water and eels leave rivers and marshes for the sea to spawn.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: migration type for grey mullets and the European eel

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: European eel assessments of the downstream spawning migration

obstacles: Several mullet species differ in how far they penetrate fresh water.
Aristotle's mullet is a mugilid group, not one modern species.
assessments.rationale: FishBase codes catadromy and related movements for the European eel and for grey mullets, and ICES assessments document the eel's migration to sea. Direction of travel is the whole empirical content. Species-level differences among mullets affect how far inland they go, not the sea-to-lagoon direction the claim states.

assessments.operationalization: Identify the small fry Aristotle derives from mud or sand and determine whether they hatch from eggs of known parents and later grow and reproduce. A closed life cycle from eggs would refute spontaneous origin; fry that never recruit would be required for the sterility clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle and early-stage records for candidate anchovies, gobies and mullets

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence records of larval fishes in coastal shallows

obstacles: Aphya and the mullet near Cnidos are insecurely identified.
Cannot grow or reproduce needs cohort data, not just a species name.
assessments.rationale: Once a fry type is identified, FishBase life-cycle records test whether it comes from eggs and whether adults reproduce. That is the observable content of a spontaneous-generation claim. The ancient fry names do not map cleanly, so the same data can refute the claim for a candidate species and still miss the population he saw.

assessments.operationalization: Examine gonads of European eels across the yellow and silver stages for milt, eggs and genital ducts. Any eel with identifiable milt, roe or reproductive passages would refute the universal negative.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode, maturity and gonad notes for Anguilla anguilla

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: assessments and cited studies of silver-eel maturation and spawning

obstacles: Yellow eels in rivers have undeveloped gonads, so a river-only sample repeats Aristotle's observation.
Fully ripe oceanic adults remain rarely sampled.
assessments.rationale: The claim is a universal negative about milt, spawn and ducts. Silver-eel studies and FishBase reproductive records document developing gonads and an oviparous life cycle, which is the observation that would refute it. A sample restricted to feeding-stage river eels would miss that stage, so the test has to include maturing migrants.

assessments.operationalization: Trace European eel early life from supposed mud worms versus from eggs and leptocephalus larvae. Origin from a identified worm in mud would support the claim; a life cycle through marine larvae and eggs would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: life cycle of Anguilla anguilla from leptocephalus to spawning adult

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: stock biology of the oceanic spawning migration

obstacles: The worm called earth's guts has no secure modern species name.
The eel life cycle does not depend on naming that worm.
assessments.rationale: The observable prediction is that eels arise from worms generated in mud. The European eel life cycle, from leptocephalus to silver eel and oceanic spawning, is documented in FishBase and in the assessment literature. That life cycle is a direct alternative to origin from earth's guts, whether or not the worm name can be matched.

assessments.operationalization: Collect incubation or gestation lengths in days for fishes and test whether every value is at most 30 and divisible by 7. Any well-measured duration outside that set refutes the universal rule.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: incubation and gestation lengths for bony and cartilaginous fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for sharks and rays

obstacles: Gestation may mean pregnancy or egg incubation.
Development time changes with temperature, and many records are ranges.
assessments.rationale: Day counts of incubation and gestation are widespread in FishBase and Sharkipedia. A rule that every duration is a multiple of seven and no longer than 30 days fails as soon as reliable counts fall elsewhere, which those tables contain. Temperature ranges make single-day precision uneven, and they do not rescue a seven-day numerology if the ranges themselves miss those values.

assessments.operationalization: Compare annual fecundity or litter size, offspring size and, where measured, juvenile mortality between cartilaginous fishes and other fishes. Lower fecundity and higher early survival in selachians would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity, offspring size and reproductive mode across fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: litter size, offspring size and natural mortality for sharks and rays

obstacles: Juvenile survival is far sparser than litter size.
Viviparity and shared ancestry confound a raw selachian-versus-bony contrast.
assessments.rationale: Litter size and offspring size are tabulated well enough to test the fecundity contrast and the claim that the young are large. Survival is the clause that existing data cover only in part: natural-mortality estimates exist for some sharks and are not comparable across fishes generally. Body size and reproductive mode have to be controlled before the contrast is read as a selachian effect.

assessments.operationalization: Score aggression by sex and reproductive state for the named mammals, with females compared just after birth and males compared in rut versus other seasons. Higher female aggression postpartum and higher male aggression in rut would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: behavioral accounts of rut and maternal aggression in the named mammals

obstacles: Bad-tempered is not a standard ethogram variable.
Quantitative series cover livestock and deer far better than bear, lion or camel.
assessments.rationale: Rut aggression and postpartum defense are described for several of the named species in natural-history accounts and livestock studies. They are not in a comparative behavior table with a common scale, so the test is a compilation for a subset. The universal timing rule across horse, boar, bull, ram, camel, bear, wolf, lion and dog is wider than those series.

assessments.operationalization: Compare birth or hatching month with the month when juveniles become independent, against local resource or temperature peaks. A match between rearing time and a pre-registered favorable season would support the observable pattern; the adapted-so-as wording needs that match to beat alternative timings.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: breeding and rearing traits across amniotes

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: age at maturity and weaning as rearing-time measures

obstacles: Convenient season and adapted so as are loose.
Birth month and resource peaks are often missing from the trait tables.
assessments.rationale: Life-history tables record rearing periods more often than the seasonal food peak those periods are supposed to meet. Where both exist, alignment can be tested for a subset of species. Many different schedules can be called convenient, and phylogeny and body size predict seasonality without a separate adaptive test, so discrimination stays weak.

assessments.operationalization: Link wind direction at mating of sheep and goats to the sex of the offspring, with season and breed controlled. A higher male fraction after north winds and a higher female fraction after south winds would support the claim.
obstacles: No public table pairs wind direction at conception with lamb or kid sex.
Separate weather archives and flock books are not linked.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is specific enough to test with flock books and wind records. Those two data streams are not published as a joined dataset, and sex-ratio studies of sheep do not carry wind direction. Confirming or refuting the rule requires that linkage, which is not available now.

assessments.operationalization: Compare survival curves of male and female horses and of stable-kept versus herd-kept horses, then test whether mating load explains the male deficit after age and management are controlled. Shorter male life confined to breeding stallions, plus longer stable life, would support both clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity records and sources for the horse

obstacles: AnAge does not split horse lifespan by sex or by stable versus herd.
Sexual service is confounded with other sex differences and with workload.
assessments.rationale: A species-level longevity record exists, and veterinary cohorts in the literature discuss sex and management. They are not an open survival table with mating history, so the causal clause cannot be separated from other differences between stallions and mares. Stable-versus-troop longevity is similarly scattered.

assessments.operationalization: Compare mule gestation (jack × mare) and hinny gestation (stallion × jenny) with horse and donkey gestations, and score foal size and morphology against sire and dam. Gestation matching the sire's species, and foals closer to the dam, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation lengths of horse and donkey as the parental baselines

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of horse, donkey and mule reproduction

obstacles: Hybrid gestations are in veterinary case series, not in AnAge.
Resemblance in looks and vigour needs a pre-set morphometric score.
assessments.rationale: Horse and donkey gestation lengths are tabulated, which supplies the two parental baselines. Mule and hinny gestations and parent-offspring resemblance are in case series rather than a public hybrid table, so both clauses can be examined only after a compilation. The comparison itself is discriminating once those lengths and measurements are aligned.

assessments.operationalization: Compile veterinary cases of female mules with confirmed pregnancy and record whether any reached parturition. Pregnancies that end without birth fit the stated case; live births limit a reading on which pregnancy never continues to birth.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive accounts of mules, including sterility and rare fertility reports

obstacles: The sentence is one historical case, which modern series do not identify.
Rare live mule births and failed pregnancies are both reported, so the universal reading and the existential reading diverge.
assessments.rationale: Species accounts and case reports document mule pregnancy and the usual failure to produce a foal, which is the general phenomenon behind the sentence. They do not identify Aristotle's particular mule. Reading the claim as never carried to birth is testable in those reports; reading it as a single ancient anecdote is not.

assessments.operationalization: Place red-deer gestation, juvenile growth and maximum longevity on the mammalian life-history plane, and test whether short gestation and fast maturity predict short maximum lifespan. Deer longevity inside the ordinary mammalian range, rather than a multi-century life, would support the negative conclusion about fabulous ages.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation, age at maturity and maximum longevity for deer and other mammals

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length, body mass and life-history traits for the same comparison

obstacles: Extreme longevity has no numeric cutoff in the text.
Maximum-longevity records are often from captivity.
assessments.rationale: Gestation, growth schedule and longevity for red deer and for mammals at large are in open databases. Those fields test both the deer facts Aristotle uses and the inference that short gestation and fast growth count against extreme age. The correlation has exceptions, so it supports a comparative argument rather than a deduction that every short-gestation mammal is short-lived.

assessments.operationalization: Rank mammals by neonate mass divided by adult female mass, and compare absolute neonate mass of the brown bear with mouse and weasel masses. The claim also requires newborn bears to be hairless, blind and incompletely formed; mass ranks and neonatal descriptions can each fail separately.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal and adult body mass across mammals, including bears

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: birth weight and adult weight for bears, mice and mustelids

obstacles: Marsupials have still smaller neonate-to-mother ratios if they are included.
Hair, vision and limb completeness are in species accounts rather than the mass tables.
assessments.rationale: Neonate and adult masses are standard mammal-trait fields, so the relative-size ranking and the mouse-to-weasel absolute comparison can be computed directly. Altricial features of bear cubs are described in the same literature the databases draw on. Whether bears are the smallest of all animals depends on including marsupials, which a pre-registered taxon scope has to state.

assessments.operationalization: Dissect or image male and female striped hyenas and score whether each sex has one functional genital opening plus a blind look-alike, or two functional sets of organs. Functional organs of both sexes in every individual would refute Aristotle's denial of hermaphroditism.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical and reproductive accounts of striped and spotted hyenas

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: open specimen media for carnivoran anatomy, including hyenas where deposited

obstacles: Striped and spotted hyenas differ in the female genitalia.
The blind part has to be matched to a pseudopenis, pouch or duct before the description can pass or fail.
assessments.rationale: Hyena reproductive anatomy is described in detail in open species accounts and anatomical papers, which is enough to test true hermaphroditism against a single functional sex. Specimen repositories add images where hyenas have been deposited, with uneven coverage. The striped hyena, the likely referent, does not match the spotted hyena's extreme female masculinization, so the species map changes the anatomical target.

assessments.operationalization: For the European hare, compile litters per year, breeding months, gestation and evidence of a second conception during pregnancy. Year-round breeding with a litter every month and superfetation would support the claim; a seasonal schedule or fewer than about twelve litters a year would fail the frequency clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litters per year, litter size and gestation for Lepus europaeus

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive schedule and litter frequency for hares

obstacles: Superfetation is not a column in the trait tables.
Breeding season length changes with latitude.
assessments.rationale: Litters per year and gestation are tabulated and can refute a literal birth every month. Superfetation in the European hare is reported in reproductive studies that are not in those tables, so that clause needs the primary papers. Latitude shifts the breeding season, which matters for the all-seasons wording.

assessments.operationalization: Rank mammals and other small vertebrates by litter size and by litters per year, or by their product, and place mice on that ranking. The claim stands if mice are at the extreme of the pre-registered metric and fails if other species clearly exceed them.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size, litters per year and interbirth interval across mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and reproductive frequency, including mice and other rodents

obstacles: Most prolific can mean litter size, frequency or annual offspring.
Captive rodents inflate reproductive output relative to wild mice.
assessments.rationale: Litter size and reproductive frequency are filled widely enough to rank mice against other mammals. That ranking confirms or refutes an extremal claim once the metric is fixed in advance. Mice sit near the top on several metrics, and other rodents can outrank them, which is a result the same tables can show.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the age at which boys first produce semen and the age at which pubic hair reaches a defined stage, in more than one population. The claim stands if both cluster near fourteen, and fails if the central ages lie well away from fourteen or the two events do not coincide.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: age at sexual debut in national surveys, a proxy rather than spermarche or pubic-hair stage

obstacles: Open survey data record sexual debut more often than first semen or Tanner pubic hair.
Age at puberty has shifted across populations and centuries.
assessments.rationale: Semenarche and pubic-hair stage are measured in pediatric cohorts, and those cohorts are scattered rather than released as one open table. Demographic surveys supply age at sexual debut, which is a later and different event. The age-fourteen claim can be probed with the published series and is not settled by the survey proxy alone.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate median ages at thelarche and menarche and test whether both fall near fourteen and coincide with male puberty. A large shift of either event away from fourteen, or a wide gap between breast development and menarche, would fail the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: women's reproductive calendars, including age at first birth as a later marker

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility showing when childbearing begins in historical and modern populations

obstacles: First birth is later than menarche and thelarche.
Secular change means modern medians are a poor stand-in for a single ancient age without the historical series.
assessments.rationale: Menarche is widely studied, and fertility databases show the ages at which births begin, which bounds puberty from above. Breast development and first menses are separate events, and open surveys rarely store both Tanner stages. The age-fourteen conjunction is testable from compiled cohort studies for some populations and is not a single downloadable global table.

assessments.operationalization: Measure male fertility and births at ages under 21, and compare birth weight and congenital-anomaly rates by parental age. Any substantial fertility before 21 refutes infertility of the seed; a monotone penalty in offspring size or viability at young parental ages would support the second clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility rates, including ages under 21

candidate_datasets.name: WHO adolescent pregnancy fact sheet
candidate_datasets.role: births to adolescents and associated offspring risks

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: maternal age, birth weight and child outcomes in survey microdata

obstacles: Imperfect covers more outcomes than birth weight.
Paternal age under 21 is less complete than maternal age.
assessments.rationale: Age-specific fertility rates include the teenage years, so a claim that semen is infertile until 21 is directly testable. Survey and WHO summaries also relate young maternal age to birth weight and neonatal risk, which is the offspring clause. The infertility wording and the milder size-and-viability wording can fail independently, and both have public numbers.

assessments.operationalization: Pair semen consistency (thin versus granular or clotted) with subsequent offspring sex in a large series, holding count and motility fixed. A higher male fraction from granular samples and a higher female fraction from thin samples would support the claim.
obstacles: No public andrology table links semen consistency to offspring sex.
Small clinical series are confounded by the rest of the semen analysis.
assessments.rationale: Consistency and offspring sex are measurable, and a large paired series would discriminate the rule. Existing public fertility data do not carry both variables together. Scattered clinical notes are too small and confounded to confirm or refute the sex prediction.

assessments.operationalization: Score visible menstrual bleeding across birds, reptiles, fishes, viviparous quadrupeds and women. Bleeding confined to women would support the discharge clause; regular menstruation in other species would refute only women. Conversion of a residue into feathers, scales, hair or urine is a separate claim and needs a tracer the bleeding data do not supply.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode across vertebrates as context for which groups menstruate

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive accounts noting menstruation or its absence

obstacles: Residue converted into feathers or scales is not distinguished from simply lacking a discharge.
A few non-human mammals menstruate, and estrous bleeding can be mistaken for menstruation.
assessments.rationale: Who shows a menstrual discharge is an observable pattern, and species accounts plus comparative reviews cover it for many taxa. The further claim that the same material becomes feathers, scales, hair or urine has no measurement that separates it from the bare absence of bleeding. The distribution is partly testable; the conversion mechanism is not.

assessments.operationalization: From ultrasound series, record the gestational age of first fetal movement and the side of the uterus, split by fetal sex. Movement of males near day 40 on the right and females near day 90 on the left would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: Carnegie-stage ages and morphology, not the side of quickening

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: timetable of human embryonic and fetal movement

obstacles: Maternal quickening is later than the first movements seen on ultrasound.
Side of implantation by sex is not a field in open atlases.
assessments.rationale: First movement and fetal sex are routine ultrasound variables, and published series report when movement begins. Open embryo atlases fix ages and morphology and do not code uterine side by sex. The 40-versus-90-day and right-versus-left rules can be checked in those clinical series, which still have to be compiled.

assessments.operationalization: At Carnegie stages corresponding to about 40 days, measure crown-rump length against a large ant and score limb buds, genital tubercle or penis, and relative eye size. The claim fails if the embryo is far from that size or if a penis is not yet distinguishable.

candidate_datasets.name: Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: Carnegie-stage photographs and sizes around day 40

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: stage tables for length, limbs, eyes and external genitalia

obstacles: Staged embryos at this age are not labeled by genetic sex.
Penis versus undifferentiated genital tubercle is an anatomical judgment.
assessments.rationale: Open Carnegie atlases give length and external anatomy for the stage that falls near forty days. Size, limb visibility and relative eye size can be scored from those images. Sex-specific penis development is the clause the same stages are least able to support, because the external genitalia are still shared, and that is itself a result.
