assessments.operationalization: Compare, by fetal sex, the gestational age at which defined organs reach a maturity criterion, and the distribution of gestational length at birth. Slower completion of parts in females and a higher share of female births at ten months would support the two clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: human developmental timetable against which sex differences would have to be shown

candidate_datasets.name: Eurostat
candidate_datasets.role: European birth statistics that include gestational age where the perinatal tables report it

obstacles: Sex-specific organogenesis timing is sparse in open atlases.
Ten months needs a declared lunar or calendar definition.
assessments.rationale: Gestational-age distributions by sex exist in perinatal statistics, which can test whether female births more often reach a ten-month term. A slower completion of parts in female embryos is a finer claim and is not a standard open table. The term clause is the one current civil-registration extracts can address; the organ-timing clause stays thinly measured.

assessments.operationalization: Compare within-species spread of gestation in humans with the spread in other mammals and other vertebrates, counting delayed implantation as real variation. The claim fails if other species have gestation ranges as wide as the human span from seven to eleven months, or if humans lack that span.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length across mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation and incubation across mammals, birds and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: Eurostat
candidate_datasets.role: European birth statistics that report gestational age, for the spread of human pregnancy length

obstacles: Many species are stored as a single gestation length, so within-species variance is under-reported.
Delayed implantation has to be counted as variation rather than dropped.
assessments.rationale: Human gestation is known to vary across months, and mammal and amniote databases record gestation for thousands of other species, including groups with delayed implantation and wide ranges. That comparison tests the claim that only humans vary. Single-value entries hide some variation, and the species with published ranges are already enough to test uniqueness.

assessments.operationalization: Using a pre-registered map of Aristotle's months onto weeks of gestation, estimate survival of infants born before that cutoff and at the seven-month boundary. Any survivors before the cutoff refute never; survival at the boundary with high morbidity would address the weakly clause.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO preterm birth fact sheet
candidate_datasets.role: gestational-age classes and survival of preterm infants

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Global Health Observatory
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal mortality indicators related to preterm birth

obstacles: Seven months can be read as lunar or calendar months.
Intensive care raises survival relative to ancient conditions, which still bears on under no circumstances.
assessments.rationale: WHO summaries report survival for very preterm and extremely preterm infants, which is the observation a universal never-survive claim has to meet. Mapping his months onto modern weeks is a declared assumption, and once it is fixed the survival figures confirm or refute the cutoff. Modern care changes the absolute rates and does not erase documented survival before a seven-month boundary.

assessments.operationalization: Compare survival of infants at a pre-registered eight-month gestational age in Egypt and Greece, in a period without modern neonatal intensive care if the historical claim is the target. Higher survival in Egypt and high mortality in Greece would support the geographic contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Global Health Observatory
candidate_datasets.role: country neonatal mortality, a coarse proxy for eight-month survival

obstacles: No ancient cohort records eight-month survival in Egypt versus Greece.
Modern hospital care removes the contrast the claim describes.
assessments.rationale: Country neonatal statistics exist, and they do not isolate an eight-month gestational class in classical populations. A modern Greece-Egypt comparison is a proxy dominated by medical care. The geographic claim as Aristotle states it lacks the cohort that would confirm or refute it.

assessments.operationalization: Find the maximum number of infants in one birth in civil-registration tables and documented case series. Any birth of six or more refutes five as the maximum; a ceiling of five in complete registries would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Eurostat
candidate_datasets.role: European birth statistics, including multiple deliveries

obstacles: Aggregate tables may top-code the highest multiplicities, so the extreme tail also depends on case series.
Assisted reproduction raises higher-order births relative to ancient conditions.
assessments.rationale: Civil-registration systems publish multiple-birth statistics, and a single reliable confinement of six or more refutes a maximum of five. Eurostat's birth tables are the open aggregate; case reports fill in the extreme tail. Assisted reproduction changes the frequency and is not required for the existence proof if unassisted higher-order births are also on record.

assessments.operationalization: Code whether females mate during an established pregnancy, for humans, horses, hares and a sample of other species. The claim stands if women and mares do so commonly, other species refuse, and hares are the superfetation exception.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mating and pregnancy accounts for horses, hares and other mammals

obstacles: Mating during pregnancy is not a standard trait column.
All other animals is far wider than existing ethograms.
assessments.rationale: Behavioral accounts document estrus, pregnancy and mating for horses, humans and hares, which covers the positive examples. A universal refusal by every other pregnant animal is not in any comparative table and fails as soon as further species with pregnancy mating are compiled. The test is feasible for the named species and open-ended for the universal clause.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the age distribution of final menses and the oldest maternal ages at birth in natural-fertility populations. The claim stands if most women stop near 40, the tail reaches about 50, and births after 50 are absent.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility through the forties and fifties

obstacles: SWAN is a modern cohort with a later menopause than the age of about forty.
Rare late births depend on how natural fertility is separated from assisted reproduction.
assessments.rationale: Cohort studies measure age at final menses, and the Human Fertility Database measures births by maternal age into the late reproductive years. Together they test the typical age, the upper tail near 50, and whether births occur beyond it. Modern menopause is later than forty in these series, which is a result rather than a barrier to the test.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate male fertility or documented paternity by age through 60 and 70. Continued paternity at 70 would support the upper example; a collapse of fertility well before 60 would refute the usual limit.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility, including paternal age in the series that record it

obstacles: Most fertility series are maternal age only.
Sexually competent is broader than documented paternity.
assessments.rationale: Where paternal age is recorded, births to men in their sixties and seventies test the upper ages directly. Many open fertility tables omit the father's age, so coverage is a subset of populations. Competence without a recorded birth is the clause those tables do not measure.

assessments.operationalization: Split the claim into congenital conditions and acquired marks. For named congenital traits, measure parent-child recurrence; for scars and pimples acquired in life, measure recurrence in children who did not share the injury. High recurrence of genetic conditions and none for scars would split the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: ClinVar
candidate_datasets.role: inherited congenital conditions with parent-child transmission

obstacles: Scars and acquired pimples are not in genetic databases.
Lame and blind mix injuries with heritable diseases.
assessments.rationale: ClinVar and pedigree studies catalogue congenital conditions that do recur in children, which tests the heritable half. Acquired scars have no corresponding public concordance table, and a hereditary reading of scars would require that table or a documented mechanism. The two halves do not stand or fall together.

assessments.operationalization: In three-generation pedigrees, count traits present in a grandparent and a grandchild and absent in the intervening parent. Recurring cases would support skip-generation resemblance; a pre-registered set of traits with no such cases would undermine the existential claim.

candidate_datasets.name: ClinVar
candidate_datasets.role: recessive and other pedigrees in which a phenotype reappears after a generation

obstacles: Open three-generation phenotype tables for ordinary resemblance are mostly restricted.
ClinVar covers medical traits, not facial resemblance in general.
assessments.rationale: Recessive pedigrees are a direct case of a trait visible in a grandparent and a grandchild and not in the parent, and those pedigrees are public for many conditions. General family resemblance, as distinct from a diagnosed trait, sits in cohort studies with controlled access. The existential genetic claim is testable; the everyday wording is broader than ClinVar.

assessments.operationalization: Compare staged embryos of a bird, a fish, a placental mammal and a placental shark on a pre-set list of early structures, and record where the nutritive cord attaches. The cord clause is supported by yolk-sac, uterine, or dual attachment in the groups named; the same-way clause needs those stages to match under the pre-set list.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish embryonic staging

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA chicken-embryo gene-expression atlas
candidate_datasets.role: chick embryonic stages and tissues

candidate_datasets.name: Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: human Carnegie stages for the viviparous comparison

obstacles: Develop in the same way is broad enough that early similarity and later difference both fit.
Placental-shark attachment is not in the model-organism atlases.
assessments.rationale: Public atlases make early development comparable across a fish, a bird and a human, and they show different nutritive attachments. That is the sharp part of the claim. A statement that all animals develop in the same way has no single mismatch that would retire it, because the stages one chooses change the answer.

assessments.operationalization: Record presentation at birth for humans and other viviparous animals, treating each species' usual presentation as the natural course. Universal head-first birth would support the claim; a species whose normal birth is tail-first, such as many cetaceans, would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: cetacean birth behavior, including usual presentation

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: birth descriptions for whales, dolphins and other mammals

obstacles: Natural course can be defined so that breech births do not count.
Presentation is well described for humans and cetaceans and sparse for most other mammals.
assessments.rationale: Usual presentation is recorded for humans and for whales and dolphins, and tail-first birth is the normal cetacean pattern in those accounts. That single group tests a claim about all animals. Livestock and wild mammals are less systematically tabulated, so the universal is vulnerable to the well-described exceptions and incompletely surveyed elsewhere.

assessments.operationalization: Count blood vessels in the umbilical cord of cattle, of a smaller mammal, and in the yolk-sac stalk of the chick. Four, two and one, in that order, would support the size rule; other stable counts would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: umbilical vessel counts in human and comparative developmental anatomy

candidate_datasets.name: Digimorph
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical imaging of vertebrate specimens where cords or yolk sacs are visible

obstacles: Published counts cover a handful of species, not a size series.
The chick uses paired vitelline vessels rather than a single umbilical cord.
assessments.rationale: Vessel number is a direct count, and veterinary and embryological descriptions give it for cattle, humans and the chick. Those descriptions are not a size-ordered trait table, so the three-step rule has to be assembled from them. The chick is the clearest potential mismatch because its yolk-sac circulation is not a single vessel.

assessments.operationalization: From eruption series, estimate the age of the first tooth and which tooth it is, and test whether warmer nurse's milk advances that age. Eruption in the seventh month, incisors first, would support the timing clauses; no milk-temperature effect would refute the last clause.

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: timing of human primary-tooth development and eruption

obstacles: Milk temperature is not in eruption tables.
Seventh month needs a declared starting point from birth.
assessments.rationale: Deciduous eruption order and age are standard pediatric measurements, and open developmental references state that the incisors come first around the middle of the first year. The effect of the nurse's milk temperature is not in those tables. Timing and order can be checked; the milk clause cannot.

assessments.operationalization: In nationally representative surveys, estimate the rate of menses during breastfeeding versus after weaning, with time since birth held fixed. A large drop in bleeding while milk is produced, with a minority of exceptions, would support the general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: breastfeeding and postpartum amenorrhea in survey microdata

obstacles: Survey amenorrhea is reported bleeding, not a hormone assay.
The moisture-in-one-direction explanation is not identified by the association alone.
assessments.rationale: Demographic and Health Surveys record breastfeeding and the return of menses for large samples of women. That is the general rule Aristotle states, including room for exceptions. The physiological story that moisture cannot flow in two directions at once is not what the survey association identifies, and the regularity itself is.

assessments.operationalization: No outcome distinguishes traces of gentleness, fierceness, courage, timidity or sagacity from their absence, because any behavioral difference can be called a trace, differing from humans in degree or by analogy.
obstacles: Psychical qualities and by analogy have no refuting observation.
Animal-personality scores would still count as traces under the wording.
assessments.rationale: The sentence asserts that most animals show some trace of human mental qualities, with the difference allowed to be either of degree or of analogy. Every measured behavior fits that wording, and no dataset result would show the traces to be absent. The claim is conceptual rather than a statement with a confirming and a refuting measurement.

assessments.operationalization: Place sponges, ascidians, sea anemones and sessile shellfish on current classifications of animals, plants and non-living things. A stable assignment to one kingdom would undermine cannot be assigned; the further claim that nature proceeds little by little from the lifeless has no separate metric in those names.

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: classification of sponges, ascidians, anemones and sessile molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Taxonomy
candidate_datasets.role: placement of the same intermediate forms in Metazoa

obstacles: Nature proceeds little by little is a scheme, not a measurement.
Modern kingdoms answer the assignment question and leave the continuum claim open.
assessments.rationale: The named intermediate organisms now have stable taxonomic placements, which tests the clause that they cannot be assigned to one side or the other. A gradual passage from lifeless things to animals is not fixed by those placements. Taxonomy resolves the examples; it does not operationalize the whole scala.

assessments.operationalization: Proxy intelligence and memory by brain size or by documented performance, and parental association by weaning age or time to independence, then test the correlation with body size and phylogeny controlled. A positive partial association would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: weaning age and age at maturity as association-time proxies

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: weaning age and life-history timing across mammals

obstacles: Weaning age ends nutritional dependence and not social life with the young.
Brain size and memory tests are separate compilations and are confounded by body size.
assessments.rationale: Duration of offspring dependence is tabulated widely. Intelligence and memory are not columns in those tables, so the test uses a proxy and inherits the proxy's confounds. A correlation of weaning with brain size can be assembled and would still leave memory, as distinct from brain size, weakly measured.

assessments.operationalization: For sea turtles, crocodiles, hippopotamus, seals, freshwater turtles and frogs, record respiratory organ and survival during forced submersion, plus whether they breed on or near land. Death or distress without access to air, and terrestrial or shoreline breeding, would support the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: respiration and breeding habitat for turtles, crocodiles, hippos and seals

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: frog respiration and breeding sites

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: sea-turtle and seal biology, including air breathing and haul-out or nesting

obstacles: Some turtles and frogs exchange gas through cloaca or skin and endure long submersion.
Drown is a graded outcome, not a single submersion time.
assessments.rationale: Lung breathing, the need to reach air, and breeding on or near land are documented for each named group in open species accounts. Those accounts also record cutaneous or cloacal gas exchange, which qualifies how quickly a frog or turtle is distressed. The named list is small enough to score species by species.

assessments.operationalization: For dolphins, confirm lungs and air breathing, time to suffocation in nets, survival in air, and whether sleep occurs with the blowhole above water. Each clause fails on its own measurement: gills instead of lungs, prolonged survival underwater in a net, immediate death in air, or submerged sleep without access to air.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: dolphin respiration, entanglement and surface behavior

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: lung anatomy, surfacing and parental behavior of dolphins

obstacles: Time-to-suffocation and time-alive-in-air are reported as observations more often than as a single trial table.
Sleep posture is described for a subset of species.
assessments.rationale: Lungs, entanglement asphyxia, haul-out or deck survival and surface breathing during rest are standard items in dolphin species accounts. The anatomical clause is settled by dissection and by those accounts together. Durations and sleep posture are quantitative details inside the same literature, with fewer formal trials than the lung claim.

assessments.operationalization: Separate two clauses: gilled fishes pass water over the gills, and blowhole animals take in water while feeding rather than as their respiratory medium. Physiology then has to show that gill flow functions to cool the blood rather than to exchange gases, for example by survival in warm oxygenated water versus cold oxygen-poor water.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gill and respiratory-mode records for fishes

obstacles: Cooling versus oxygen uptake is not a FishBase field.
The purpose clause needs experiments that are scattered in physiology papers.
assessments.rationale: Presence of gills versus a blowhole is anatomical and is widely recorded, including the point that cetaceans breathe air. The claim that water is taken in to cool the blood is a function that gas-exchange experiments can in principle separate from oxygenation. Those experiments are not assembled as a comparative dataset, so the function remains weakly tested.

assessments.operationalization: For each candidate identification of the cordylus, record gills, lungs and terrestrial locomotion, and test uniqueness against other amphibians. The claim stands only if one animal has gills, lacks lungs, walks on land and is the only such animal.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: respiration and habitat of newts, salamanders and other amphibians with gills

obstacles: Cordylus may be a newt larva, a salamander or an aquatic proteid.
Several amphibians have external gills, and larvae also have developing lungs.
assessments.rationale: AmphibiaWeb records gills, lungs and habitat for the animals that might be the cordylus. Uniqueness and the combination of no lungs plus land walking can be checked once the name is fixed, and the plausible identifications do not share that combination. The limit is the name, not the absence of amphibian life-history data.

assessments.operationalization: Score secondary sexual traits before and after castration in a pre-set list of species, and separately test whether embryo sex tracks the size of an early organ rather than chromosomal or environmental sex determination. A shift toward female form after removal of the gonad would support the castration clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of sexual dimorphism and, where described, effects of castration

obstacles: Castration outcomes are in livestock studies more than in a trait database.
Mammalian sex is not decided by the size of an embryonic organ, and that contrast is in developmental papers.
assessments.rationale: The castration example is a concrete before-and-after comparison, documented for several domestic species and not gathered in one open table. The general claim that any minute organ can reshape the whole animal is too open to fail. Embryonic sex determination by organ size is a distinct mechanism and is addressed by developmental studies rather than by the castration records.

assessments.operationalization: Lower an empty thin wax vessel into seawater for 24 hours and measure the volume and salinity of any water inside. A drinkable yield would support the claim; an empty vessel or a saline yield would refute it.
obstacles: Ocean salinity archives do not run the wax-vessel procedure.
No public replication series with volume and salinity was located.
assessments.rationale: The procedure and the pass-fail measurement are fully specified. Public salinity data describe seawater and do not substitute for water recovered inside a wax vessel. Resolving the prediction requires a reported replication, which is not available as a dataset.

assessments.operationalization: In diet records with identified prey, code intraspecific predation for fishes and for mullets, and compare the conger with other species. The universal fails if well-studied species have no conspecific prey; the mullet exception fails if mullets eat conspecifics.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet items, including conspecifics where recorded, for fishes and mullets

obstacles: Missing cannibalism records are not evidence of absence.
Diet studies over-represent commercial species.
assessments.rationale: FishBase food-item records include conspecific prey for many species, which can refute a ban and can check mullets and the conger. Most species lack a diet study thorough enough to treat a zero as real. The exception and the especially ravenous clause are testable in the studied subset; the word all is not.

assessments.operationalization: In dissections or scans, measure whether an esophagus separates the mouth from the stomach across a phylogenetic sample of fishes. A stomach immediately behind the mouth and no esophagus would support the claim; a distinct gullet in ordinary teleosts would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: morphological notes on the alimentary tract where species accounts include them

candidate_datasets.name: Digimorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT imagery of fish specimens for mouth, esophagus and stomach position

obstacles: Esophagus presence is described in anatomical papers more often than as a FishBase field.
Digimorph includes few fish species.
assessments.rationale: Presence or absence of a gullet is a dissection finding, and comparative anatomy covers it for many fishes. Open databases hold that fact unevenly: species accounts sometimes describe the gut, and scanned specimens are few. A short esophagus can be scored as present or absent under a pre-set length rule, which is enough to test the universal in a compiled sample.

assessments.operationalization: Code Mediterranean fishes for cyclic oral or pharyngeal reprocessing of food, using Sparisoma cretense as the scarus, and ask whether any other fish shows the same behavior. A second fish with cud-like rechewing would refute uniqueness; restriction of that behavior to the scarus would support it.
obstacles: Chewing the cud must be mapped either to true regurgitation or to the parrotfish pharyngeal mill, and those readings can disagree.
FishBase records diet and teeth, not a rumination ethogram, so the behavioral criterion still has to be taken from papers.
assessments.rationale: The scarus is securely Sparisoma cretense, and FishBase covers its herbivory and that of other grinding fishes. Uniqueness is a universal negative, and the dataset does not record whether food is regurgitated and rechewed. The test can challenge uniqueness among well-studied taxa, not close it for fishes as a whole.

assessments.operationalization: Compare otolith and captive ages of Anguilla anguilla with a threshold of about seven to eight years. The claim is an existence statement, so any reliable ages in that range confirm it, and a maximum well below seven years would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and life-history records for the European eel

obstacles: The wording 'in some cases' is confirmed by a few old eels and is not a claim about typical or maximum age.
Captive maxima and wild otolith ages are not the same distribution.
assessments.rationale: Age of the European eel is a standard variable, and both AnAge and FishBase compile it. Because the claim only says that some eels reach seven or eight years, existing age samples can confirm it directly and would refute it if eels never approached that age. Longer lifespans do not contradict the wording.

assessments.operationalization: Treat hooked-talon birds as the raptor orders, and score each species' diet from plant versus vertebrate percentages. Any species with substantial seed or fruit use refutes 'carnivorous without exception'; a purely animal diet across the group would support that clause.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: species-level diet proportions for birds, to test whether every hooked-talon species is strictly carnivorous

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak and body measurements used with taxonomy to delimit the hooked-talon comparison set

obstacles: Diet percentages record what is eaten in nature, not whether a bird physically cannot swallow grain placed in the bill.
Parrots have hooked bills but not raptorial talons, so the group boundary needs an explicit rule.
assessments.rationale: EltonTraits gives diet fractions for essentially all birds, so the universal carnivory claim can be confirmed or refuted by a direct count of plant-eating exceptions. The further claim that these birds cannot swallow grain is a capacity test absent from the diet table. One documented non-carnivorous exception is enough to reject the statement as a whole.

assessments.operationalization: Score free-water drinking as present or absent for birds of prey, treating the kestrel and kite as the named exceptions. Repeated drinking by another raptor would refute 'never'; a systematic absence outside those exceptions would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts that sometimes record drinking, for a subset of kites, falcons and other raptors

obstacles: Drinking is rarely tabulated, so absence of a mention is not evidence that a species never drinks.
The claim is about a near-universal negative, which scattered anecdotes can refute but not establish.
assessments.rationale: Drinking is a clear behavior, but no open trait table records it. Species accounts and papers mention it for some raptors, which is enough to test the 'never' clause for those species only. A full test of birds of prey would require new, systematic observations.

assessments.operationalization: For oviparous vertebrates, score lung architecture as sac-like and poorly vascularized versus parabronchial and richly vascularized, and separately score drinking rate. A bird lung with a rich blood supply refutes the claim that every oviparous animal has a scantily blooded spongy lung.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and mesh data for reptile and bird torsos that show lung form in a subset of oviparous vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: digital anatomical slices used to compare lung structure across a few reptiles, birds and other amniotes

obstacles: Scans show gross lung shape better than how richly the tissue is supplied with blood.
Drinking rate is not in these anatomical archives, and 'all oviparous animals' includes birds as well as reptiles.
assessments.rationale: Lung type is measurable, and bird lungs are the obvious discriminating case against a single spongy, blood-poor lung for every egg-layer. Public scans and anatomical series cover only a subset of taxa and almost never quantify vascularity or drinking. The anatomical half can be tested for well-scanned species; the drinking half cannot.

assessments.operationalization: Among jag-toothed carnivorous mammals, compare plant eating in healthy versus clinically ill animals, and record whether the bout ends in vomiting. Regular grass eating by healthy dogs or wild carnivores would refute 'only when sick' and the purge explanation.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: plant versus vertebrate diet percentages for Carnivora, showing which supposed carnivores eat vegetation at all

obstacles: Diet percentages do not say whether the animal was ill or whether it vomited.
The purge story is a purpose claim; only the timing of grass eating relative to sickness is observable.
assessments.rationale: EltonTraits can show that many carnivores include plant matter, which already strains 'never eat grass'. It cannot tie those meals to illness or vomiting. Veterinary and behavioral papers on dogs fill part of that gap but are not a single open table, so the sickness clause is only partly testable.

assessments.operationalization: Compute dressing percentage as carcass or saleable flesh divided by live weight for domestic pigs, and compare relative fattening rate with other livestock of similar size. A dressing percentage far from five-sixths would refute that ratio; a match within ordinary breed variation would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service
candidate_datasets.role: live weight and dressed-weight statistics from livestock slaughter, for a modern estimate of the pig's flesh fraction

candidate_datasets.name: FAOSTAT
candidate_datasets.role: international livestock production and carcass statistics used to compare pig yields with other domestic species

obstacles: Modern dressed weight excludes different parts from Aristotle's 'flesh', and commercial breeds are not ancient Greek pigs.
Comparative fattening rate across 'any other animal' is much broader than slaughter statistics.
assessments.rationale: The five-sixths ratio is a direct dressing percentage, and slaughter statistics contain the two weights. Those series cover modern commercial pigs and a modern carcass definition, so they test a proxy for the ancient husbandry claim rather than the full comparative fattening statement. The ratio can still be accepted or rejected for present-day Sus scrofa domestica.

assessments.operationalization: Compare recorded longevities of Camelus dromedarius and Camelus bactrianus with a typical lifespan near thirty years and a maximum near one hundred. Records clustered around a few decades without any approach to a century would refute the hundred-year instances; ages near thirty would support the ordinary figure.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity records for dromedary and Bactrian camels

obstacles: 'About thirty years' is a vague central figure, while captive records are maxima rather than wild averages.
Failure to find a hundred-year camel is strong evidence against that instance, not a logical proof that none ever lived so long.
assessments.rationale: Camel longevity is tabulated in AnAge from zoo and husbandry records. Those records can check both the ordinary lifespan and the claimed century. Coverage is good for captive animals and thinner for free-ranging ones, but it is enough to accept or reject the extreme figure.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the honey bee's use of carrion or fermented substrates with that of other insects. Another insect that invariably avoids rotten food would refute uniqueness; regular use of rotten material by the honey bee would refute the bee clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: recorded feeding links for Apis mellifera and other insects, including some associations with decaying substrates

obstacles: Uniqueness across all insects cannot be read out of an incomplete interaction graph.
'Invariably' and 'rotten' are stricter than the presence of a nectar or pollen link.
assessments.rationale: GloBI and the entomological literature can show that the honey bee is a nectar and pollen feeder and that many insects are not saprophages. They cannot survey every insect for invariable avoidance of decay. The test works for well-recorded groups and leaves the universal 'only' open.

assessments.operationalization: Use breeding and wintering locations of Grus grus from the Pontic-Caspian steppe and ask whether those birds winter in the marshes at the headwaters of the Nile. Tracks or ringing recoveries ending there would support the route; wintering consistently elsewhere would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: GPS and satellite tracks of common cranes, for breeding areas on the steppe and winter destinations

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal occurrence of Grus grus from eastern Europe and western Asia through Africa

obstacles: Modern flyways need not be identical to fourth-century routes.
The 'source of the Nile' has to be fixed as a geographic region before tracks can be scored.
assessments.rationale: Crane migration is now tracked, and occurrence data show where steppe populations winter. That is a direct test of a flight from Scythia to the marshes south of Egypt. Adequacy is short of the ancient period, but present-day routes are enough to confirm or reject the stated destination for the species Aristotle describes.

assessments.operationalization: Compare body mass or fat score of the same migratory populations at autumn departure from the breeding range and at spring return, with the common quail as the worked example. Higher autumn condition would support the claim; the reverse pattern in a well-sampled species would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: EURING databank
candidate_datasets.role: ringing encounters and, where recorded, body mass of migrants including quail at seasonal passages

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: tracking studies that sometimes include body-condition measurements at departure and arrival

obstacles: Autumn and spring samples differ in age, sex and stopover, so mass is confounded with more than travel direction.
'All creatures' is far wider than the passerines and quail that ringing stations actually weigh.
assessments.rationale: Fat at the two ends of migration is measurable, and ringing and tracking archives hold masses for some species, especially the quail's general class of migrants. Coverage is seasonal and taxonomic rather than universal, and condition is confounded with breeding state. The quail clause can be examined; the claim about all migrants cannot.

assessments.operationalization: For hooked-talon birds, measure relative neck length and tongue flatness and code vocal mimicry as present or absent. A hooked-talon species that is long-necked or that does not mimic would weaken the joint rule; the rule would hold if those three traits co-occur.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak, tarsus, wing and tail measurements as a partial morphological frame; neck and tongue are not themselves columns

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of vocal mimicry and qualitative neck and tongue descriptions for raptors, owls and parrots

obstacles: No open table jointly records neck length, tongue shape and mimicry.
Aristotle's hooked-talon set mixes raptors with mimics such as parrots, which do not share talon morphology.
assessments.rationale: Each trait is measurable, but they live in different sources and mimicry is not a standard morphological variable. AVONET can support a restricted morphological comparison, and species accounts can score mimicry for many species. The three-part rule can be challenged for familiar families, not confirmed across every hooked-talon bird.

assessments.operationalization: Once the trichia is assigned to a modern clupeid or shad, test whether that fish moves from the Black Sea up the Danube and down a branch into the Adriatic. Occurrence on that path, plus a real river connection, would support the account; a drainage divide with no such fish movement would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: HydroSHEDS
candidate_datasets.role: river networks and drainage divides, to test whether the Danube has a branch that reaches the Adriatic

obstacles: The trichia is not a secure modern species, and different clupeids give different distributions.
A hydrographic divide can refute a surface bifurcation without identifying the fish.
assessments.rationale: The route is a concrete migration hypothesis, and river networks plus fish occurrences can test it. The name is the limiting step: several sardines and shads are plausible, and they do not share one Danube-to-Adriatic path. Hydrography can reject a navigable bifurcation even while the species stays uncertain.

assessments.operationalization: Score dormancy in response to heat and to cold separately, using land snails, the purple murex and the scallop as the stated cases. Activity through the hottest season, or through winter, in a named case would refute that case; retreat in both extremes would support the general claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE mammal trait database
candidate_datasets.role: hibernation and phenology flags for mammals, a subset of the animals said to hide from cold

obstacles: Mammal hibernation tables do not cover snails, murex or scallops.
Aestivation of shellfish is described qualitatively and is not a downloaded seasonal activity series.
assessments.rationale: Heat and cold dormancy are real natural-history variables, and mammal hibernation is compiled. The claim's worked examples are molluscs, for which seasonal retreat is scattered through life-history notes rather than a trait column. The mammal half and a few shellfish can be examined; 'animals' as a class cannot.

assessments.operationalization: For snakes, lizards, geckos and the Nile crocodile, measure months without feeding and without surface activity in the cold season. About four months of aphagia in winter would support the claim; winter activity or feeding, especially in the crocodile, would refute it for that animal.

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame and distribution for the named reptile groups

obstacles: Occurrence month is a proxy for activity, not a record of fasting.
Four months of hiding is latitude-dependent, so a single duration cannot fit both Greek snakes and the Nile crocodile.
assessments.rationale: Winter retreat and fasting are measurable, and seasonal occurrences can show that some reptiles remain active when Aristotle has them hidden. Fasting duration is not a column in these databases, so the 'eat nothing' clause depends on scattered herpetological studies. The crocodile in a mild winter is the clearest partial test.

assessments.operationalization: For the swallow, kite, stork, turtle-dove and the other named birds, compare winter locations with the breeding range. Wintering in sub-Saharan Africa or another distant region refutes hiding in local holes; recovery of marked birds in winter roosts on the breeding grounds would support concealment.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: migratory tracks of swallows, storks, kites and turtle-doves through the winter

candidate_datasets.name: EURING databank
candidate_datasets.role: ringing recoveries linking European breeding sites to winter locations

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal presence and absence of the named species on the breeding grounds

obstacles: A few individuals could still roost locally without making concealment the species' winter strategy.
Aristotle's list mixes long-distance migrants with birds whose winter behavior differs.
assessments.rationale: Tracking and ringing locate these birds in winter, which is exactly the contrast between migration and local hiding. Swallow tracks to Africa refute the claim that swallows pass the winter featherless in holes. The same archives cover the kite, stork and turtle-dove well enough to judge the list species by species.

assessments.operationalization: For female brown bears, record birth date, den-emergence date relative to the winter solstice, and whether they feed in the den. Birth in mid-winter and emergence about three months after the solstice, with no feeding, would support the claim; summer birth or regular den feeding would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and life-history notes for Ursus arctos

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE mammal trait database
candidate_datasets.role: hibernation and reproductive traits for bears

obstacles: Trait tables give gestation and a hibernation flag, not birth day, emergence day or den fasting.
Den studies are concentrated in a few monitored populations.
assessments.rationale: The three clauses are standard bear natural history and are measured in published den studies, but they are not columns in AnAge or COMBINE. A team can compile the timing for well-studied populations in weeks and leave other bear species and the strict 'eats nothing' claim less tightly covered. That is a partial test of a claim that is otherwise unambiguous.

assessments.operationalization: Count ecdyses across the life of crabs, spiny lobsters and clawed lobsters. A size series with more than one soft-shell moult confirms repeated shedding; a single terminal moult for those groups would refute it.
obstacles: Moult number is often inferred from growth stages rather than stored as a single count.
The claim is about the groups Aristotle names, not every crustacean species.
assessments.rationale: Repeated moulting is a direct life-history variable for the crabs and lobsters in view, and fisheries biology has published stage series for them. SeaLifeBase organizes those life histories. A small team can confirm multiple moults for the named groups without new fieldwork, which is enough to resolve the claim as stated.

assessments.operationalization: Compare documented multi-host or population-level disease outbreaks in fishes with the epidemic diseases of humans, horses and cattle. A fish epidemic with spreading mortality refutes the claim that no pestilential disease attacks fishes; only isolated individual illnesses would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Organisation for Animal Health
candidate_datasets.role: listed aquatic and terrestrial animal diseases and outbreak reporting, including epidemic fish pathogens

obstacles: Modern aquaculture surveillance is denser than ancient observations of wild sea fish.
Aristotle allows individual illness, so only spreading, population-level disease counts against him.
assessments.rationale: Epidemic fish disease is now a reported category, parallel to the livestock diseases he names. WOAH records include viral and bacterial outbreaks that kill many fish, which is the contrast the claim denies. Surveillance is biased toward farmed and managed stocks, but those outbreaks are enough to refute a universal absence.

assessments.operationalization: Expose Bolinus brandaris or Hexaplex trunculus to fresh water and record survival at one day, using occurrence in fully marine versus estuarine salinities as a weaker proxy. Death within a day would support the claim; survival well beyond a day at low salinity would refute the stated time.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences of purple-dye murex species relative to the coast, as a proxy for avoidance of fresh water

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic identity and marine habitat of Bolinus brandaris and Hexaplex trunculus

obstacles: Distribution shows that these snails are marine, not that they die within a day of tasting fresh water.
The one-day lethality comes from scattered tolerance experiments, not a compiled survival table.
assessments.rationale: The one-day claim is a precise toxicity statement. Occurrence data can show that the purple murex does not live in rivers, which is only a proxy. Timed survival after fresh-water exposure is published piecemeal, so the numerical claim stays only partly testable.

assessments.operationalization: Identify 'measles' with muscle cysticerci visible in the flesh and under the tongue, then ask whether any non-pig host, and any suckling pig, carries the same lesions. Cysticerci in cattle, sheep or suckling pigs would refute the corresponding exclusivity; restriction to weaned pigs would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Organisation for Animal Health
candidate_datasets.role: listed cysticercosis of pigs and cattle, the modern diseases corresponding to flesh 'measles'

obstacles: 'Measles' is Aristotle's lesion name; cysticercosis is the historical identification, not a label he used.
Other skin pustules could be meant, and they would be scored differently.
assessments.rationale: If the pimples in the flesh are cysticerci, livestock-disease reports show the condition in more than the pig and can address age. That identification is standard but not certain, so the test resolves the parasitological reading rather than every possible skin disease. Suckling versus weaned status is less completely tabulated than host species.

assessments.operationalization: Use confirmed rabies cases after bites by rabid dogs, and compare fatality in humans with fatality in other mammals. Any human death from rabies refutes the exception for man; survival of a bitten non-human species that Aristotle would have counted would refute universal fatality outside man.

candidate_datasets.name: World Health Organization rabies topic
candidate_datasets.role: human rabies deaths and the transmission path from rabid dogs

candidate_datasets.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rabies pages
candidate_datasets.role: case surveillance for human and animal rabies after bites

candidate_datasets.name: World Organisation for Animal Health
candidate_datasets.role: animal rabies occurrence across mammals

obstacles: Modern post-exposure treatment prevents some human deaths, so untreated outcome is the relevant comparison.
Reservoir species are not invariably killed by infection, which complicates 'any animal whatever'.
assessments.rationale: Rabies after a dog bite is a diagnosed, reported outcome in people and in other mammals. Human deaths directly contradict the claim that man is the exception who does not take the fatal disease. Surveillance is extensive enough, and the analysis is a straightforward comparison of reported cases.

assessments.operationalization: Rank the donkey against the horse and mule by lower critical temperature or cold-related mortality, and test historical absence on the Black Sea shore and in Scythia. Greater cold mortality in donkeys plus genuine ancient absence would support the claim; feral donkeys thriving in comparable climates, or ancient donkey remains in those regions, would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: range accounts for wild asses and horses

obstacles: Modern absence can be husbandry rather than physiology, and ancient absence needs archaeological evidence.
A physiological ranking against the horse and mule is not a field in occurrence databases.
assessments.rationale: Occurrence data can map where donkeys live now, including cold regions, but they do not measure cold tolerance or fourth-century distribution. The causal link from intolerance to absence on the Euxine is confounded by transport and farming. The claim is only partly approachable with public biogeographic data.

assessments.operationalization: Score mortality of insects after external oil application, with a faster endpoint when the head is oiled in sun. Universal death would support the claim; survival of any oiled insect would refute 'without exception'.

candidate_datasets.name: ECOTOX Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: curated chemical toxicity tests, including oils and petroleum products, for a subset of aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates

obstacles: Toxicity tests cover pest and indicator species, not insects without exception.
Household oil smeared on the cuticle is not the same exposure as the mixtures in a toxicity archive.
assessments.rationale: The mortality claim is experimentally sharp, and oil toxicity has been measured for many insects in pest control and ecotoxicology. ECOTOX and the trial literature still omit most of the insect fauna, and protocols differ from Aristotle's smear-and-sun method. A counterexample would refute the universal, but the existing tests only sample pests.

assessments.operationalization: Map Holocene and ancient presence of lion and leopard in Libya, Asia Minor, Greece between the Achelous and the Nessus, and the rest of Europe. Lions in that Greek district and leopards absent from Europe would support the claim; European leopard records, or no Greek lions, in the relevant period would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil and archaeological-age occurrences of Panthera leo and Panthera pardus around the Mediterranean

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: historical and present range summaries for lion and leopard

obstacles: 'More numerous' is a density claim, while fossils record presence.
Europe's boundary in the Caucasus and the date of extinction both change the scoring.
assessments.rationale: Presence of lions in the southern Balkans and of leopards in Anatolia is a historical-biogeographic question with fossil, archaeological and range data. Those sources are uneven in time and do not measure abundance. They can test presence and absence for the named regions and cannot settle 'more numerous'.

assessments.operationalization: Among mammal species pairs, predict viable hybridization from similarity of body mass and gestation length, holding phylogenetic distance aside as a rival. Pairs matched in size and gestation that never hybridize, or mismatched pairs that do, would weaken the rule; a positive association beyond relatedness would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for mammal species used in the pairing rule

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE mammal trait database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and reproductive traits for a taxonomically matched mammal list

obstacles: Hybrid records are scattered, and relatedness confounds size and gestation.
The Libyan watering-place story is not itself in these tables.
assessments.rationale: Size and gestation are compiled for thousands of mammals, so the predictors exist. Documented hybrids are not in one open matrix of comparable quality, and close relatives tend to share both traits and the ability to interbreed. The association can be explored and will stay confounded.

assessments.operationalization: Test wolf-dog and fox-dog ancestry with genome-wide markers and chromosome compatibility. Wolf ancestry in dogs, or fertile wolf-dog offspring, supports the first cross; no fox ancestry in Laconian-type dogs and no viable Vulpes-Canis hybrid would refute the second.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: public canid genomes and sequences for dog, wolf and fox ancestry tests

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: assembled dog, wolf and fox genomes used to compare ancestry and karyotype compatibility

obstacles: The ancient Laconian hound is not a living breed with a type specimen, so the fox cross is tested on dogs generally and on historical sighthounds.
Wolf-dog gene flow does not by itself prove the Cyrene anecdote.
assessments.rationale: Wolf-dog hybridization and the absence of fox-dog hybrids are genetic questions with public genomes. Admixture methods can confirm wolf ancestry in dogs and reject fox ancestry for the supposed Laconian cross. The particular Cyrene pairing is a local story; the biological possibility of the two crosses is what the data resolve.

assessments.operationalization: Regress known age, from otoliths or annuli, on scale size and scale hardness in scaly fishes. A tight relationship would support reading age from those two traits; wide overlap of size and hardness across ages would refute 'may be told'.

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: fisheries survey ages and lengths that show how well body and scale size predict age

obstacles: Age is routinely read from scale circuli, not from hardness, which is rarely measured.
Size-at-age overlap means size alone is a noisy proxy even when growth curves exist.
assessments.rationale: Fisheries archives pair age with length for many scaly species, and scale size tracks length. Hardness is not a stored variable, so half of Aristotle's criterion is missing. The analysis can show that size is informative but not sufficient to 'tell' age, which tests the claim only in part.

assessments.operationalization: Use sex differences in aggression or boldness as a proxy for 'spirit', and test whether females score lower in every gonochoric species except bears and leopards. A higher female score in another species would refute the universal; the reverse pattern in bears and leopards would be required to support the exceptions.
obstacles: 'Spirited' and 'courageous' have several behavioral translations, and they are not a trait-database field.
Published sex differences cover a small, biased set of vertebrates and are confounded by size and season.
assessments.rationale: A sex difference in aggressiveness can be defined, but it only partly matches Aristotle's spirit, and no public dataset scores it across animals. Existing ethological papers allow a check in a few mammals and birds, including the bear and leopard as special cases. The universal, and the claim that those two are the only exceptions, is not resolvable with what is compiled.

assessments.operationalization: Score agonistic interactions between species that share a site or a prey, and among conspecifics when food is experimentally or seasonally short. More fighting in shared-food pairs than in non-overlapping pairs would support the claim; peaceful coexistence on the same food, or no increase in fighting when food is short, would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: recorded interspecific interactions, including some antagonistic and trophic links

obstacles: 'Enmity' can be read as a definition of competition, which makes the test circular.
Interaction archives record that a link exists, not how often animals fight when food runs short.
assessments.rationale: GloBI compiles biotic links, so shared prey and some antagonistic relationships can be counted. The archive does not measure fighting rates under food shortage, and many co-occurring species are not enemies in any observable sense. The claim can be probed as a statistical tendency and cannot be cleanly separated from the definition of competition.

assessments.operationalization: Treat supplemental feeding and long-term provisioning as a proxy for unlimited food, and measure approach distance to humans and rates of aggression among animals. Loss of fear and of fighting under sustained surplus would support the prediction; persistent wariness or aggression despite abundant food would refute it.
obstacles: No real setting supplies unlimited food, so experiments are proxies.
Tameness is confounded with individual habituation and with which species people choose to feed.
assessments.rationale: The sentence is a counterfactual about wild animals in general. Provisioning studies and a few classic fed populations, including Nile wildlife, record approach distance and aggression, but they are scattered and never match 'no lack of food'. They can reject the prediction for particular species and cannot establish it for animals at large.

assessments.operationalization: For known-age male Cervus elaphus, compare antler points with year of life through age six, and test whether point number still predicts age afterward. The stated sequence (none, spike, fork, three points, then no further age information) is confirmed by a match and refuted by systematic departures.
obstacles: Known-age antler series sit in wildlife-agency reports and papers, not in one open global table.
Nutrition and population change point number independently of age.
assessments.rationale: Point number by known age is exactly the wildlife measurement needed, and red deer have been aged from teeth while their antlers were counted. Those series are public but dispersed, and they vary by habitat, so they test the schedule for studied populations rather than for every stag. The 'after six years, antlers no longer indicate age' clause is part of the same comparison.

assessments.operationalization: At red-deer births, record whether the hind ingests the placenta before it reaches the ground. Consistent immediate swallowing would support the claim; placentas left on the ground or not eaten would refute the universal 'at once'.
obstacles: Placentophagia is described in ungulate natural history but is not a downloaded behavioral dataset.
Births are rarely observed closely enough to score 'before it falls'.
assessments.rationale: The behavior is specific and has been reported for deer and other ungulates, so published observations can support or challenge it for watched births. There is no systematic open dataset of hind parturitions. The claim is testable for a handful of observed births and not for hinds in general.

assessments.operationalization: For dogs, compare grass eating and subsequent vomiting in animals scored as ill versus healthy. Grass eating restricted to illness and followed by vomiting would support self-treatment; routine eating by healthy dogs without vomiting would refute that reading.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: plant fraction of canid diets, showing that dogs and wild canids eat plant matter, without health context

obstacles: Self-medication is an intention; the data can show only health state, grass eating and vomiting.
The dittany story about Cretan goats is a separate anecdote and is not in these tables.
assessments.rationale: Dog grass-eating has been quantified in behavioral studies, which can separate healthy from ill animals and record vomiting. EltonTraits only shows that canids eat plants. The observable pattern is partly testable; calling it treatment of an ailment adds a purpose that the counts do not decide.

assessments.operationalization: Watch gaping Nile crocodiles and score whether a small bird enters the mouth, takes material from the teeth, and leaves unharmed. Repeated entries of that kind would support the claim; systematic observation without them would refute it as a normal behavior.
obstacles: The trochilus has been guessed to be the Egyptian plover, but the identification is not secure.
Co-occurrence of crocodiles and shorebirds does not record tooth-cleaning.
assessments.rationale: The behavior is observable in principle and would be decisive if filmed at scale. What exists is anecdote and a long argument that the behavior has not been reliably seen. No public dataset contains mouth-entry events, so the claim cannot be resolved without new observation.

assessments.operationalization: Follow marked pairs of domestic pigeons, ring-doves and turtle-doves across years and record whether the pair bond ends only at death, allowing the occasional extra-pair mating Aristotle notes. Divorce of both living partners would refute strict pairing for life; bonds broken only by death would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: compiled mating-system accounts for Columba and Streptopelia, including pair-bond duration

candidate_datasets.name: EURING databank
candidate_datasets.role: mark-recapture of pigeons and doves, a frame for pair studies rather than a pair-bond table

obstacles: Ringing archives do not store mate identity.
Domestic pigeons, ring-doves and turtle-doves do not share one mating system.
assessments.rationale: Pair fidelity is routinely measured in pigeon and dove studies, and species accounts summarize it. The raw mate histories are study-specific, so a team can test familiar species and not every bird Aristotle grouped as a pigeon. Occasional extra-pair mating is already built into the claim and should not be scored as a refutation by itself.

assessments.operationalization: Classify nests of quails, partridges and similar heavy ground birds as constructed nests versus ground scrapes. A scrape on level ground would support Aristotle's description; an elevated or woven nest in those species would refute 'build no nests'.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: nest-site and nest-structure descriptions for quails, partridges and other galliforms

obstacles: A scrape can be counted as a nest, so the contrast depends on defining 'build'.
The purpose clause, that a nest would be useless to a poor flier, is not tested by nest structure alone.
assessments.rationale: Nest form for quails and partridges is described in standard species accounts and is a ground scrape rather than a constructed nest. That resolves the structural claim for those birds. The further claim that nest building would be useless because they fly poorly is a functional gloss that nest descriptions do not test, and similar galliforms are only partly compiled.

assessments.operationalization: When a person approaches a partridge or quail brood, score injury-feigning, the direction of the display away from the chicks, and the return call. A stereotyped distraction display would support the claim; flushing without feigning, in the same circumstances, would refute it as a general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: behavioral accounts of injury-feigning and brood defense in partridges and quails

obstacles: The display is well described qualitatively and rarely stored as an ethogram dataset.
Quails and partridges may not share the behavior to the same degree.
assessments.rationale: Distraction displays are a standard, scored behavior, and handbooks record them for partridges. The evidence is narrative and video rather than a reusable table of trials, so the claim can be checked for the best-known species and not quantified across all broods. It is a partial but genuine test.

assessments.operationalization: Code palmation of the feet from taxonomy and handbooks, then test whether every web-footed species' habitat or occurrences fall by sea, river or pool. A web-footed species whose range is consistently away from water would refute the universal; universal association with water would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: habitat and geographic attributes for all birds, joined to a coding of webbed feet

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging stratum, including water-surface and pelagic categories

obstacles: Foot webbing is not a column in AVONET and has to be coded by family.
'Near water' is broad, so only strongly terrestrial web-footed species would count as exceptions.
assessments.rationale: Habitat and occurrence are compiled for all birds, and the web-footed orders are a known set. Joining those two is a standard analysis that can confirm or refute a universal association with water. The purpose clause about structure is not separately tested, but the distributional claim is.

assessments.operationalization: Compare vocal rates of swans in ordinary life with rates in animals known to be dying, and check whether dying birds fly out to sea to sing. Song throughout life, with no concentration at death, would refute 'chiefly at the approach of death'.

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: recordings of living whooper, trumpeter and mute swans, showing whether song is confined to dying birds

obstacles: Archives are not linked to the singer's imminent death, so they cannot directly measure 'chiefly'.
Mute swans and northern swans differ so much in voice that the species Aristotle meant matters.
assessments.rationale: Routine recordings of healthy swans can show that some species sing in ordinary life, which cuts against song being chiefly a death behavior. They do not sample dying birds, and the flight out to sea is unmeasured. The claim is only weakly and partially testable.

assessments.operationalization: For Cuculus canorus, record whether it builds a nest, how many eggs it lays in each host nest, and whether the host incubates and rears the young. One egg per host nest, no nest of its own, and host rearing would support the claim; a cuckoo nest or regular multi-egg clutches in one nest would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian brood parasite-host relationships
candidate_datasets.role: compiled parasite-host list, including the common cuckoo and the hosts that rear its young

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: breeding accounts of clutch size per host nest and absence of a cuckoo nest

obstacles: 'Lays only one egg' can be misread as one egg per season; the test uses one egg in a given host nest, which is what the passage describes.
Host lists include occasional hosts, so frequency matters as well as possibility.
assessments.rationale: Brood parasitism of the common cuckoo is compiled as host relationships and breeding details, including the lack of a nest and the host's role in rearing. Those data can confirm or qualify the one-egg-per-nest description directly. The analysis is a tabulation of existing host records, not new fieldwork.

assessments.operationalization: Compare escape distance and nest defense of the common cuckoo with those of nesting birds of similar size. Exceptional timidity would match the stated mechanism; ordinary boldness would weaken it. The comparison still would not show that cowardice is why the bird parasitizes nests.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: qualitative accounts of cuckoo parental care and response to disturbance, set beside host behavior

obstacles: Awareness of one's own cowardice is not an observation distinct from the absence of parental care.
Low nest defense is a consequence of parasitism as much as a cause, so the test is confounded.
assessments.rationale: The observable residue of the cowardice explanation is that cuckoos defend young less than nesting birds. That difference is described, but it does not distinguish cowardice from other reasons for brood parasitism, including the loss of parental care itself. The mental-state wording has no separate measurement.

assessments.operationalization: Measure eagle home-range size, natal dispersal of fledged young, and whether other birds settle inside the territory. Large exclusive ranges and expulsion of young would support the maintenance claim; small overlapping ranges, or tolerance of neighboring birds, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: GPS ranges of breeding eagles and dispersal of their young

obstacles: Tracks show space use, not active expulsion of other species.
Eagle species differ, and Aristotle's eagle is not a single modern species.
assessments.rationale: Home range and juvenile departure are measured for several eagles and can test the need for a large area. Interspecific exclusion of 'other birds' is a stronger claim than conspecific territoriality and is not what the tracks record. The spatial half is testable; the expulsion mechanism is only partly so.

assessments.operationalization: At sea-eagle nests before fledging, record whether adults orient chicks toward the sun, strike those that look away, and kill chicks whose eyes water. Repeated sequences of that kind would support the claim; nests without them would refute it as a normal practice.
obstacles: The sea-eagle may be the white-tailed eagle or another large eagle, but the behavior is undescribed for either.
Nest videos that exist were not collected to score this ordeal, and they do not amount to a dataset.
assessments.rationale: The ordeal is a specific behavioral sequence and could be confirmed or refuted by nest observation. It is not present in tracking archives, trait tables or a compiled ethogram. Resolving it requires new or purposefully reviewed nest records that do not yet exist as data.

assessments.operationalization: Describe the illicium and esca of Lophius and test whether prey approach the lure and are taken while the fish is buried. A lure that is anatomically present and attracts fish would support the claim; absence of the filaments, or no attraction, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen imagery of anglerfish heads for the filaments in front of the eyes

obstacles: Attraction of prey is behavioral, whereas most open records are morphological.
Several Lophius species fit 'fishing-frog', and lure use should be checked for the Mediterranean species.
assessments.rationale: The filaments and their use as bait are standard anglerfish biology, documented in FishBase and in anatomical specimens, with prey approach described in the fisheries literature. A team can confirm both the structure and the feeding sequence from existing sources. Species identity within Lophius is a minor ambiguity, not a barrier.

assessments.operationalization: Measure electric-organ discharge of Torpedo during prey capture and during contact with people, and record whether prey are immobilized. Discharge that stuns prey and is felt by humans would support the claim; prey capture without a shock, or no effect on people, would refute the corresponding part.
obstacles: Quantitative discharge traces live in physiology papers more than in a single fisheries table.
Several Mediterranean torpedo rays fit the name.
assessments.rationale: The shock, its organ, and prey immobilization are measured properties of electric rays, and FishBase points to the species and the literature that report them. Human numbness is likewise recorded. The data are more scattered than a trait column, but they are public and sufficient for a direct confirmation or refutation.

assessments.operationalization: For Silurus aristotelis, record which sex remains with the eggs, whether small fish are driven off, and the days until the young leave. Male care lasting about forty to fifty days would support the claim; female-only care, no guarding, or a very different duration would refute it.
obstacles: Guarding duration is in species studies, not a FishBase numeric field.
The sheat-fish has sometimes been confused with Silurus glanis, which does not show the same care.
assessments.rationale: Male guarding and its duration are concrete and have been re-observed for Silurus aristotelis. FishBase records parental care only in summary, so the forty-to-fifty-day figure has to be taken from the primary studies. The behavior can be checked for this species and is not a general fish dataset.

assessments.operationalization: Classify Mediterranean fishes by diet as carnivorous or not, check the grey mullet, saupe, red mullet and chalcis as the named exceptions, and compare a movement metric between carnivores and the others. Further herbivores or detritivores would refute 'all except a few'; greater ranging by carnivores would support the second clause.
obstacles: 'Wander most' is not a standard FishBase column and is only loosely matched by migration or depth range.
The chalcis is not a single secure species.
assessments.rationale: FishBase diets cover the fauna Aristotle is discussing and can accept or reject the short list of non-carnivores. That universal is the main clause and is directly testable. The claim that carnivores wander most is less cleanly measured, which lowers discriminating power without blocking a decision on the diet statement.

assessments.operationalization: Compare ink release of Sepia, octopus and squid in threat trials with and without a pursuit or a need for cover. Ink used as a screen during escape in cuttlefish and also in squid or octopus would refute 'the sepia alone'; ink only as a startle in the latter two would support the contrast.
obstacles: Concealment and fear are not separate observable causes when the animal is disturbed in both cases.
Inking experiments are study-specific and not a comparative dataset.
assessments.rationale: All three groups release ink when disturbed, and that fact is recorded. Experiments that try to separate a smoke screen from a startle response exist as papers, not as a table, and the two functions are hard to tell apart. The uniqueness claim is only weakly testable.

assessments.operationalization: Place Octopus vulgaris on backgrounds of known color and measure skin match while foraging and while alarmed. A spectral or pattern match in both contexts would support the claim; fixed color, or matching only in one context, would refute the corresponding part.
obstacles: Quantitative match scores are in experimental papers and image supplements, not in a life-history database.
Laboratory backgrounds are simpler than the stones Aristotle names.
assessments.rationale: Color matching at rest and under threat is a measured cephalopod behavior, with public experimental records for Octopus vulgaris. SeaLifeBase only summarizes it. A team can adjudicate the claim from those studies for this species, which is a partial scope relative to octopuses in general and relative to a single downloaded trait.

assessments.operationalization: Compare age at death of Octopus vulgaris, especially females after spawning, with a one-year limit. Deaths before a year would support the rule; routine survival well past a year would refute 'does not live the year out'.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: longevity records for octopus and other cephalopods

obstacles: Aquaculture and captive ages can exceed wild ages.
The claim says 'as a rule', so a few older individuals do not refute it, whereas a typical life past a year would.
assessments.rationale: Octopus lifespan and post-spawning death are reported in AnAge and SeaLifeBase and in the growth studies they draw on. Those sources can show whether a year is the usual limit for Octopus vulgaris. Female decline after spawning is part of the same life-history record.

assessments.operationalization: Film Argonauta argo at the surface in a breeze and score whether the web between the arms is held as a sail and other arms are used as oars or rudders. That posture while making way would support the claim; a web used only as a shell cover, with no sailing, would refute it.
obstacles: The sailing account rests on few observations and is not a behavioral dataset.
The thin web is also the shell-secreting arms, so structure and the sailing function must be scored separately.
assessments.rationale: Surface posture of the argonaut can be filmed and has been re-described in a small modern literature. SeaLifeBase identifies the animal and its shell but does not contain sailing trials. Existing observations can challenge the sail-and-oar story and are too sparse to count as a resolved dataset.

assessments.operationalization: Locate the origin of the silk thread in spiderlings and adults: external sloughing from the body surface, or secretion from abdominal silk glands through spinnerets. Glandular secretion would refute 'not from their interior as an excretion'; silk shed like bark with no glands would support Aristotle against Democritus.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: microCT of spider abdomens showing spinnerets, for a subset of species

obstacles: Histology of the silk glands, not external shape alone, decides secretion versus a surface slough.
Scans and sections cover a minority of spider families.
assessments.rationale: The dispute with Democritus is anatomical: where the thread comes from.
