They do not supply a neutral definition of true horn that would let the restriction to viviparous animals be tested rather than stipulated. Fighting use is documented for some egg-laying animals and is not a complete dataset.

assessments.operationalization: For every living family that bears a head weapon called a horn or antler, score whether the weapon is solid bone and whether it is shed. Solid or deciduous weapons outside deer refute the corresponding only; hollow permanent antlers in deer would refute the deer side.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: antler bone and shedding in deer, horn sheaths in bovids, pronghorn shedding, and rhino and giraffe weapons

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: enumerates the horn-bearing families so the only-claims have a closed list

obstacles: Pronghorn sheaths and giraffe ossicones force a prior decision about what counts as a horn.
Antlers are bone and bovid horns are a keratin sheath over a core, which is the solidity contrast to be coded.
assessments.rationale: The living families with horns or antlers are few, and open accounts already say whether the structure is solid bone and whether it is cast. Pronghorns, bovids, rhinoceroses and giraffes are the decisive contrasts and are described at family level. A team can tabulate that closed set from existing references and decide both uniqueness claims.

assessments.operationalization: For every horned mammal, score upper incisors or canines in the front of the jaw. Any horned species with those teeth refutes the exclusion. The material-transfer explanation, teeth sacrificed to make horns, is not tested by the correlation.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental formulas of bovids, deer, pronghorn, rhinoceroses and giraffes

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: closed list of living horned species so the universal can be bounded

obstacles: Rhinoceros horns and giraffe ossicones may or may not be included; the decision changes which dentitions are in scope.
Loss of tooth material into horn is a developmental claim the presence-absence table does not test.
assessments.rationale: Dental formulas for the horn-bearing mammal families are standard content of open species accounts, and the species list is finite. A single horned species with upper front teeth decides the universal negative. The causal story that horn material is tooth material diverted is a further claim and is not resolved by those formulas.

assessments.operationalization: Score lungs and a cervical region between head and pectoral girdle across vertebrates, with fishes as the stated case. A lungless animal with a neck, or a lunged animal with none, refutes the biconditional if neck is defined in advance.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gills, lungs and body form of fishes, including lungfish

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: skeletal characters of the fish pectoral region and occiput

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: definitions of lung and neck used to keep the two variables distinct

obstacles: A fish neck is anatomically disputed, so the absence can be made true by definition.
Lungfish have lungs and a poorly marked neck, which is the sensitive case.
assessments.rationale: Lung presence in fishes, including lungfish, is recorded in fish databases. Whether fishes lack a neck depends on a landmark definition that those databases do not apply uniformly. The association can be examined for tetrapods and fishes once that definition is fixed, and it is not a clean download.

assessments.operationalization: Score an epiglottis, a flap covering the laryngeal opening, across hairy mammals, birds and scaly reptiles. An epiglottis in a bird or reptile, or its absence in a hairy lunged mammal, refutes the restriction.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: laryngeal anatomy in mammal, bird and reptile accounts where it is described

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: the anatomical class epiglottis, so a laryngeal fold is not counted differently in each clade

obstacles: Epiglottis presence is not a filled trait column and must be compiled from anatomical descriptions.
Some reptile and bird laryngeal structures are easy to force into or out of the category.
assessments.rationale: The structure is well defined and is described for the major land-vertebrate classes in comparative anatomy. Those descriptions are not a single open matrix, so the universal only is a compilation across orders. Discriminating power is high once the flap is coded consistently, and the data-collection step is the limit.

assessments.operationalization: Score heart, lung, liver, spleen and kidney, or agreed homologues, in vertebrates and in cephalopods, crustaceans, molluscs and insects. A heart or digestive gland in a bloodless animal refutes the claim if homologues count; if only vertebrate organs count, the claim is nearly true by the definition of viscera.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: internal anatomy of cephalopods, crustaceans and other bloodless marine animals

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: presence of hearts and digestive glands in invertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: the vertebrate viscera used as the blooded side of the contrast

obstacles: Whether a cephalopod systemic heart or an insect dorsal vessel counts as a heart decides the result.
Bloodless does not line up perfectly with invertebrates.
assessments.rationale: Internal organs of both vertebrates and the main invertebrate groups are described in open databases. The claim's force depends on refusing those invertebrate organs the name viscera, which is a homology decision rather than a missing observation. Under a strict reading the test is weak; under a homologue reading it is straightforward and unfavorable to a total absence.

assessments.operationalization: In staged embryos of blooded animals, record the first visible organ and whether blood is present in the heart at that stage. Another organ appearing before the heart, or a heart that is bloodless when first formed, refutes the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish developmental stages for the timing of heart formation and circulation

obstacles: Open staging databases cover zebrafish and a few other models, not all blooded animals.
First formed depends on the imaging method and on when a heart rudiment counts as a heart.
assessments.rationale: Vertebrate model embryos, especially zebrafish, have public stage tables that order the heart relative to other organs and show when blood cells circulate. That tests the claim in those species. It does not extend, without new comparative embryology, to every sanguineous animal Aristotle includes.

assessments.operationalization: Test whether pain, pleasure and sensation are abolished by inactivation of the heart but not of the head, using lesion, stimulation and pathway data. The opposite pattern refutes the heart as the primary seat.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: sensory and affective pathways mapped in the brain

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: human brain recordings during sensory and affective tasks

obstacles: The archives are human and model-mammal resources, not a survey of all blooded animals.
Pleasure and pain are inferred from behavior and neural markers, not observed as motions ending in the heart.
assessments.rationale: Existing brain maps and task recordings localize sensation in the head and can be set against the heart-centered alternative directly. They do not include a comparable experimental inactivation of the heart as a sensory center across taxa, because that experiment is not how the data were collected. The primary-seat claim is decidable for the studied vertebrates and not for every sanguineous animal.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the heart's midline offset in humans and in other blooded animals from dissections or imaging. A leftward apex in a non-human, or a midline human heart, refutes the corresponding uniqueness or human clause. The cold-side explanation is not part of the position test.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: human thoracic anatomy for the leftward position in one male and one female

obstacles: Veterinary imaging of heart position is published as papers, not as one comparative file.
The Visible Human sample cannot speak for other species or for humans in general.
assessments.rationale: Heart position is a routine anatomical fact, and human imaging shows the leftward tilt, but open archives do not line up the same measurement across mammals, birds and other blooded animals. A unique-to-humans claim needs that comparative series. It can be begun from textbooks and papers and cannot be finished from a single public dataset.

assessments.operationalization: Score an os cordis, a bone or cartilage in the heart skeleton, as present or absent in the horse, cattle and other mammals. Presence outside the horse and ox refutes the restriction; absence in both refutes the positive claim.
obstacles: Cardiac bones are reported in veterinary pathology papers for cattle, sheep, deer and otters, not in a trait database.
A certain kind of ox is vague, and horse records are inconsistent.
assessments.rationale: The structure is unambiguous when a heart is dissected, and published reports already name several species. Those reports are not an open survey of mammalian hearts, so the only-clause cannot be closed without compilation, and even then unsurveyed species remain. The data exist as a scattered literature rather than a dataset that contains the variable.

assessments.operationalization: Count chambers only after stating whether Aristotle's cavity is an atrium, a ventricle or a recess, then regress that count on body size. Modern four-chamber hearts in both large and small mammals refute a three-versus-two size rule under the straightforward mapping, but a different mapping can be made to fit.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: chamber anatomy of a small vertebrate heart

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: heart chamber counts in mammal, bird, reptile and fish accounts

obstacles: Aristotle's three cavities do not match the four modern chambers, so the count is unstable.
Large and small are not tied to a size cutoff.
assessments.rationale: Chamber number is basic vertebrate anatomy and is available for every class. It does not decide the claim until cavity is translated, and more than one translation is live. Under the usual modern count the size rule fails; under a charitable recount it can be preserved. That ambiguity is the main limit on discriminating power.

assessments.operationalization: Residual heart mass, after body size, is compared with a pre-registered boldness or flight-initiation measure for the hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard, marten and a broader sample. Timid animals with small residual hearts, or bold animals with large ones, refute the direction.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: body mass for the named mammals; it does not contain heart mass or a timidity score

obstacles: Heart mass and boldness are published separately and for different species sets.
Large heart is confounded with body size unless residuals are used, and timidity is not a standard trait.
assessments.rationale: Both variables exist somewhere in the literature for some of the named species, and neither is in a joint open table. Body-size databases fix the confound only if heart weights are compiled first. The comparison is possible as a partial literature synthesis and is not a clean test with current files.

assessments.operationalization: Use fate maps to ask whether solid organs and the body wall differentiate from blood, as opposed to blood merely supplying them. A tissue lineage that does not pass through blood refutes the material claim for that tissue. Vessel layout alone does not decide it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish developmental anatomy and cell-lineage resources for whether organs arise from blood

obstacles: Lineage data are from model species, not all blooded animals.
Supply of nutrients by blood is a weaker reading that the fate maps were not designed to separate from Aristotle's stronger material claim.
assessments.rationale: Public developmental atlases of vertebrate models record germ-layer origins and can show that organs are not formed out of blood. That is a real test of the strong reading in those species. It is not a survey of every sanguineous animal, and a weak reading on which blood only nourishes the body would not be touched by lineage.

assessments.operationalization: Score gills and lungs across fishes, treating a lung in any fish as a refutation of never, and separately ask whether gill ventilation is required for cooling rather than only for gas exchange. The anatomical score and the cooling score can come apart.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gills, lungs and air-breathing in fishes, including lungfish

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: respiratory phenotypes that separate gills from lungs

obstacles: Cooling by water is a physiological role that fish databases do not measure.
Lungfish and other air-breathers break a universal about fishes only if they are inside Aristotle's fishes.
assessments.rationale: Gill and lung presence is tabulated well enough to test the anatomical universal directly, including the lungfish counterexamples. The claim that the water is a cooling agent, rather than the medium of gas exchange, is not a field in those databases. Anatomy is resolvable with current files; the thermal function is not.

assessments.operationalization: Compare lung volume, blood content and the change in volume when inflated between mammals and the egg-laying groups, birds and reptiles. A small blood-rich mammal lung, or a large blood-filled bird lung, refutes the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: soft-tissue or contrast scans of lungs where they exist; most specimens are skeletons

obstacles: Lung volume and blood content are in anatomical papers, not a comparative file.
Spongy and capable of great expansion need a shared inflation protocol that older descriptions do not use.
assessments.rationale: The contrast is anatomically specific and has been described for mammals, birds and reptiles. Open scan archives are dominated by bone and rarely quantify pulmonary blood or inflation. A partial comparison can be compiled from the literature; it is not a standard analysis of an existing table.

assessments.operationalization: At the level of vertebrate classes, score presence of heart, liver, lung, spleen and kidney. Absence of heart or liver in any blooded class refutes the positive claim; presence of kidney, lung or spleen in every class refutes the claim that heart and liver alone are invariable.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: class-level presence of heart, liver, lung, spleen and kidney

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: a fish reference for which of those viscera are present in a blooded animal that lacks lungs

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: confirms lung absence across most fishes while the other viscera remain in play

obstacles: Spleen tissue in jawless fishes is histologically debatable.
Class-level presence does not certify every species, but the invariable claim is already decided by class differences.
assessments.rationale: Which of these organs occur in fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals is standard anatomy in open species accounts and model-organism databases. Lungs are already coded as absent in most fishes, which is enough to test the only-these-two wording. A team can score the five organs by class from existing references without new dissection.

assessments.operationalization: Score a urinary bladder in birds, fishes, scaly reptiles and turtles. A bladder in a lizard, snake, bird or fish refutes the only-tortoises wording; absence in turtles refutes the exception.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: urinary bladder presence in birds, turtles, lizards, snakes and crocodilians

candidate_datasets.name: Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic coverage of the scaly reptiles and turtles in the scope

obstacles: Bladder presence is in prose accounts, not a character column, and is unstated for many species.
Some fishes have urinary bladders that are easy to overlook in general fish databases.
assessments.rationale: Urinary bladders of turtles and of many lizards are described in open herpetological accounts, which is enough to test the only-exception wording at group level. The character is not tabulated for every species, and fish bladders are inconsistently recorded. The group-level contrast can be compiled; a species-level universal cannot be downloaded.

assessments.operationalization: Score kidneys in birds, fishes, scaly reptiles and turtles. Kidneys in any bird, fish or non-chelonian reptile refute the absence claim; absence in turtles refutes the stated exception. Flattened avian kidneys still count as kidneys if they produce urine.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: kidney presence in birds, reptiles and fishes

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: the kidney of a teleost as a direct counterexample to absence in scaly or fish-like blooded animals

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: keeps kidney distinct from a vaguely kidney-like body

obstacles: Aristotle allows flattened kidney-like bodies in some birds, so a coder must decide whether those count as the organ he says is lacking.
assessments.rationale: Kidneys are class-level organs of fishes, birds and reptiles, and that fact is recorded in open anatomical accounts and in a model-fish database. The tortoises-only exception is therefore decidable without new dissection. The only real ambiguity is whether a lobulated avian kidney is the organ named in the claim, and that can be fixed from the same descriptions.

assessments.operationalization: In animals with paired kidneys, compare the craniocaudal position of the right and left organs. A species in which the left kidney sits higher refutes the universal. Humans are one species inside the scope, not the whole of it.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: right and left kidney position in one male and one female human

obstacles: Comparative positions are in veterinary anatomy papers, not a multi-species file.
Two human bodies cannot represent all animals that have kidneys.
assessments.rationale: Which kidney sits higher is a direct measurement, and it is known for humans and for a scatter of domestic mammals. Only the human pair is in a public image dataset, and even there the sample is two individuals. The universal over all kidney-bearing animals needs a compilation that does not yet exist as a dataset.

assessments.operationalization: Define laughter as a play vocalization elicited by tickling, then search for that response in humans and other mammals, especially apes and rodents. A tickle-evoked play call outside humans refutes uniqueness. A looser definition that requires propositional humor makes the claim nearly untestable.
obstacles: Laughter is not a field in trait databases, and ape and rat play vocalizations are in experimental papers.
Whether those calls are laughter is the operational dispute that decides the unique-to-humans claim.
assessments.rationale: Tickle-evoked play sounds in apes and rats are published observations, so a behavioral reading can be confronted without new experiments. There is no comparative dataset of the response, and a stricter reading on which only human laughter counts makes every non-human case irrelevant by definition. The assessment stays partial because the word laughter does not fix the criterion.

assessments.operationalization: For viviparous mammals with upper and lower incisors, count stomach chambers. More than one chamber in any such species refutes the single-stomach universal. The named genera are the minimum set; the universal requires the other incisor-bearing orders as well.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: stomach form and incisor presence for carnivores, perissodactyls, pigs, primates and rodents

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: diet and taxonomy of the mammals in scope; it does not itself count stomach chambers

obstacles: Stomach chamber number is prose in species accounts, although it is stable at the level of mammalian orders.
Incisors in both jaws excludes ruminants and must not be confused with camels, which lack upper incisors.
assessments.rationale: Monogastric versus multi-chamber stomachs, and the presence of upper incisors, are described for every mammalian order in open accounts. The pattern is uniform enough within orders that a team can score the incisor-bearing groups from those accounts. Chamber number is not a life-history column, but it does not need to be, because the ordinal anatomy is already published and consistent.

assessments.operationalization: Score horn presence, upper incisors and stomach-chamber number for bovids, deer, camels and chevrotains. Several stomachs in a hornless species, or a single stomach in a horned one, refutes the stated link. The chewing explanation is supported only if the extra chambers occur exactly where foregut fermentation compensates for dentition.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: rumen structure, horns and upper incisors in deer, bovids, camels and chevrotains

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: lists the living ruminant and camelid families so hornless multi-stomach species are not omitted

obstacles: Camels and musk deer are hornless and multi-chambered, so they test the because-horned clause rather than the anatomy of sheep and cattle.
Chamber counts vary among foregut fermenters and need a threshold for several.
assessments.rationale: Stomach complexity, horns and upper teeth are all described for the relevant families in open mammal accounts, and the family list is closed. Hornless ruminants and camelids are in that list, so they discriminate a horn-based explanation from a dentition or fermentation explanation. The named livestock can be scored directly, and the rivals that lack horns can be scored from the same sources.

assessments.operationalization: Define rumination as regurgitation and rechewing of foregut contents, then search feeding observations for Sparisoma cretense and for other fishes. Oral scraping or pharyngeal milling without regurgitation does not count. Another ruminating fish, or no regurgitation in the parrotfish, refutes the corresponding part.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet and feeding notes for the Mediterranean parrotfish and other fishes

obstacles: Aristotle says apparently ruminates, and pharyngeal chewing is easily mistaken for cud-chewing.
The ancient Scarus may not be only Sparisoma cretense, and quantitative feeding observations are few.
assessments.rationale: Fish diet databases record that parrotfishes scrape and mill food, which is a proxy, not regurgitation. True rumination is rarely observed in fishes and is not a coded behavior. The single-exception claim can be probed with existing feeding notes and cannot be settled by them, because the notes do not use Aristotle's criterion.

assessments.operationalization: Score milk-clotting gastric enzyme activity, or a chymosin ortholog as a proxy, across species with multi-chambered stomachs and in hares. The claim holds if both groups have it, and fails if a clear multi-chambered lineage or the hare lacks it.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: chymosin and related gastric aspartic proteases, as a molecular proxy for rennet across sequenced mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: orthologs of the chymosin gene in ruminants, camelids, cetaceans and lagomorphs

obstacles: Multi-chambered stomachs occur in several unrelated groups, so the taxon set has to be defined before the enzyme is scored.
Gene presence is a proxy for the secreted rennet Aristotle meant, and hare data are sparse.
Lepus covers several species whose stomach biochemistry is not equally known.
assessments.rationale: Chymosin orthologs are openly listed for many mammals, which is enough to test a molecular proxy in the main ruminant lineages and in lagomorphs. Enzyme activity in the stomach, especially of the hare and of non-ruminant multi-chambered species such as cetaceans, still has to be compiled from physiological papers. That compilation can decide the named cases and leaves the universal quantifier only partly covered.

assessments.operationalization: Code reproductive mode as oviparous or internally brooded then live-bearing for Viperidae and for sharks and rays. The generalization holds only if both groups develop eggs internally and then bear live young; oviparous species in either group refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of elasmobranchs, separating egg-laying from live-bearing after internal egg development

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: life-history traits for sharks and rays, including reproductive mode

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for Viperidae stating whether a species lays eggs or bears live young

obstacles: Viperidae is mixed: some genera lay eggs, and Aristotle's viper may have been the European Vipera only.
Skates and some sharks lay egg cases, so the selachian universal is decidable and sensitive to how the group is bounded.
assessments.rationale: FishBase and Sharkipedia record reproductive mode for elasmobranchs in a form a small team can tabulate directly. Viper reproductive mode is stated in species accounts rather than one column, but the genera are few enough to compile in weeks. Together those sources can confirm or refute both halves of the generalization as a claim about the modern groups named in the scope.

assessments.operationalization: Score gallbladder presence and its attachment, liver versus intestine, across a phylogenetic sample of fishes. Universal presence fails if any major fish lineage lacks a gallbladder; the attachment clause fails if the liver is the usual site.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: computable fish anatomical phenotypes from curated systematic matrices, where gallbladder characters were coded

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts for exemplar fishes that mention the gallbladder and its position

obstacles: Attachment site is rarely a coded character, so most records speak only to presence.
Published matrices cover selected clades rather than fishes as a whole.
Aristotle's fishes include cartilaginous fishes, lampreys and bony fishes, which are not one anatomical sample.
assessments.rationale: Presence or absence of a gallbladder is a discrete anatomical character, and some fish matrices already code organ phenotypes. Coverage is a subset of clades, and the claim that the bladder is usually on the intestine rather than the liver is much thinner in those matrices. A team can test exemplar lineages now and would need a long compilation before the universal is settled.

assessments.operationalization: Record gallbladder presence or absence, and for the camel the presence of only small biliary vessels, in horse, mule, ass, deer, roe deer, camel, seals and dolphins. Each named case is confirmed by absence, or by reduced ducts in the camel, and refuted by a normal gallbladder.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical and natural-history accounts for the named ungulates, seals and dolphins

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen media for the named species, useful where soft-tissue or contrast imaging shows the biliary tract

obstacles: The gallbladder is soft tissue and is often missing from skeletal scans, so accounts carry more weight than bone libraries.
Deer and seal each name a family, and a single species with a gallbladder would limit how far the group claim reaches.
assessments.rationale: The claim is a short list of presence, absence and duct reduction, and each named animal has a published visceral anatomy. A small team can score the list from species accounts and veterinary anatomy in days. Imaging repositories help where the biliary tract was actually scanned, and they are secondary to those accounts.

assessments.operationalization: Compare gallbladder presence and size in sheep and goats from Naxos with animals from the Chalcis district of Euboea, against the usual presence of a gallbladder in those species. The locality claim holds if Naxos animals are extreme and Euboean animals lack the organ.
obstacles: No public survey records gallbladder size or presence for sheep and goats by Greek locality.
Modern island breeds need a demonstrated link to the ancient stocks Aristotle named.
Routine slaughter statistics do not retain gallbladder measurements.
assessments.rationale: The variables are straightforward, presence and size by locality, and a dedicated survey could decide them. Nothing now in open trait databases or breed registries records gallbladder anatomy for Naxos versus Euboea. Existing livestock data identify breeds and places, and they omit the organ the claim is about.

assessments.operationalization: Regress size-corrected maximum longevity on gallbladder absence across mammals, with deer, horses, asses, camels and dolphins marked. The claim holds if absence predicts longer life after body size and phylogeny are accounted for, and fails if the association is flat or reversed.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and adult body mass for mammals with and without a gallbladder

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and life-history covariates used to residualize longevity

obstacles: Gallbladder presence is not a column in the longevity databases and has to be compiled for the species that have longevity records.
Body size and phylogeny both predict lifespan, so an uncorrected comparison is uninformative.
Roe deer are short-lived for a 'deer' example, so the group label hides heterogeneity.
assessments.rationale: AnAge supplies the longevity side of the comparison for a large set of mammals, including the named kinds. The gallbladder character is real but scattered through anatomical sources, so only a subset of the longevity table can be scored quickly. Even on that subset, a clean result needs a phylogenetic model, which keeps the test informative and confounded.

assessments.operationalization: Score ink-sac presence across cuttlefish, squid and octopuses, and compare ink quantity or ink-sac volume scaled by body size, asking whether Sepia ranks highest. Universal presence fails if a cephalopod in that set lacks ink; the ranking fails if another genus stores more.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species pages for cephalopods compiling published notes on the ink sac

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for cuttlefish, squid and octopuses so ink records can be attached to names

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of ink use and the ink sac in common cephalopods

obstacles: Ink volume is described far more often than measured on a common scale.
Nautiluses lack an ink sac, so the result depends on whether 'all cephalopods' includes them or only Aristotle's coleoids.
assessments.rationale: Presence of an ink sac in the familiar coleoids is documented well enough to test that half of the claim from species accounts. A quantitative ranking of ink amount is not in any trait table, and the published measurements cover a handful of genera. The test can settle presence for the named kinds and only illustrate the 'most ink' ranking.

assessments.operationalization: Score a gastric mill, a second set of teeth in the stomach, in spiny lobsters, crayfish and crabs. The distributional claim holds if Carabi and only some crabs have one; the functional clause needs a further comparison of animals whose mouthparts already chew well.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: decapod species pages that summarize stomach anatomy where it has been published

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: name matching for Carabi, lobsters, crayfish and crabs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of the decapod foregut and gastric mill

obstacles: Carabi maps uncertainly onto spiny lobsters, which lack chelae, and onto crayfish, which have them.
A gastric mill is widespread in decapods, so 'some crabs' needs an explicit species list.
Presence of the mill does not show that the mouthparts were insufficient.
assessments.rationale: The gastric mill is a standard decapod character and can be scored for the main groups from carcinological descriptions. Name matching for Carabi changes which animals enter the test, and the 'because' clause is a functional claim that presence data leave open. Existing accounts can test the anatomical distribution on a restricted set of families.

assessments.operationalization: Track gonad index across the lunar month in Mediterranean edible sea urchins, with nighttime sea temperature and feeding rate as covariates. The size claim holds if gonads peak at full moon; the warmth explanation holds only if temperature, rather than feeding, accounts for that peak.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive notes for echinoids, including lunar spawning where a species page records it

candidate_datasets.name: World Echinoidea Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for the edible sea-urchin species in Aristotle's scope

obstacles: Lunar gonad series exist for some tropical species and are sparse for the Mediterranean species he would have seen.
Moonlight does not supply a sea-temperature treatment, and tides, spawning cycles and feeding move together.
No open dataset holds gonad index, intake and temperature on the same lunar calendar.
assessments.rationale: A lunar peak in gonad size is measurable and has been published for particular urchins, so a subset of the pattern can be reviewed now. Those series rarely pair feeding and nighttime temperature with gonad size, which is what would separate Aristotle's warmth explanation from a feeding explanation. The mechanism half of the claim stays out of reach of the existing tables.

assessments.operationalization: Count gonads ('eggs'), lantern teeth and stomach compartments across regular and irregular echinoids. The claim holds if every sea urchin has five of each; any order with a different gonad count or without a lantern refutes the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: World Echinoidea Database
candidate_datasets.role: classification of regular and irregular echinoids whose diagnoses state lantern and gonad patterns

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: scans and photographs of tests and lanterns from which tooth count can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of Aristotle's lantern, gonads and gut compartments in sea urchins

obstacles: Aristotle's eggs are gonads and his stomachs are the five pouches around the lantern, so the counts have to follow that anatomy.
Irregular echinoids often reduce the lantern and the gonad number, and skeletal repositories show teeth more readily than gonads.
assessments.rationale: Five-part organization of regular sea urchins is standard morphology and can be checked from diagnoses, accounts and lantern specimens. Irregular groups are in the same taxonomic database and are the natural refuting cases if 'all sea urchins' is taken at face value. Gonad counts are soft-tissue records, and order-level descriptions already state them well enough for a decision.

assessments.operationalization: The passage asserts an unbroken natural scale from lifeless things through plant-like beings to animals, with neighbours scarcely different. No measurement of disparity or of phylogenetic distance supplies a threshold that would confirm or refute that picture without replacing it.
obstacles: 'Unbroken sequence' and 'scarcely any difference' have no decision criterion.
A tree, a life-versus-nonlife boundary, or a disparity statistic would test a modern stand-in for the claim.
assessments.rationale: This is a statement about how nature is arranged, not a comparative measurement with a confirming and a refuting result. Phenotypic and phylogenetic datasets can describe gaps and clusters, and any degree of similarity can still be called a close approach. The claim therefore has no empirical resolution that preserves what it says.

assessments.operationalization: Identify the food of adult cicadas by gut contents, feeding traces or stable isotopes. The claim holds if atmospheric moisture accounts for their intake, and fails if they feed on plant sap.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: species-interaction records linking cicadas to food plants where those records exist

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: feeding accounts for Cicadidae, including xylem feeding versus dew

obstacles: GloBI's coverage of cicadas is incomplete, so species accounts still have to be read.
Occasional dew drinking can sit alongside sap feeding, and the claim requires moisture from the air as the food.
The aside that insects eat little because they are cold is a separate, non-measured explanation.
assessments.rationale: Cicada diet is a standard natural-history variable, documented in accounts and in interaction records that point to plants. A small team can score the family well enough to decide whether air-deposited moisture is their food. The cold-nature gloss does not add a second observable beyond that diet.

assessments.operationalization: Compare wing count, two versus four, with body size across flying insects, treating flies and bees as the named anchors. The claim holds if a small size class has two wings and larger fliers have four, and fails if tiny four-winged insects or large two-winged insects are common.

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for insect orders whose wing counts are stable, to be joined to body-size records

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: exemplar accounts stating wing number for flies, bees and other flying insects

obstacles: No open table pairs wing count with body size across insects.
'Very small' has no stated cutoff.
Minute wasps have four wings and large flies have two, so order-level proxies answer a different question from the size rule.
assessments.rationale: Wing number is discrete and, for exemplar orders, already written in ordinary descriptions, so counterexamples can be assembled. A fair test of 'very small implies two wings' needs a size-stratified sample that does not exist as a dataset. Existing sources can refute a crude version on well-known orders and cannot yet carry a quantitative rule for flying insects as a whole.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the frequency of a larger right claw in crabs, in Carabi, and in clawed lobsters. 'Invariably' requires a right-claw bias indistinguishable from all individuals; the lobster clause holds if side is about even.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: decapod accounts that report claw asymmetry where it has been studied

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: matching of Carabi, crabs and lobsters to modern families

obstacles: Carabi is an unstable name, and spiny lobsters do not have crushing claws.
Laterality frequencies are published for a few crabs and for Homarus, not for crabs as a class.
A single left-handed individual refutes 'invariably' if that word is taken literally.
assessments.rationale: Claw laterality is measurable and already counted in papers on shore crabs and the European lobster. Those studies cover a small slice of the groups named, and the identity of Carabi changes the hypothesis. The existing counts can test a few genera and leave the universal over crabs unresolved.

assessments.operationalization: Count arms in cuttlefish, squid and octopuses, and compare arm length scaled by mantle length. The claim holds if all three have eight arms and the arms are short in cuttlefish and squid and longer in octopuses.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: cephalopod species pages describing arm and tentacle counts and relative arm length

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for Sepia, teuthids and octopods

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of arm number and proportion in the common genera

obstacles: Squid and cuttlefish also have two tentacles, which must be kept distinct from the eight arms.
Relative length is often qualitative in accounts.
Nautiluses fall outside the eight-arm pattern if the claim is read as all cephalopods.
assessments.rationale: Arm counts for the three groups Aristotle compares are standard and repeated in public species accounts. Relative length is described consistently enough, even without a morphometric table, for a small team to score the contrast he draws. Extending the same count to nautiluses is a boundary choice, and within the stated scope the comparison is decidable.

assessments.operationalization: Count cervical vertebrae, and any fusion into one element, in wolves and lions, and compare that count with other mammals that have a neck. The claim holds only if the wolf and lion neck is a single bone.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skeletal scans of Canis lupus and Panthera leo from which cervical counts can be taken

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: digital cranial and cervical anatomy of mammals, including large carnivores where digitized

candidate_datasets.name: VertNet
candidate_datasets.role: museum skeletal specimens of wolves and lions with vertebral series

obstacles: Cervical count is scored from specimens or accounts rather than a precomputed longevity-style column.
The named species are the whole scope, and both are well represented in collections.
assessments.rationale: A single neck bone versus several vertebrae is directly visible on skeletons, and wolves and lions are in open morphology repositories and museum indexes. Scoring a few specimens decides the claim. The same collections supply the comparison with other necked mammals.

assessments.operationalization: Compare withers height of foals with adult withers height, and test whether the hind hoof reaches the head in foals and fails to do so in adults. The claim holds if young solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed animals are nearly adult in height because the limbs are disproportionately long.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: juvenile and adult limb elements of horses and other ungulates for relative leg length

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: growth and proportion notes for horses and other hoofed mammals

obstacles: Withers-height series live in husbandry papers rather than one open growth table.
The hind-hoof-to-head movement is a flexibility observation and is rarely measured.
The claim also covers cloven-hoofed quadrupeds, which are less completely measured than the horse.
assessments.rationale: Relative limb length of young versus adult ungulates can be approached with museum specimens and with published horse growth curves. Those sources cover the horse better than the whole hoofed scope, and they rarely record the reaching movement. The height comparison is partly testable now; the behavioral clause is thinly documented.

assessments.operationalization: The claim assigns hands to humans because they are intelligent enough to use them. Co-occurrence of hands and intelligence does not separate that final-cause order from the opposite story, and a phylogenetic sequence of dexterity and brain size would be a different claim.
obstacles: No observation distinguishes nature's assigning hands for the sake of intelligence from the bare conjunction of the two traits.
Replacing the final cause with an evolutionary order changes the claim.
assessments.rationale: This is a teleological ranking of causes. Human hands and human intelligence are both observable, and nothing in existing data says which exists for the sake of the other. The passage is therefore not empirically resolvable on its own terms.

assessments.operationalization: Count digits, including the dewclaw, on each forefoot and hind foot of wolves, lions, dogs and leopards. The claim holds if forefeet have five digits and hind feet have four.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: pedal skeletons of the named carnivores

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: digit anatomy for mammal specimens that have been digitized

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: toe-count statements in species accounts for canids and felids

obstacles: Domestic dogs often carry a hind dewclaw, so 'dogs' is not a single count.
The forelimb dewclaw is a reduced digit and has to be included on purpose.
assessments.rationale: Digit number in these four carnivores is elementary anatomy and is visible on skeletons and written in species accounts. A small team can score the named species, and the dog dewclaw is the main within-group complication. The claim as restricted to these animals is decidable with current specimens and accounts.

assessments.operationalization: Pair teat number and position, inguinal versus abdominal, with litter size across viviparous quadrupeds. The claim holds if animals with small litters have two inguinal teats and litter-bearers have many teats along the belly.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and adult body mass for mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and reproductive traits for the named ungulates and carnivores

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: teat number and position in species accounts for horse, camel, deer, ox, goat, pig, dog and lion

obstacles: Teat number and position are not columns in the life-history tables and have to be compiled.
Shared ancestry tracks both litter size and teat pattern.
Primates, with two pectoral teats and usually one young, sit outside the thigh-versus-belly wording.
assessments.rationale: Litter size for the relevant mammals is in open life-history databases, and teat counts for the familiar livestock and carnivores are in species accounts. Joining the two for a phylogenetic test is a real compilation, feasible for the named species and incomplete for viviparous quadrupeds at large. The data can test the stated examples and a partial comparative version of the rule.

assessments.operationalization: Record the direction of the urine stream, rearward versus forward or lateral, in female quadrupeds, in lynx, lion, camel and hare males, and in solid-hoofed males. The universals hold only if every female and no solid-hoofed animal directs urine backward, with the named males as the male exceptions.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: elimination and urogenital notes for the named genera

obstacles: 'Backwards' has no standard angular criterion.
Quantitative records exist for a few domestic and zoo species, while most quadrupeds are undescribed on this point.
The orientation of the urethral opening is an anatomical proxy for the behavior.
assessments.rationale: Direction of urination is observable and is described for horses, camels, lions and a few other familiar species. Those accounts can speak to the named exceptions and to solid-hoofed animals. They do not cover female quadrupeds as a class, so the universal remains untested.

assessments.operationalization: Score external tail presence and a distinct buttock, a fleshy gluteal mass used in upright posture, in humans and in quadrupeds. The anatomical claim holds if humans lack a tail and quadrupeds lack buttocks; the nourishment story has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: caudal regions and pelves of humans and quadrupeds

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: tail and locomotor descriptions across mammals, including apes

obstacles: A buttock is a soft-tissue shape, whereas skeletal collections show caudal vertebrae.
Many mammals lack an external tail, so 'man alone' is a broad comparative claim.
Diversion of tail nourishment into the buttocks yields no distinct observation.
assessments.rationale: Tail reduction and pelvic form can be compared with skeletons and species accounts, which is enough to test whether tail loss and buttocks are uniquely human. The nutritional explanation of that pattern does not differ observationally from the anatomy itself. The result is a partial test of the anatomical clauses.

assessments.operationalization: Score a huckle-bone as the double-pulley astragalus, and tabulate it against polydactyl, solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed feet. The claim holds if polydactyl quadrupeds lack that bone, solid-hoofed animals usually lack it, and the animals that have it are mostly cloven-hoofed.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: ankle skeletons across artiodactyls, perissodactyls and multi-toed mammals

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: astragalus morphology for digitized mammal specimens

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: foot-type and ankle descriptions for the main ungulate and carnivore groups

obstacles: Every tetrapod has a talus; the claim is about the dice-shaped artiodactyl astragalus.
Foot categories have to be applied the same way to each specimen.
assessments.rationale: The double-trochlea astragalus is a standard osteological character and is visible in open skeletal collections. Foot type is likewise standard. A small team can cross-tabulate the two across living quadruped orders and decide the generalization.

assessments.operationalization: Score tongue presence in the Nile crocodile and in other oviparous quadrupeds and snakes. The claim holds if every such animal has a tongue except the river crocodile, which has only an empty space.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: oral-cavity accounts for crocodilians, lizards, turtles and snakes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: head specimens of Crocodylus niloticus, informative where soft tissue is preserved

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: cranial anatomy of crocodilians and other reptiles

obstacles: The crocodile tongue is soft tissue and is easy to miss on a dry skull.
A tongue that is present and immobile still counts as a tongue under a presence criterion.
assessments.rationale: Tongue presence in reptiles is ordinary anatomy and is stated in species accounts for crocodilians, lizards, turtles and snakes. The river crocodile is the single exception the claim needs, and it is well described. Skeletal scans are supplementary because the character is soft tissue.

assessments.operationalization: Score which eyelid closes the eye in lizards, turtles, crocodilians and birds. The claim holds if these animals lack a functional upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower lid.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: eye and eyelid descriptions for lepidosaurs, turtles, crocodilians and birds

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: orbital anatomy for reptile specimens where the lids can be interpreted

obstacles: Snakes have a spectacle rather than mobile lids.
Crocodilians, geckos and birds differ from typical lizards in how the upper lid and the nictitating membrane work.
Family-level scoring still has to be compiled from descriptions.
assessments.rationale: Eyelid mechanics are described at the level of the major groups the claim covers, and those descriptions are public. A small team can score lizards, turtles, crocodilians and birds as groups and decide whether lower-lid closure is general. Within-group exceptions are part of that same literature, so they narrow the claim rather than leaving it untestable.

assessments.operationalization: In the Nile crocodile, measure which element rotates at the jaw joint relative to the braincase, and separately how the head moves relative to the ground during a bite. The claim holds if the upper jaw is the element that moves on the skull; movement of the head on the neck is a different result.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: cranial and jaw-joint models of crocodilians

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skulls of Crocodylus showing the jaw articulation

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: functional accounts of crocodile feeding and jaw movement

obstacles: Relative to the skull the mandible is the mobile element; relative to the ground the whole head lifts.
Published kinematic series cover few individuals.
Aristotle's observation matches the head-lifting frame, so the criterion has to be stated before the data decide anything.
assessments.rationale: The jaw joint itself is visible on specimens and is enough to say which bone articulates. Feeding kinematics that would match Aristotle's frame, the head rising while the lower jaw stays near the substrate, exist for a few animals and are not a systematic dataset. The anatomical test is feasible, and the reference frame keeps it from being a clean decision.

assessments.operationalization: Score milk or mammary glands against reproductive mode. The claim holds if milk and mammae occur only in internally viviparous animals, and fails if any egg-laying or otherwise non-internally-viviparous animal lactates.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal species list and life history, including monotremes and therian mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and longevity records that identify monotremes, marsupials and placentals

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: lactation and reproductive-mode accounts, including monotremes and birds that produce crop secretions

obstacles: Monotremes lay eggs and lactate, so they are the decisive case and must be inside the taxon set.
Pigeon crop milk is a different secretion and has to be kept outside mammary milk by the definition used.
assessments.rationale: Reproductive mode and lactation are both standard, and monotremes are present in mammal life-history databases and species accounts. A small team can ask whether any non-internally-viviparous animal has milk. That comparison decides the universal as stated.

assessments.operationalization: Correlate neck length with leg length across birds, coding webbed feet as the stated exception. The claim holds if neck and leg lengths track each other once web-footed birds are set aside, and if those web-footed birds break the pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: tarsus length, wing and mass for birds, covering the leg side of the comparison; neck length is not a column

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: bird skeletons from which neck length can be measured for a sample

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts describing neck, leg and foot type, including webbed feet

obstacles: Neck length is absent from the main open avian morphometric table.
Web-footed birds range from long-necked swans to short-necked auks, so the exception class is heterogeneous.
A phylogenetic model is required before the correlation can be read as a rule.
assessments.rationale: Leg length and foot type are available for essentially all birds, and neck length can be measured on a skeletal sample or taken from accounts for a subset. That is enough to test the rule in part. A full-scope test waits on a neck-length compilation joined to the existing leg data.

assessments.operationalization: Code tarsal or wing spurs and predatory talons as two binary traits across birds. The co-occurrence claim holds if no species has both; the remark that nature makes nothing superfluous has no further observation.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts describing spurs, claws and feet for galliforms, jacanas, screamers and raptors

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: foot descriptions for exemplar gamebirds and birds of prey

obstacles: Spur and talon need explicit definitions before a species is scored.
Full species accounts are partly paywalled.
The final-cause sentence is not a separate measurable claim.
assessments.rationale: Spurs and talons are described in standard bird accounts, and the relevant groups are few enough that a team can search them. There is no open character column for either trait, so the work is a compilation rather than a download. The mutual-exclusion clause can be tested on a well-defined subset; the teleological gloss cannot.

assessments.operationalization: Count toes on each foot across birds, with the ostrich set aside as the claim allows. The claim holds if every other bird has four toes.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: toe counts in species accounts across bird families

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: foot descriptions for ratites, shorebirds, woodpeckers and other groups that vary in toe number

obstacles: Toe number is written in descriptions rather than in the AVONET measurement table.
Three-toed ratites, some shorebirds and some woodpeckers remain inside the claim once the ostrich is excluded.
assessments.rationale: Toe count is a discrete, universally described bird character. Setting the ostrich aside is explicit in the claim, and the remaining families can be scored from handbooks and accounts in weeks. Exceptions outside the ostrich decide the universal.

assessments.operationalization: Code toe arrangement as two-forward-two-back versus three-forward-one-back for the wryneck and for other birds. The claim holds only if Jynx is the sole two-and-two species.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: toe arrangement for wrynecks, other woodpeckers, parrots, cuckoos, toucans and trogons

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: zygodactyl and heterodactyl foot descriptions for the main bird groups

obstacles: Zygodactyly, heterodactyly and a reversible outer toe have to be distinguished.
Woodpeckers other than the wryneck are the closest comparison, and parrots and cuckoos are further two-and-two cases.
assessments.rationale: Foot arrangement is standard in bird descriptions, and the wryneck's identity is unambiguous. A small team can list the other two-and-two and two-back arrangements from family accounts. That list decides whether the wryneck is unique.

assessments.operationalization: Count paired pectoral and pelvic fins, which are the four fins in this passage, across fishes, treating broad flat batoids as the stated exception. The claim holds if non-flat fishes have four and no fish has more than four.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: pectoral and pelvic fin fields, from which paired-fin presence and counts can be taken

obstacles: Median fins are outside the four Aristotle is counting.
A blank fin-ray field has to be separated from a genuinely absent pelvic fin.
Eels and other non-flat fishes often lack pelvic fins, which bears on the 'have four' clause.
assessments.rationale: FishBase records paired-fin rays for a very large fraction of fish species and can be downloaded and scored with ordinary filters. The maximum of four paired fins and the claim that non-flat fishes have all four are both decidable from those fields. Batoids are identifiable in the same table and can be set aside as the text does.

assessments.operationalization: Score an operculum against skeleton type for elasmobranchs, chimaeras, sturgeons and bony fishes. The distributional claim holds if selachians lack gill covers; the 'because cartilage' clause holds only if cartilaginous-skeleton fishes in general lack them.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: classification of cartilaginous and bony fishes, with gill-cover details in the morphology sections of bony fishes

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxon matching for selachians, chimaeras and chondrosteans

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: gill-slit and operculum descriptions for sharks, rays, chimaeras and sturgeons

obstacles: Chimaeras have a soft opercular flap on a cartilaginous skeleton.
Sturgeons have an operculum and a largely cartilaginous skeleton, which is the comparison that bears on the causal clause.
assessments.rationale: Operculum presence is a group-level character already reflected in fish databases and in elasmobranch trait compilations. The selachian half can be read off directly. The causal half is decided by the same character in other cartilaginous-skeleton fishes, which are in the same taxonomic systems.

assessments.operationalization: Code mouth position as ventral versus terminal in dolphins and in selachians, and code whether feeding requires rolling onto the back. The claim holds if both groups have an underslung mouth and turn over to eat.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: mouth position for sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: dolphin and whale species pages describing mouth position and feeding posture

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: feeding accounts for dolphins and for sharks that roll or do not roll while taking prey

obstacles: Dolphin mouths are described as terminal on the beak, so the cetacean half may not match the shark coding.
Belly-up feeding is a behavior and is not a FishBase field.
Many sharks feed without rolling over, so mouth position alone does not establish the posture clause.
assessments.rationale: Mouth position for sharks and rays is a coded morphological field and can be tested now. The turning-over clause, and the inclusion of dolphins, depend on behavioral and anatomical accounts that cover common species and leave most selachians undescribed. The claim is decidable in part.

assessments.operationalization: Score sperm-producing testes, external or internal, in fishes and in snakes and other footless vertebrates. The claim holds only if those animals lack testes and have only sperm ducts.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive biology of fishes; male gonads are described in species summaries and the anatomical literature rather than a single presence column

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: snake species accounts and anatomical literature pointers for male reproductive organs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: testis descriptions for fishes and snakes

obstacles: Aristotle treated elongate gonads as ducts, so the criterion has to be a sperm-producing organ rather than a compact scrotal testis.
Footless animals include caecilians and eels as well as snakes, and coverage is best for fishes and snakes.
assessments.rationale: Male gonads of fishes and snakes are described throughout comparative anatomy and are reflected in reproductive sections of public databases and accounts. A presence criterion decides the universal. The duct-versus-testis wording is a relabeling that the histology and gross anatomy can still address, because the organs produce sperm.

assessments.operationalization: Test whether the cetacean blowhole is connected to water taken in by the mouth, using airway-versus-esophagus anatomy and the composition of the blow. The claim holds if expelled water is swallowed seawater, and fails if the blow is respiratory vapor from a separate airway.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: respiratory and feeding anatomy of dolphins and whales, including the blowhole and the separation from the mouth

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: cetacean species pages summarizing the blowhole and lung

obstacles: The decisive anatomy is in descriptions rather than a trait column.
Chemical samples of the blow exist for a few species.
The claim covers dolphins, porpoises and whales, and the common species are the ones with detailed anatomy.
assessments.rationale: The connection between mouth, lungs and blowhole is established anatomy for the cetaceans the claim names, and it is written in public species accounts. That anatomy decides whether the blowhole vents swallowed seawater. Direct assays of blow composition add a second line of evidence for a smaller set of species.

assessments.operationalization: The claim says nature avoids the infinite because the infinite is incomplete, and therefore seeks an end. No dataset distinguishes that principle from any particular finite life cycle.
obstacles: 'Avoids the infinite' and 'seeks an end' state no confirming or refuting observation.
The application to spontaneous generation, that new kinds do not form an endless series, is a different and narrower claim.
assessments.rationale: This is a metaphysical constraint on nature. Finite generation, extinction and bounded clutch sizes are all compatible with it, and so are their opposites if one redescribes the end nature is said to seek. The sentence has no empirical decision criterion.

assessments.operationalization: Score sexual system, separate sexes versus hermaphroditism versus no gametes, in sessile shelled molluscs and in attached animals such as barnacles, sponges and ascidians. Separate males and females refute a claim of no sexes; hermaphroditism matches his plant comparison only under that reading.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for bivalves, gastropods, barnacles, sponges and ascidians where pages record it

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for testaceans as shelled molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: names and higher classification for attached marine animals in the scope

obstacles: Testaceans map to a mixed set of shelled molluscs, and attached animals add further phyla.
Hermaphroditism can be scored either as combined sexes or as the 'no sex' condition he attributes to plants.
Many bivalves have separate sexes, which is the clearest opposing outcome.
assessments.rationale: Sexual systems of common bivalves, snails, barnacles and ascidians are in marine species compilations and in the taxonomic literature those compilations summarize. Coverage is good for commercial and coastal genera and thin elsewhere. The test can decide the claim for those genera once hermaphroditism is given an explicit reading.

assessments.operationalization: The claim assigns the efficient cause of generation to the male and the material cause to the female. Those are Aristotelian causal roles, and an observation that the egg contributes cytoplasm or that the sperm contributes a genome replaces the claim with a different one.
obstacles: Efficient cause and material cause are not measurements.
Embryological and genetic datasets become relevant only after the four causes are translated away.
assessments.rationale: The sentence states a principle of explanation. Modern reproductive data describe contributions of egg and sperm in chemical and genetic terms, which do not confirm or refute 'efficient' versus 'material' as he uses those words. The claim stays conceptual.

assessments.operationalization: Compare sexually dimorphic traits before and after castration in males, asking whether most of them move to the female mean. The claim holds if the whole form shifts toward the female, and fails if only a few traits change or the animal remains clearly male in overall form.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: notes on secondary sexual characters, including antlers and other traits known to depend on the testes, for exemplar species

obstacles: 'Nearly the whole form' and 'seems female' need a declared trait list and a distance.
Published castration effects are concentrated on livestock, deer, horses and a few birds.
Age and breed confound before-after comparisons.
assessments.rationale: Effects of castration on particular dimorphic characters are documented for domestic animals and deer, so a partial test is possible from that literature. There is no cross-species table of whole-form change. The strong wording, that the animal becomes female or nearly so in form, can be assessed only for those well-studied species.

assessments.operationalization: Score testes versus sperm ducts alone in fishes and snakes. The claim holds if males of both groups lack testes and possess only two spermatic ducts.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive biology of fishes; testis anatomy is in species summaries and standard comparative anatomy

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: snake accounts pointing to internal male reproductive organs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: testis descriptions for fishes and serpents

obstacles: Elongate gonads are the structures Aristotle called ducts; the decision criterion is whether those structures are testes.
Coverage is broad for fishes and adequate at family level for snakes.
assessments.rationale: The same anatomical sources that describe fish and snake reproduction identify paired male gonads. That identification decides a claim of absence. Compiling the score from databases and standard accounts is ordinary work for a small team.

assessments.operationalization: Record whether testes are internal and lie near the kidneys in birds and in oviparous quadrupeds such as lizards, turtles and crocodiles. The claim holds if both location conditions are general in those groups.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: urogenital anatomy for birds, lizards, turtles and crocodilians

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic and account coverage for oviparous reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: species lists and life history confirming which birds and reptiles fall in the scope

obstacles: 'Near the loin, by the kidneys' is a position claim, not mere absence of a scrotum.
Species accounts mention position unevenly, while group-level anatomy is consistent.
assessments.rationale: Internal testes beside the kidneys are group-level characters for birds and for the oviparous reptiles Aristotle includes. Public accounts state them, and the groups themselves are listed in life-history and taxonomic databases. A small team can score the groups and decide the generalization.

assessments.operationalization: Score the uterus or its analogue as paired or single across females, including mammals, birds and the invertebrate groups in the surrounding discussion. The claim holds if the organ is always double in the same sense that testes are two.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: uterus and oviduct descriptions for mammals, birds and other vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal species for which uterine type can be joined from anatomical accounts

obstacles: 'Double' can mean two horns, two oviducts or two chambers, and a simplex uterus is a fused pair.
Most birds have one functional oviduct.
Crustacean, cephalopod and insect gonoducts are a further mapping.
assessments.rationale: Uterine form is well described for mammals and birds, so those classes can be scored from accounts, with life-history lists supplying the species frame. The word 'always' reaches invertebrates whose paired ducts are described unevenly, and the criterion of doubling is itself ambiguous. The vertebrate portion is testable; the full universal is only partly so.

assessments.operationalization: Compare copulation duration of fishes, snakes, birds and oviparous quadrupeds with that of mammals that have external testes. The claim holds if every internal-testis or duct-only species is faster than the external-testis species.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mating descriptions that sometimes give copulation duration for exemplar vertebrates

obstacles: Duration data are scattered through behavioral papers and cover a biased subset of species.
Some snakes with internal testes mate for hours, which is a serious confound for a simple ranking.
Mating system and body size track duration along with testis position.
assessments.rationale: Copulation duration is measurable and published for many vertebrates, including both internal-testis and scrotal species. There is no open comparative table, and the studies that exist are enough to inspect a biased sample rather than to rank all of the groups. Phylogeny and mating system keep even that sample from being a clean test.

assessments.operationalization: Compare testis mass in the breeding season with testis mass afterward for seasonally pairing birds. The claim holds if testes enlarge sharply at copulation and then shrink to near invisibility.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: breeding-season summaries for birds, with testis-cycle notes where accounts include them

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history timing for birds, including clutches per year and age at maturity, as context for published seasonal testis series

obstacles: Testis-volume series sit in avian endocrinology papers rather than one repository.
Year-round breeders are outside the seasonal clause.
'Almost indiscernible' needs a size threshold.
assessments.rationale: Seasonal growth and regression of bird testes is a repeatedly measured variable, especially in temperate passerines and in poultry. A team can compile those series for a solid subset of seasonal breeders. A dataset that already holds testis size for birds at large does not exist, so the full scope stays partial.

assessments.operationalization: Record mating posture in Erinaceus, upright and face to face versus a posterior mount, and relate that posture to the spines. The posture claim holds if they copulate standing upright; a posterior mount with lowered spines fails it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-behavior account for the European hedgehog

obstacles: Posture is described in natural-history narratives and films, not in a measurement archive.
The spine explanation is settled only once the posture itself is known.
Other hedgehog genera are poorly described compared with Erinaceus europaeus.
assessments.rationale: The European hedgehog's mating posture is described in public natural-history accounts, which is enough to examine the upright-stance claim for that species. The records are few and qualitative. Other hedgehogs, and a measured link between spine length and posture, are much thinner.

assessments.operationalization: Code whether cartilaginous fishes and vipers form eggs internally and then bear live young. The claim holds for a group only if that two-step mode is general in it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: elasmobranch reproductive mode

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: shark and ray reproductive mode as a trait

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: Viperidae accounts stating egg-laying versus live birth

obstacles: Oviparous skates, catsharks and some viper genera decide the universals if the groups are taken at modern scope.
Yolk-sac and placental live birth both begin with an internal egg, which matches the wording if the egg stage is real.
assessments.rationale: This is the same reproductive-mode comparison as the Parts of Animals passage on vipers and selachians, and the same open sources cover it. Elasmobranch mode is tabulated; viper mode is in species accounts that can be compiled quickly. The generalization can be confirmed or refuted for both groups.

assessments.operationalization: Compare body temperature and egg-covering rigidity of live-bearing sharks and vipers with their egg-laying relatives. The cold-nature explanation holds if the live-bearers are colder and their coverings are soft because of that cold.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: preferred temperature and reproductive mode for sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of sharks and rays, to be set beside FishBase temperature fields

obstacles: 'Cold nature' is not a body-temperature measurement.
Regionally warm-bodied sharks that bear live young cut against a cold-cause story.
Eggshell thickness and maternal temperature are rarely measured in the same study.
assessments.rationale: Temperature preferences and reproductive mode can be joined for many sharks, which tests a thermal proxy for 'cold nature'. Viper body temperatures and the softness of their egg coverings are scattered, and a temperature difference would still leave the causal story confounded with phylogeny. The data support a partial, proxy test.

assessments.operationalization: Locate the testes of elephants and hedgehogs as scrotal or internal. The location claim holds if both are internal; the claim that their skin cannot form a scrotum is not decided by location alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: male reproductive anatomy of elephants and hedgehogs

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
