candidate_datasets.role: abdominal scans or dissections, where soft tissue shows testis position

obstacles: Testis position is documented in accounts; skin suitability is a functional gloss.
Skeletal repositories often omit the soft-tissue location.
Other testicond mammals show that internal testes occur with more than one skin type.
assessments.rationale: Internal testes in the elephant and the hedgehog are standard mammalogy and are stated in species accounts, so the location half can be decided now. The explanation from unsuitable skin does not make a prediction that location data can separate from other reasons for testicondy. The claim is only partly resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: Code mating posture in octopuses, cuttlefish and squid as mouth-to-mouth with intertwined arms, or as some other approach. The claim holds if that posture is the cephalopod mode.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-behavior notes for common cephalopods

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mating descriptions for octopus, cuttlefish and squid

obstacles: The three groups do not mate in one posture.
Many species have never been seen mating, so published observations are biased toward coastal genera.
Insertion of an arm into the mantle can co-occur with a head-to-head approach.
assessments.rationale: Mating has been described for the common octopus, cuttlefish and several squids, and those descriptions are summarized in public accounts. They can test the posture claim for those genera. They do not establish a single mode for cephalopods, and unobserved species remain a large share of the group.

assessments.operationalization: Examine the octopus arm that enters the female's funnel for a sperm groove or spermatophores, and for a connection to the male's seminal passage. The claim holds if that arm is only a holdfast and carries no generative role.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: notes on the hectocotylus and spermatophore transfer in octopuses

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of the specialized octopus arm

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for Octopus and related genera with a hectocotylus

obstacles: The spermatophore groove is described for common species and is not a filled column for every octopus.
Aristotle's poulp is the common octopus and its relatives, which are the best-described cases.
assessments.rationale: The specialized arm and its role in passing spermatophores are described in detail for the octopuses Aristotle would have meant, and those descriptions are public. Anatomy that shows sperm on the arm, or a groove continuous with the male system, decides whether the arm is outside generation. A small team can score the well-known species and settle the claim as he framed it.

assessments.operationalization: Trace life cycles of fleas, flies and blister beetles from egg to adult, and ask whether adults appear from putrefying matter with no parents. The claim holds only if those insects arise without conspecific parents and, when they do unite, fail to produce their own kind.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle accounts for fleas, flies and blister beetles

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: interaction records tying these insects to hosts, dung or carrion, as context for where eggs are laid

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: name matching for Siphonaptera, Diptera and Meloidae, including cantharides

obstacles: Cantharides maps to blister beetles, whose parasitic larval stages are easy to confuse with generation from carrion.
Flies lay eggs on putrefying matter, so substrate and parentage have to be scored separately.
Complete life cycles are in handbooks rather than one life-cycle table.
assessments.rationale: The life cycles of fleas, flies and blister beetles are fully described in public entomology, including the eggs and the role of rotting substrates. Those accounts decide whether the animals arise from putrefaction without parents. The work is compilation of known cycles, not a search for missing data.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate the proportion of copulating insect species in which female body length exceeds male body length. The claim holds if that proportion is a majority under a stated species universe.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: body-size and sex notes for exemplar insect orders

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: the taxonomic universe of insect orders against which published size samples can be matched

obstacles: Sexual size dimorphism is published in papers and supplements, with a bias toward a few orders.
No single open table covers insects that mate.
'Most' requires a sampling frame and a phylogenetic weighting.
assessments.rationale: Female-larger and male-larger insects are both well measured in scattered datasets, so a partial comparative test can be assembled. Those samples do not constitute a downloadable census of mating insects. The majority claim is testable on studied orders and remains open as a statement about insects in general.

assessments.operationalization: Score, across insects that copulate, whether the female inserts a part into the male or the male inserts a part into the female. The claim holds if female insertion is the majority pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: copulatory-anatomy accounts for major insect orders

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: order-level frame for sampling genitalia descriptions

obstacles: Genital orientation is described in taxonomic papers and is not a cross-order table.
A few groups with a female intromittent organ do not settle 'most'.
Building a fair sample across orders is months of compilation.
assessments.rationale: Which sex inserts is a discrete anatomical fact and is described for enormous numbers of species. Existing syntheses cover orders well enough to inspect the pattern, and they are not a dataset from which a prevalence can be computed directly. The claim is partly testable and laborious at full scope.

assessments.operationalization: In multi-generation human pedigrees, score traits that are absent in the parents and present in a child and in a more remote ancestor. The claim holds if such skipping occurs, and fails if resemblance is confined to parents.

candidate_datasets.name: ClinVar
candidate_datasets.role: clinical assertions with inheritance patterns, including autosomal recessive conditions expressed in offspring of unaffected parents

obstacles: The woman of Elis and the Ethiopian story is an anecdote, not a dataset.
Skipping can be recessive inheritance, incomplete penetrance or coincidence, and the claim only requires that skipping happens.
Open pedigree detail is richer for clinical traits than for ordinary family resemblance.
assessments.rationale: Reappearance of ancestral traits after a gap is a standard pedigree pattern, and public clinical-genetic archives document recessive transmission of that form. A small team can treat those records as a test of whether resemblance can skip generations. The particular ancient anecdote is not recoverable, and the general claim is.

assessments.operationalization: Compare acquired parental injuries, such as amputations, with the corresponding body part in the offspring. The claim holds if offspring are not always mutilated in the parental way, and would fail only if acquired mutilation were reliably inherited.
obstacles: Acquired injury has to be separated from congenital malformation.
There is no single registry of parental trauma and offspring phenotype; the evidence is the breeding, surgical and experimental record.
The claim is a negative generalization and is decided by documented non-transmission.
assessments.rationale: Non-inheritance of acquired mutilations is documented across animal breeding, surgery and experimental amputations. A small team can assemble decisive cases from that published record without new observation. The absence of one dedicated dataset limits convenience and does not leave the question untestable.

assessments.operationalization: Ask whether semen and sperm contain contributions drawn from every parental organ, as pangenesis requires, or a germline genome plus accessory-gland secretions. The claim holds if semen is not a sample of all body parts.

candidate_datasets.name: ProteomeXchange
candidate_datasets.role: seminal-plasma and sperm protein datasets with tissue attributions

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: proteins of semen and sperm, with tissue specificity

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: sperm and testis expression datasets contrasted with other organs

obstacles: Public molecular datasets are dominated by humans and a few model animals.
A restatement in which the genome 'comes from the whole body' would change the claim.
Seminal plasma mixes several glands, which is still far short of every part.
assessments.rationale: Proteomic and expression archives identify the tissues that contribute to semen and show a haploid germline plus a short list of accessory glands. That composition decides a claim that semen is withdrawn from all parts of the body. One or a few well-studied species are enough, because the claim is universal.

assessments.operationalization: Regress offspring number, litter size, clutch size or fecundity, on adult body mass across animals. The claim holds if larger species have fewer young, as a general negative relationship.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and litter or clutch size across vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal body mass and litter size

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: body length and fecundity for fishes, the high-fecundity end of the comparison

obstacles: The pattern is a correlation with exceptions, so 'have few' and 'have many' need a stated transform.
Phylogeny and offspring size both track fecundity.
Invertebrates outside fish and amniote tables are less evenly covered.
assessments.rationale: Body size and offspring number are core fields in open life-history databases for mammals, other amniotes and fishes. A standard comparative regression can be run in days to weeks and will confirm or refute a general inverse relationship. Remaining gaps are invertebrate coverage and the need to control phylogeny, which qualify the result and do not block the test.

assessments.operationalization: From human growth standards, compare stature gained from birth to about age five with stature gained from age five to adulthood, and with total postnatal gain. Either reading of 'half the height gained in the rest of life' can be accepted or rejected against those curves.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: length and height by age from birth to five years

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: measured stature by age in a population sample, including children and adults

obstacles: The phrase can mean half of later growth or half of all lifetime growth, and both are computable.
Modern standards are cross-sectional and secular change shifts adult height.
The claim is about humans in general, and the open standards are modern populations.
assessments.rationale: Age-specific human stature is in public growth standards and in NHANES measurements. Computing the fraction of lifetime height gained by age five is a short analysis. Wording ambiguity and secular change affect the interpretation, and they are handled by reporting both readings on the same tables.

assessments.operationalization: Compare fertility, time to pregnancy or live births, across adiposity classes in women and men. The fertility clause holds if fatter people are less fertile; the concoction clause needs semen volume or menstrual loss to fall as fat stores rise.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: body-mass index together with reproductive-history items for women and men

obstacles: Survey fertility items are coarse, and age, disease and low body weight confound a fat-versus-fertile contrast.
The diversion of secretion into fat is not measured by a fertility rate.
Clinical cohorts with semen analysis and adiposity exist as papers and are often access-restricted.
assessments.rationale: NHANES links body composition to reproductive history in an open sample, which can test whether higher adiposity goes with lower fertility. The design leaves serious confounds, and it does not contain the physiological diversion Aristotle proposes. The fertility association is partly testable; the mechanism is not in that survey.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the composition of semen with urine and with a glandular secretion that supplies nutrients to sperm. A nutritive secretion is supported if semen is rich in sperm nutrients from accessory glands; 'the last stage of nutriment' has no further chemical criterion.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: seminal proteins and their glandular origins

candidate_datasets.name: ProteomeXchange
candidate_datasets.role: seminal-plasma composition datasets

obstacles: 'Last stage of useful nutriment' is a concoction category.
A secretion that feeds sperm is compatible with more than one theoretical label.
Composition data are strong for humans and weak for animals at large.
assessments.rationale: Seminal biochemistry can show that semen is a glandular product containing sugars and proteins used by sperm, which bears on 'secretion' and on 'useful'. The same measurements do not isolate a final stage of nutriment or refute every rival description of a secretion. The claim is only partly turned into a test.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the age distribution of spermarche, voice change and first ejaculation in boys with the age of menarche and breast development in girls. The claim holds if those events fall in the same span of life.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: age at menarche and adolescent development items

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: adolescent growth and pubertal reference context for the same ages

obstacles: Spermarche is poorly represented in the surveys that record menarche.
'The same time of life' allows a window of years rather than a shared birthday.
Secular trends differ by sex and population.
assessments.rationale: Age at menarche is a standard public variable, and male pubertal timing is available in a smaller published literature that can be set beside it. The two are not one harmonized open table. A restricted comparison of modern populations can test whether the events coincide in life stage.

assessments.operationalization: Compare female and male adult mass in viviparous mammals, and ask whether female-smaller dimorphism is confined to species that menstruate. The size clause holds if females are smaller in this class; the menstrual explanation holds only if non-menstruating viviparous species lack that dimorphism.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and life history for viviparous mammals, as the species frame for a sex-size comparison

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: body-mass records for the same mammals, including monotremes and therians

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts that state male and female size, and whether a species menstruates or has an estrous cycle

obstacles: Female-larger mammals are common, so the size clause is an empirical distribution rather than a definition.
Menstruation is known from few clades and is not a field in the mass tables.
Sexual selection predicts size dimorphism independently of menstrual loss.
assessments.rationale: Adult body mass for mammals is downloadable, and many species accounts give male and female sizes, so the claim that viviparous females are smaller can be tested for a large subset. Sex-specific mass is not a single column in the main life-history tables, and menstruation is a separate character known for few clades. The size pattern is therefore partly testable now, while the menstrual explanation needs a compilation those tables do not contain.

assessments.operationalization: The claim defines the female as an impotent male who cannot concoct the final nutriment into semen. Failure to produce semen is the definition being used, and it does not add a measurement that could come out against the claim.
obstacles: Inability to concoct semen is how this passage says what a female is.
Hormone, gamete and genetic comparisons become a different claim once 'impotent male' is redescribed.
assessments.rationale: The sentence is a definitional theory of sex. Females' lack of semen is the observation it builds in, so that observation cannot test it. Datasets of gametes and endocrinology would answer a reconstructed physiological hypothesis, not this wording.

assessments.operationalization: Score cyclic menstrual shedding across humans and viviparous quadrupeds, with the mule as the stated defective case, and compare the amount of discharge with that of women. The claim holds if all non-defective members of the class menstruate, in smaller quantity than women.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: the species list of viviparous quadrupeds against which menstruation records can be joined

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-cycle accounts distinguishing estrus, menstruation and pregnancy bleeding

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history coverage of the mammal groups in the claim, including equids and the mule's parents

obstacles: Menstruation has to mean cyclic endometrial shedding, kept distinct from estrus.
Abundance relative to women is qualitative in most accounts.
Horses do not menstruate, so the mule's sterility is not the only equid case.
assessments.rationale: Which mammals menstruate is a reviewed comparative fact, and the species frame of viviparous quadrupeds is in open mammal databases. Species accounts separate estrus from menstruation for the main orders. A small team can decide whether menstruation is general in the class and merely lighter than in women.

assessments.operationalization: Relate breast projection at first menses to a length of about two finger-breadths. The claim holds if menarche usually coincides with that degree of breast rise.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: age at menarche and adolescent anthropometry, as a coarse public proxy for pubertal stage

obstacles: Two fingers' breadth is not a Tanner stage or a recorded breast measurement.
Cohorts that link breast stage to menarche are published and are not one open table.
Finger breadth varies with the observer.
assessments.rationale: Public surveys date menarche and record some adolescent body measures, which can place menarche in a stage of development. They do not record breast rise in finger-breadths. Pediatric studies come closer and still have to be compiled, so only a loose proxy of the timing claim is available.

assessments.operationalization: Ask whether any material from the male, genome, centriole or sperm proteins, becomes part of the embryo, or whether the male contributes only a motion and a form. The claim holds if normal embryos contain nothing material from the father.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Genome
candidate_datasets.role: reference genomes and parent-offspring genetic data showing paternal DNA in offspring

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: gene models and comparative genomics for the paternal contribution to the zygote

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: sperm and zygote proteins, including paternal contributions retained in the embryo

obstacles: The wording 'need not' is modal; a normal requirement for paternal DNA answers it for actual animal generation.
Coverage is best for humans and model species, which is enough for a universal denial of male material.
Centrioles and proteins are material in a broader sense than DNA alone.
assessments.rationale: Parentage and genome databases show that offspring carry a paternal genome, which is material from the male inside the embryo. That result can be read off existing genetic resources without new experiments. It decides the claim that nothing material from the male need enter the offspring and that his role is only motion and form.

assessments.operationalization: Classify hens' eggs by stage at mating, ovarian or freshly ovulated yolk versus an oviductal egg that has albumen, and record which of those eggs hatch as fertile. The claim holds if a mating while the egg is still entirely yellow converts a wind-egg into a fertile egg.
obstacles: Fertilization timing in the hen is established in poultry physiology rather than a downloadable trial table.
Sperm-storage tubules fertilize later ovulations, which can resemble fertilization of an egg already under way.
Wind-egg means an unfertilized ovum, and farm records rarely time the mating to yolk color.
assessments.rationale: The timing of fertilization relative to albumen secretion is known in detail for the domestic fowl, so the yellow-versus-white criterion can be interpreted and checked against that physiology. The original observation, a particular mating converting a specified yolk, is not stored as a reusable dataset. The claim is testable from the published experimental record for the chicken and only by analogy for other birds.

assessments.operationalization: Assign paternity in clutches where a second cock mates while eggs are still yolk, and measure the share of chicks sired by the second male. The claim holds only if the whole brood resembles, and is sired by, the second cock.
obstacles: Sequential-mating trials in poultry exist as papers, not as a public database.
'The whole brood' is stricter than a statistical last-male advantage.
Plumage resemblance and genetic paternity can diverge.
assessments.rationale: Sperm competition and second-male paternity in chickens have been measured, so the all-or-none claim about a second cock can be compared with those results. The trials are scattered and small. They can refute or qualify 'the whole brood' for the fowl and do not constitute a standing dataset.

assessments.operationalization: Among externally fertilizing fishes, compare fertilization of eggs that sperm reach with eggs from the same spawning that sperm do not reach. The claim holds if only the contacted eggs are fertilized.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fertilization mode, external versus internal, and reproductive guild for oviparous fishes

obstacles: FishBase codes the mode of fertilization and does not store egg-by-egg exposure trials.
Those trials are published for model and commercial teleosts.
Internally fertilizing oviparous fishes sit outside the milt-sprinkling description.
assessments.rationale: External fertilization, with sperm meeting eggs after laying, is a coded life-history field for a large share of fishes. Experimental embryology of teleosts records that unexposed eggs are not fertilized. Together the database and those studies decide the claim for the oviparous, externally fertilizing fishes it describes.

assessments.operationalization: Score gonochorism versus hermaphroditism in animals that locomote, and compare that with sessile animals. The claim holds if every motile species has separate male and female individuals.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sexual system of fishes, including simultaneous and sequential hermaphroditism

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems of motile invertebrates such as gastropods, and of sessile groups for the contrast

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for the motile and attached animals being compared

obstacles: Wrasses, hamlets, slugs and earthworms are motile hermaphrodites and are the deciding counterexamples if present.
Invertebrate sexual systems are less completely coded than those of fishes.
Separate sexes should be distinguished from the mere occurrence of sexual reproduction.
assessments.rationale: FishBase records hermaphroditism as a reproductive trait, and marine invertebrate compilations cover many motile hermaphrodites. A small team can list motile species that are not gonochoric and thereby confirm or refute the universal. Remaining uncertainty is coverage of terrestrial invertebrates, not the existence of a test.

assessments.operationalization: The claim says animals generate so that the kind can be eternal as a species, since the individual cannot be. That assigns a purpose to generation. Species durations and extinctions would test a different assertion, that species in fact last forever.
obstacles: 'Eternal as a species' is offered as the end for which generation exists.
A fossil record of extinction speaks to species' actual durations, which this modal and teleological wording does not assert.
assessments.rationale: The passage explains why there is generation, by a goal of species-level eternity. No measurement of births, deaths or extinctions distinguishes that goal from generation simply occurring. The claim is conceptual.

assessments.operationalization: Compare adult body-size distributions of vertebrates with invertebrates, and of motile animals with sessile ones, using medians and maxima. The claim holds if, taken generally, blooded animals are larger than bloodless ones and mobile animals larger than fixed ones.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass for vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: body length for a wide range of fishes, as the vertebrate aquatic sample

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: body size for marine invertebrates, including sessile and motile forms where length is recorded

obstacles: Aristotle's blood is approximately vertebrate blood, and some invertebrates exceed many vertebrates.
Colonial sessile animals have an ambiguous individual size.
Medians and maxima answer 'taken generally' in different ways, and invertebrate size coverage is biased toward large or commercial species.
assessments.rationale: Vertebrate body sizes are well tabulated, and marine invertebrate lengths are available for many species, so both contrasts can be sketched. Sessile and bloodless animals are the poorly standardized side, especially colonies. The result can support or weaken a general tendency and cannot yet match the full scope of animals.

assessments.operationalization: Measure egg diameter at laying and again during development for fishes, crustaceans and cephalopods, and for birds and oviparous reptiles. The claim holds if only the first three groups' eggs enlarge after they are produced.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg diameters and reproductive mode for fishes; the post-laying change itself is in embryological sources rather than the diameter field

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg and brood notes for crustaceans and cephalopods

obstacles: Teleost swelling is largely water uptake into the perivitelline space, which still counts as an increase in size.
Bird and reptile eggs are widely described as fixed in size after laying, while paired measurements are species-specific.
Brooded crustacean embryos are unevenly measured.
assessments.rationale: The contrast between cleidoic eggs and eggs that swell after laying is established for model fishes, poultry, a few reptiles and common cephalopods. Those published series can test the claim on a restricted set of species. There is no multi-group dataset of before-and-after diameters, so full taxonomic coverage remains out of a single analysis.

assessments.operationalization: Score live birth against the presence of vertebrate blood, and score vertebrates as viviparous, oviparous or sterile. The claim holds if every viviparous animal has blood and every animal with blood reproduces in one of those two ways unless it is infertile.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: live-bearing versus egg-laying in fishes, a major blooded group

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive notes for invertebrates, including viviparous arthropods where recorded

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: blood, hemolymph and reproductive mode for exemplar vertebrates and for viviparous invertebrates

obstacles: Aristotle's blood is red vertebrate blood, so viviparous insects and scorpions are the discriminating cases.
Live birth is coded for fishes and scattered for terrestrial invertebrates.
Sterile hybrids such as the mule have to be listed before the 'unless infertile' clause is applied.
assessments.rationale: Reproductive mode of vertebrates, especially fishes, is in open databases, and viviparity of several invertebrate groups is in species accounts. Joining those sources tests whether live birth occurs without vertebrate blood. Invertebrate coverage is the weak side, so the universal is partly, not fully, resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: Code each species as air-breathing or gill-breathing and as internally viviparous (live birth with the embryo retained and nourished in the mother, rather than an egg laid to the outside). The claim is refuted by viviparous gill-breathers and supported if internal viviparity is confined to air-breathers in the compiled tables.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and respiration for bony and cartilaginous fishes, including viviparous species

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: elasmobranch reproductive mode, including placental and other forms of live birth

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian viviparity and gestation as the air-breathing comparison class

obstacles: Aristotle's 'internally viviparous' has to be separated from egg-laying and from yolk-only retention.
FishBase sometimes lumps ovoviviparity with viviparity.
assessments.rationale: Live birth and mode of respiration are standard fields for fishes and mammals. Open compilations cover the gill-breathing groups in which exceptions would appear, and a single well-coded viviparous shark or teleost decides the universal claim. The remaining work is a coding crosswalk, which is routine.

assessments.operationalization: Compare adult body temperature or mass-specific metabolic rate of lunged versus lungless species, and among lunged species compare richly vascularized lungs with simpler ones. Higher values in lunged animals, and the highest in soft blood-rich lungs, would support the claim; a reversal in a broad sample would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: species-level body temperature and metabolic rate, concentrated on birds and mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: metabolic and life-history parameters across animals, including many ectotherms

obstacles: Aristotle's heat is an innate quality only partly captured by body temperature or metabolic rate.
Endothermy, body size and environment are confounded with presence of a lung.
assessments.rationale: Temperature and metabolic-rate tables exist and can rank many lunged and lungless species. Coverage is thin for fishes and amphibians relative to birds and mammals, and a temperature ranking does not isolate the lung from endothermy. The test is informative for a physiological proxy on a subset of taxa.

assessments.operationalization: Assign independent proxies of heat (body temperature or metabolic rate) and of dryness (cutaneous water loss or egg water content) and test whether those proxies predict cleidoic eggs in birds and scaly reptiles versus live birth. The heat-and-moisture rule fails if reproductive mode does not track the proxies once phylogeny is taken into account.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: parity mode, clutch size and related life-history traits for birds, mammals and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: body temperature for endotherms as a proxy for Aristotle's heat

obstacles: Dryness and innate heat are largely read off the reproductive modes they are meant to explain.
Viviparity in reptiles tracks climate and phylogeny at least as closely as any moisture score.
assessments.rationale: Parity mode is tabulated for amniotes, so the pattern of complete eggs versus live birth can be plotted. Independent measurements of dryness are scattered, and heat is a poor separator once birds, mammals and reptiles are compared. Outcomes remain compatible with several causal stories, so only a proxy of the mechanism can be tested.

assessments.operationalization: Map 'scolex' to a larval stage unlike the adult, then score insects for presence of a larva and for red blood or hemoglobin, and score non-insects for larvae. Any ametabolous insect, any blooded larva-producer, or an insect with hemoglobin-bearing blood challenges the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: documented holometabolous life cycle and developmental stages for Drosophila

candidate_datasets.name: AmphiBIO
candidate_datasets.role: amphibian reproductive modes, including larval stages in blooded animals

obstacles: Aristotle's scolex is a grub that later hardens, not every modern larval type.
Insect life-history traits are not in one global downloadable matrix.
assessments.rationale: Model-organism and amphibian trait tables can test pieces of the conjunction: fly metamorphosis, and blooded animals with larvae. A full survey of insect orders, and of which insects lack hemoglobin, still has to be compiled from the literature. The universal quantifiers are decidable on a subset, which is why the claim is only partly resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: No measurement separates a 'right' ranking by perfection and innate heat from the bare list of reproductive modes, because perfection and heat are assigned from those same modes.
obstacles: 'More perfect' and 'hotter' are not defined independently of the reproductive series.
A teleological claim that nature orders generation rightly has no rival-excluding observation.
assessments.rationale: Reproductive modes can be listed, and life-history databases already list them, but the claim is that nature grades animals by perfection and heat. Those ranks are not additional observations. Any outcome of a mode table can be read as fitting the scale, so the claim is not empirically decidable.

assessments.operationalization: Using staged embryo series, record whether distinct organs are present together at the earliest stage or appear across successive stages. Simultaneous presence of the later organs at the first morphological stage would refute successive formation; a repeated sequence of appearance would confirm it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish staging series showing organs appearing across developmental stages

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick gene-expression and anatomical stages through organogenesis

obstacles: Public staging atlases cover model species rather than every animal phylum.
assessments.rationale: Successive versus simultaneous appearance of parts is directly visible in open staging series for fishes, amphibians and birds, and the same contrast can be checked in insect resources. That is enough to confirm or refute the general embryological claim with standard inspection of existing images and stage tables. Remaining taxa would widen coverage rather than change the decision criterion.

assessments.operationalization: In lunged vertebrates, record the stage of first morphological appearance of the heart and of the lung bud, and their relative sizes at those stages. Heart-before-lung despite a larger lung confirms the claim; lung-before-heart, or a lung that is smaller when it first appears, refutes the stated contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick stages covering early heart and later respiratory-tract markers

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: timed mouse developmental series for early organ landmarks, strongest for the head and neural tube

obstacles: A quantitative heart-versus-lung size table is not precompiled across species.
The mouse atlas is brain-centered, so lung timing leans on chick and frog resources plus the literature.
assessments.rationale: The order of appearance and the relative size of heart and lung are observable in existing vertebrate staging series, especially chick and frog. Those series cover a subset of lunged animals rather than the full scope. The comparison itself is unambiguous once the stages are aligned, so the restricted taxonomic window is the main limit.

assessments.operationalization: Measure semen colour, viscosity and freezing behaviour at emission and after cooling, including near-freezing temperatures. Thick white semen that becomes colourless and watery on cooling, and that fails to freeze in frost, would support the claim; stable colour or ordinary freezing would refute the corresponding clause.
obstacles: Quantitative cooling curves are scattered in andrology and animal-breeding papers rather than one open table.
Most measurements are human or livestock, not animals generally.
assessments.rationale: Colour, viscosity and whether semen freezes are laboratory variables with a clear decision rule. Published descriptions and cryopreservation reports cover humans and a few domestic species, and they have to be compiled. A systematic multi-species cooling series is not a single public dataset, so only part of the scope can be checked now.

assessments.operationalization: Record ejaculate colour across human populations, including dark-skinned African populations, and across other animals. Universally white or grey semen supports the claim; a population whose semen is black refutes it.
obstacles: No open dataset stratifies semen colour by ancestry.
Clinical series are scattered and rarely designed as a population survey.
assessments.rationale: Semen colour is directly observable, and the Herodotus clause names a specific human contrast. Andrology reports describe colour repeatedly, but they are papers rather than a downloadable multi-population table. A small team can compile the human evidence; a true global sample of animals is thinner.

assessments.operationalization: Order embryonic characters by stage of first appearance and class them as shared among animals or peculiar to a species. Species-specific characters appearing after the shared ones would support the claim; early appearance of species-specific traits, under a pre-registered character list, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish stage tables for the order in which structures appear

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick expression and anatomy through stages where species characters differentiate

obstacles: Which characters count as 'generic animal' versus species-specific is contested.
Transcriptomic hourglass tests are a rival operationalization with different datasets.
assessments.rationale: Staging atlases contain the raw sequence of morphological appearance for several vertebrates. Turning that sequence into a test requires a character partition that is not in the atlases themselves. Competing partitions change the result, so the claim is testable only after a substantial coding choice and only for well-staged species.

assessments.operationalization: No observation distinguishes reason entering the embryo from outside, and being divine, from the fact that humans reason, because 'from outside' and 'divine' name no measurable variable.
obstacles: The claim is a doctrine about soul, not a prediction about organs or timing.
A strong reading that equates reason with absence of brain activity changes what Aristotle meant.
assessments.rationale: The sentence asserts an external, divine origin for reason and denies a bodily activity proper to it in his psychological sense. That is not a staging, anatomical or physiological measurement. Brain-activity datasets would test a different claim about neural correlates, not this one.

assessments.operationalization: Code chondrichthyan species for whether embryos finish development by a maternal uterine connection after yolk stores are used, and whether the egg is laid. One or more species with retained, maternally attached embryos confirms the existential claim; none in a broad elasmobranch sample would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of sharks and rays, including placental viviparity

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species-level reproductive mode for cartilaginous fishes

obstacles: 'Connection with the uterus' covers several matrotrophic modes that databases code under broader labels.
assessments.rationale: The claim is existential: some selachians keep the embryo and nourish it from the mother. Reproductive-mode fields already separate egg-laying, yolk-sac viviparity and placental attachment for many sharks and rays. A standard query of those tables can confirm or refute the existence claim without new collecting.

assessments.operationalization: Compare dates of menstrual onset with lunar phase in a large sample of cycles, and separately test whether ambient temperature is lower during the waning moon in the same records. A significant excess of onsets in the waning half would support the timing clause; a flat distribution would refute it.
obstacles: Cycle-onset dates tied to lunar phase sit in scattered studies, not one public table.
The waning moon is a weak stand-in for a colder environment, so the causal clause is confounded.
assessments.rationale: Onset versus lunar phase is a clear statistical contrast, and several published cycle series speak to it. Those series are not gathered in an open repository with broad geographic coverage. Temperature as the stated cause is a further claim that lunar phase does not measure, so only the timing clause is partly testable.

assessments.operationalization: In multi-generation hybrid pedigrees of the named crosses, score offspring shape against the two parental species and test whether later generations converge on the female parent's form. Convergence on the female line would support the claim; stable intermediacy, male-line resemblance, or sterility that stops the pedigree would refute it for that cross.
obstacles: Fox-dog and partridge-fowl crosses rarely yield the successive fertile generations the claim requires.
Hybrid pedigrees with scored morphology are scattered and often unpublished as data tables.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is a directional change in resemblance across generations and is measurable where pedigrees exist. The crosses Aristotle names are poorly represented by public multi-generation datasets. Better-documented hybrid zones, such as some canids, can serve only as a proxy and do not cover his examples.

assessments.operationalization: In staged vertebrate embryos, rank the heart against other organs by stage of first distinct appearance. The heart earliest in each series supports the claim; any blooded animal in which another organ is distinctly formed before the heart refutes the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish heart development relative to other early structures

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick stages from the heart tube onward

obstacles: 'First distinctly marked off' depends on what counts as an organ rather than a germ layer.
Model species stand in for all blooded animals.
assessments.rationale: Open staging series show when the heart becomes visible in fishes, birds and amphibians. That tests the claim on a real but incomplete sample of vertebrates. Borderline cases, such as notochord or neural tube appearing as early as the heart, keep the test from being fully clean across the whole scope.

assessments.operationalization: Once erythrinus is mapped to a modern species or genus, tally sexed specimens and the presence of testes versus ovaries or roe. A substantial sample of functional males refutes the claim; only females, or simultaneous hermaphrodites with no separate male, would support the observation he reports.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex, hermaphroditism and reproductive notes for candidate Mediterranean fishes

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic framework for matching ancient fish names to current genera

obstacles: Erythrinus is not a secure identification; serranids and sparids would give different sexual systems.
Hermaphrodites can look like 'females full of roe' without the species lacking males.
assessments.rationale: FishBase records sex and hermaphroditism for the plausible modern groups, so the biological test is standard once the name is fixed. The name itself points at more than one Mediterranean fish. Until that mapping is chosen, the same data can both confirm and refute the report.

assessments.operationalization: Score Anguilla and candidate stagnant-water mullets for separate males and females using gonad type or genetic sex. Distinct males and females refute 'neither male nor female'; a species with no sex distinction would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex, maturity and reproductive biology of eels and mullets

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems and sex-determination records for fishes

obstacles: The mullet of stagnant waters is not identified to a modern species.
Eel gonads mature at sea, so river samples under-represent sex even though the sexes exist.
assessments.rationale: Eel sexual systems are documented in open fish databases well enough to test Aristotle's example directly. The second example, a mullet of stagnant water, cannot be tied to one species with the same confidence. The claim is therefore resolvable for eels and open for the mullet.

assessments.operationalization: Among species with separate sexes, record whether females produce viable offspring with no male contribution. Facultative or obligate parthenogenesis in such species refutes the empirical clause; its absence across a broad sample would support it. The maxim that nature makes nothing in vain is not part of the measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems, including parthenogenesis, across animals

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for squamates in which facultative parthenogenesis is reported

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive notes for fishes, including rare parthenogenesis

obstacles: 'Perfectly' is undefined: a parthenogenetic offspring may or may not count as complete generation.
The teleological premise is not tested by the reproductive records.
assessments.rationale: Sexual-system compilations record parthenogenesis in animals that also have separate sexes, which is the observable part of the claim. Whether an uniparental offspring counts as perfect generation still has to be defined. The maxim that nature makes nothing in vain is not decided by those records.

assessments.operationalization: In staged embryos, compare first appearance of internal organs with external structures, and of larger structures with smaller ones. Internal-before-external and large-before-small would support the claim; a repeated external-before-internal sequence would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick stages spanning early external axial structures and internal organs

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish stage series for organ versus body-surface timing

obstacles: The boundary between internal and external parts is ambiguous for neural tube, somites and skin.
Visibility depends on staining and on which structures are scored as large.
assessments.rationale: Staging series contain the order in which structures become visible for several vertebrates. Applying Aristotle's internal-versus-external cut, and his size rule, requires a coding scheme that the atlases do not supply. The test is feasible for model species and remains sensitive to that coding.

assessments.operationalization: For many-toed quadrupeds, record whether eyelids are fused at birth and the age at eye opening. Universal birth with closed eyes in that group would support the claim; a many-toed species born with eyes open would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts stating whether carnivore young are born blind and when the eyes open

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian life-history context, including altricial development where coded

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and neonate traits used to place species as altricial or precocial

obstacles: 'Polydactylous quadrupeds' may mean fissiped carnivores or every many-toed mammal, and those scopes differ.
Age at eye opening is written in species accounts more often than in a single numeric column.
assessments.rationale: Eye opening is a standard natural-history fact for the dog, cat and their relatives, and species accounts record it. A downloadable numeric field for every many-toed mammal is lacking, so the universal has to be compiled. Within the named carnivores the test is straightforward; outside that list the category itself is the obstacle.

assessments.operationalization: Measure relative volume of head, eyes and legs at early embryonic stages. A head and eyes that dominate early, with small legs, would support the descriptive clause. The claim that lower parts exist for the sake of the upper has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: timed mouse embryo images for early head and eye proportions

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick embryo images across stages when the head is disproportionately large

obstacles: The teleological clause is not distinguished from the size pattern it explains.
Public series are model species, and morphometrics would have to be taken from images.
assessments.rationale: Early embryos in open atlases can be measured for head, eye and limb proportions, which tests the descriptive half. 'For the sake of the upper parts' adds no further observation. Image measurement is standard but has been done for only some of the animals in scope.

assessments.operationalization: Track relative eye size from first appearance to the stage when eyelids, lens and retina are complete, and test for an interval of collapse. Eyes that are disproportionately large early, then collapse, and finish last, would support the claim; eyes that are complete early or that grow steadily without collapse would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick eye development from optic vesicle to later ocular structures

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: mouse developmental series covering early optic tissues

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish eye staging from optic vesicle onward

obstacles: 'Collapse' needs a morphometric definition, not just a qualitative impression.
Completion ranks require a full organ checklist that atlases do not precompute.
assessments.rationale: Optic-vesicle stages and later eye morphology are documented for chick, mouse and zebrafish. Ranking the eye as the last organ finished, and demonstrating a collapse, needs extra measurement on those images. The pattern can be tested in those model vertebrates and not yet as a finished comparative table.

assessments.operationalization: Compare ossification timing of the cranial roof with other skull bones, and fontanelle closure age in humans versus other mammals, alongside relative brain size. A skull roof that ossifies last and stays soft longer in humans would support the descriptive clauses; an earlier-closing human fontanelle, or a later bone elsewhere, would refute them.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative notes on mammalian neonates, skulls and relative brain size

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history context for postnatal development in humans and other mammals

obstacles: Ossification-sequence matrices and fontanelle-closure ages are scattered across papers.
'Most fluid' brain has no standard variable distinct from brain size and water content.
assessments.rationale: Fontanelle closure and skull ossification order are measured in human paediatrics and in comparative ossification studies. Those measurements are not one open cross-species file. Relative brain size can be brought in from compilations, while 'most fluid' remains a loose extra clause, so the claim is only partly testable.

assessments.operationalization: Compare species with determinate versus continued bone growth on whether body size plateaus when skeletal growth stops. A tight match would support bones as the limit of size; continued body growth after skeletal maturity, or determinate size in animals whose skeleton keeps growing, would weaken that causal claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: von Bertalanffy growth parameters showing whether fishes approach an asymptotic length

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian and avian longevity and body size for determinate growers

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: body size and life-history timing across amniotes

obstacles: The counterfactual that bones could always grow is not itself a dataset.
Growth plateaus have hormonal and energetic causes that are confounded with skeletal cessation.
assessments.rationale: Asymptotic growth curves and adult body sizes are widely tabulated, so determinate and continued growth can be compared. Those tables do not show that bone is the cause of the plateau. The causal claim stays weakly separated from rival limits on growth.

assessments.operationalization: Measure hair shaft length at death and at later intervals on the same body, controlling for skin retraction. Continued elongation of the shaft would support the claim; length change explained by shrinkage of the scalp, with no new hair growth, would refute it.
obstacles: Forensic measurements are in papers and case series, not a public longitudinal dataset.
Almost all records are human.
assessments.rationale: Shaft length versus skin retraction is a decisive measurement, and forensic reports already discuss it. They are scattered case literature rather than an open table, and they barely cover hairy animals other than humans. Compilation can test the human case; a comparative dataset does not exist as a single resource.

assessments.operationalization: Classify teeth as continuously growing or finite, and compare that with other bones in the same species. Teeth that stop growing, or bones other than teeth that grow through life, refute the universal; continuously growing teeth alongside bones that stop would support it where that pattern holds.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental descriptions, including ever-growing incisors versus finite adult teeth

obstacles: Aristotle counts teeth as bones, so the comparison inherits that classification.
Continuous-growth dentition is described species by species rather than in one matrix.
assessments.rationale: Whether teeth and other skeletal elements grow through life is recorded in comparative dental accounts. Those accounts are numerous and public but not a single downloadable trait table. Misaligned teeth, his cited evidence, measure eruption and drift as well as continuous growth, which softens the test.

assessments.operationalization: Record erupted teeth or beaks at birth for humans and other toothed vertebrates, treating rare natal teeth as his 'contrary to nature' exceptions. Humans normally toothless at birth, and other toothed animals born with teeth, would support the claim; a toothed mammal or other vertebrate born toothless would refute the universal about 'other animals'.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal descriptions, including whether young are born with erupted teeth

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: altricial versus precocial life histories that correlate with natal dentition

obstacles: Natal dentition is in narrative accounts more than in a numeric column.
His 'other animals' is wider than the mammals with good birth records.
assessments.rationale: Presence or absence of teeth at birth is a yes-no trait with a clear exception class for rare natal teeth in humans. Species accounts document it for many mammals and some other vertebrates. Coverage outside familiar mammals is patchy, so the universal over all other toothed animals is only partly covered.

assessments.operationalization: Rank humans against other animals on hair cover and on nail or claw length relative to body size. Humans at the extreme of least cover and smallest nails would support the descriptive claim. 'Least earthy residue' has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass as the denominator for relative nail size where nail lengths are compiled

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian body masses for allometric comparison

obstacles: Hair cover can mean follicle density, hair length or visible nakedness, and those rankings differ.
Nail and claw lengths are not a standard column beside body mass.
assessments.rationale: Body size is tabulated, but the two traits that would decide the superlatives, hair cover and relative nail size, are scattered anatomical notes. The earthy-residue explanation is not an additional variable. A partial ranking among mammals is possible after compilation; a ranking against all animals is not.

assessments.operationalization: Count umbilical blood vessels per species and regress the count on maternal or neonatal body size. A positive size relationship matching his one-, two- and many-vessel grades would support the claim; no size trend, or vessel counts that contradict the grades, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of umbilical cord structure in mammals

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: adult and neonate body masses as the size axis

obstacles: Vessel counts are written in placentation accounts, not a comparative numeric file.
Humans, with three vessels at moderate size, may cut across a simple size series.
assessments.rationale: Vessel number and body size are both measurable, and placentation accounts plus mass tables supply them for a set of familiar mammals. The accounts have to be coded by hand. That is enough for a partial test of the size series, not a finished analysis of every viviparous species.

assessments.operationalization: Code viviparous mammals for upper incisors, horns and placental type, then test whether lack of upper front teeth, or a highly vascular uterus, predicts cotyledons. Cotyledons restricted to the groups he names would support the claim; cotyledons in incisor-bearing hornless species, or their absence in upper-incisor-less species, would refute the rules.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: placental type, including cotyledonary placentas, across mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental formulae, horns and reproductive accounts

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: species list and life-history context for joining dental and placental records

obstacles: Uterine vessel pattern, his second criterion, is less consistently recorded than placental type.
Camelids and a few other lineages are likely boundary cases for the incisor rule.
assessments.rationale: Placental type and the presence of upper incisors are recorded for many ungulates and other mammals in public accounts. Joining them tests the main cotyledon rule. The vessel-pattern clause and incomplete species coverage keep the full statement at a partial test rather than a single query.

assessments.operationalization: Measure placentome or cotyledon size across gestation in ruminants and test whether they shrink and vanish by term. Shrinkage to disappearance would support the claim; growth toward term, with separation only at birth, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: descriptions of ruminant placentomes through pregnancy

obstacles: Quantitative size-by-gestational-age series are in veterinary papers, not a shared file.
Cotyledon, caruncle and placentome are easy to conflate when coding his term.
assessments.rationale: Placentome size through pregnancy is measured in cattle and sheep and described in comparative placentation accounts. A cross-species numeric series is not downloadable as one table. The direction of size change is decidable for the main domestic ruminants after a literature compilation.

assessments.operationalization: For interspecific hybrids, record whether either sex produces offspring, and compare mules with other named crosses. Mules uniquely sterile, and every other hybrid fertile in both sexes, would support the claim; any other sterile hybrid, or a fertile mule, would refute the stated uniqueness.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of horse, ass and mule fertility

obstacles: Hybrid fertility is a literature compilation, not a global hybrid database.
Rare fertile female mules make an absolute 'sterile' claim depend on sample size.
assessments.rationale: Fertility of mules and of other hybrids is a recorded biological outcome. Public species accounts cover the equid case, while bird, canid and ray hybrids are scattered. The uniqueness claim is decidable in principle from those records and is not yet a single open analysis.

assessments.operationalization: No dataset distinguishes empty general theories from sound ones, because the claim is a rule of method rather than a statement about animals.
obstacles: The claim prescribes how natural science should argue.
It names no organism, trait or measurable outcome.
assessments.rationale: The sentence is a methodological maxim about reasoning from the principles proper to a subject. Nothing in existing biological datasets confirms or refutes it. It has no empirical decision criterion.

assessments.operationalization: Map occurrence of Equus asinus against climate, separating feral and wild records from sheltered domestic stock, and test whether breeding populations are absent from cold regions such as northern Eurasia. Absence from cold climates would support the distributional clause; established outdoor populations in cold regions would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced observations of donkeys, including records from cold countries

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: range of the African wild ass, the wild relative of the domestic ass

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history context for Equus asinus

obstacles: Domestic donkeys are moved and sheltered by people, so occurrence is not cold tolerance.
'Cold nature' is his explanation and is not the same variable as geographic range.
assessments.rationale: Occurrence data can show where asses live, including regions Aristotle called wintry. Human husbandry confounds a physiological reading of 'cannot bear cold'. The distributional clause is testable now; the innate-cold explanation is only partly constrained by those maps.

assessments.operationalization: Compare tabulated gestation lengths of horse and ass with a pre-set window around 365 days. Means and ranges inside that window for both species support a one-year gestation; a mean well outside it for either species refutes the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for horse and ass

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian gestation length at species level

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: independent compilation of gestation for the two equids

obstacles: 'One year' needs an explicit tolerance in days before the test is run.
Breed and domestication shift gestation by days to weeks.
assessments.rationale: Gestation length for both equids is a standard field in more than one open life-history database, with coverage that matches the named species. The decision is a comparison with one year and can be run directly. Only the width of the window around 365 days has to be fixed in advance.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the temperature of horse and ass semen and test whether mixing or chilling horse semen produces the sterility seen in mules. Colder ass semen, and sterility caused by that chilling, would support the mechanism; equal temperatures, or sterility unaffected by temperature, would refute it.
obstacles: No public dataset records seminal temperature of horse and ass or a chilling experiment on mule sterility.
Existing karyotype records do not measure the cold-seed mechanism.
assessments.rationale: The mechanism is a thermal prediction about the two secretions and about the effect of mixing them. That prediction is measurable, and the measurements are not in an open dataset. Sterility itself is well known, but it does not supply the temperature variable the explanation requires.

assessments.operationalization: Compile mule pregnancies and their outcomes, and record whether female mules show a menstrual or analogous uterine secretion. Conceptions that never reach birth would support the claim; a live foal would refute impossibility of birth, and an estrous rather than menstrual cycle would refute the secretion clause as he states it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mule reproductive biology, including sterility of the sexes

obstacles: Documented mule pregnancies are rare case reports.
Equids cycle by estrus, so 'menstrual secretion' is a mismatched variable.
assessments.rationale: Pregnancy outcome in female mules is an observable event, and veterinary cases plus species accounts record it. The cases are too few and too scattered for a clean rate estimate. The menstrual-secretion explanation uses a category that horse and ass reproductive physiology does not share with humans, which limits that clause.

assessments.operationalization: Code sharks, rays and chimaeras for egg-laying versus live birth and, where recorded, for shell type and egg colour. A class-wide pattern of internal eggs, live birth and a soft one-coloured egg would support the claim; oviparous species with horny egg cases would refute it as a statement about cartilaginous fishes generally.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode across sharks, rays and chimaeras

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species-level reproductive mode for chondrichthyans

obstacles: Shell hardness and egg colour are less often a separate field than reproductive mode.
Chimaeras sit at the edge of his selachian class.
assessments.rationale: Reproductive mode of cartilaginous fishes is tabulated in open trait databases with broad species coverage. Egg-laying skates and sharks are the direct counterexamples to a class-wide live-bearing claim, and they are coded. Shell colour is spottier, but the main generalization can be confirmed or refuted by a standard cross-tabulation.

assessments.operationalization: Score bird species for unfertilized eggs laid without mating, and compare ground-living prolific birds with raptors. Wind-eggs restricted to the former group would support the claim; unfertilized eggs in birds of prey, or their absence in prolific fowl, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size as a proxy for the prolific birds he contrasts with raptors

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet and foraging stratum to separate raptors from non-predatory birds

obstacles: Unfertilized-egg records themselves are concentrated in poultry science.
Diet and clutch size proxy the groups he names and do not record wind-eggs.
assessments.rationale: Open trait tables can separate raptors from prolific ground birds by diet and clutch size. Whether those groups lay unfertilized eggs is a further fact, well documented for fowl and geese and sparse for wild raptors. The group contrast is testable now; the wind-egg distribution is only partly compiled.

assessments.operationalization: Relate wing or feather investment to clutch size and copulation frequency, comparing raptors with heavy ground birds. A trade-off in the predicted direction would match the pattern. Shared 'residual matter' making both wings and semen is not measured by that correlation.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: wing and body measurements for birds as a proxy for allocation to flight

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size for the fecundity side of the contrast

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet classes that pick out birds of prey

obstacles: A correlation of wing metrics with clutch size does not show a common residual substance.
Copulation frequency is rarely tabulated beside morphology.
assessments.rationale: Wing measurements, diet and clutch size are in open bird datasets and can test whether raptors lay fewer eggs. That is the observable pattern. The material-cause story that wings and semen draw on one residue is not separated from ordinary life-history trade-offs by those variables.

assessments.operationalization: Record clutch size and nest use of Cuculus canorus against other birds. A small clutch laid in other species' nests would support the natural-history clauses. 'Cold nature' and cowardice are supported only if an independent thermal or behavioural measure predicts parasitism.

candidate_datasets.name: BirdLife Data Zone
candidate_datasets.role: species account for the common cuckoo, including brood parasitism

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size of the cuckoo relative to other birds

obstacles: Cold temperament and cowardice are not variables in ornithological trait tables.
Host-mobbing is a consequence of parasitism, so it does not independently prove a cold nature.
assessments.rationale: Brood parasitism and a small clutch are documented for the common cuckoo in public species data. Those clauses can be checked directly. The explanation from coldness and cowardice has no separate measurement in the same sources, so the claim as a whole is only partly resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: Using known-age lionesses, record litter size at each successive birth and test for the sequence from five or six down by one each year to zero. That sequence would support the claim; a different age pattern, or continued litters late in life, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: species-level litter size for the lion, a population mean rather than an age series

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: lion longevity and litter size as context for the age trajectory

obstacles: Open databases report a typical litter size, not litter size by the mother's parity.
Longitudinal lion studies exist as papers and monitoring records that still need compilation.
assessments.rationale: The predicted parity-by-parity decline is a precise, refutable series. Mean litter size in life-history databases speaks only roughly to the first-birth number. Age-specific lion reproduction is in field and zoo records that are public but scattered, so the exact sequence is partly, not immediately, testable.

assessments.operationalization: Compare egg laying in hens and geese that have never mated with birds that have mated, and score eggs as unfertilized. Eggs from never-mated females support independent origin of wind-eggs; eggs only after a prior mating would support the relic theory he rejects.
obstacles: Poultry trials are in agricultural papers and husbandry records, not one open repository.
Wild birds are outside the domestic fowl and goose evidence.
assessments.rationale: Whether a never-mated hen or goose lays eggs is a simple contrast, and poultry practice has recorded it many times. Those records are not collected as a downloadable dataset. For the domestic species he names, compilation is enough to decide the claim; it is not a ready-made analysis.

assessments.operationalization: Compare egg completeness at laying, egg size at laying versus hatching, and fecundity between birds and externally spawning fishes. Complete avian eggs and fish eggs that finish outside, with fish fecundity too high for internal completion, would support the claim; fishes that lay few complete eggs, or birds that lay unfinished ones, would challenge it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and egg size for externally spawning fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: avian clutch size and egg mass for the bird side of the contrast

obstacles: 'Incomplete' mixes swelling, fertilization and embryonic stage.
High fecundity does not by itself show that internal completion is impossible.
assessments.rationale: Fecundity and egg size are tabulated for many fishes, and clutch and egg size for birds. That supports a comparison of numbers and of how finished the egg is at laying. The causal claim that sheer number makes internal completion impossible is not settled by the correlation alone.

assessments.operationalization: Score eggs for a distinct albumen and yolk versus a single coloured yolk mass, across birds and fishes. Two-coloured bird eggs and one-coloured fish eggs would support the claim; a bird egg without that division, or a fish egg with a separate white, would refute the corresponding universal.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg descriptions and diameters for fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: bird egg sizes as context; yolk-and-white structure is only partly captured

obstacles: Yolk-versus-white structure is described in embryology texts more than in a trait column.
Shark eggs are structurally richer than typical teleost eggs.
assessments.rationale: The colour division of the egg is a visible trait with a clear contrast between birds and fishes. Fish and bird databases record egg size much more consistently than albumen-yolk structure. The contrast can be checked from existing descriptions for many species and is not a finished comparative file.

assessments.operationalization: Compare yolk mass and yolk colour between water birds and land birds, holding egg size constant. Larger and paler yolks in water birds would support the descriptive claim; equal or smaller, deeper-yellow yolks would refute it. Moister and colder nature is a separate proxy.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging and habitat classes that separate aquatic from terrestrial birds

obstacles: Yolk proportion and yolk colour are in poultry and ornithology papers, not in the habitat tables.
Domestication and diet change yolk colour independently of habitat.
assessments.rationale: Habitat classifications can pick out water birds and land birds. Yolk size and colour, the traits that decide the claim, are measured for some domestic and wild species in scattered studies. The group labels are ready; the yolk comparison still has to be compiled, and diet confounds colour.

assessments.operationalization: Record which end of the egg emerges first at oviposition in domestic fowl and other birds. The blunt end first, sharp end last, would support the claim; sharp end first in a majority of layings would refute it.
obstacles: Orientation at laying is in poultry observations and films, not a public dataset.
Other bird species are much less often recorded than the hen.
assessments.rationale: Which pole emerges first is a binary observation with a decisive count. Poultry research has recorded it for the domestic fowl, in scattered reports rather than an open table. Extending the same count to birds generally would need further compiled observations.

assessments.operationalization: Measure shell hardness and mineral content at the moment of laying and over the following minutes, and test whether hardening is produced by cooling and evaporation. A soft shell at exit that rigidifies by cooling would support the claim; a shell already hard in the shell gland, with no post-laying mineral jump, would refute it.
obstacles: Shell-gland timing is in poultry physiology papers, not a shared dataset.
Cooling and evaporation need to be separated from calcification that happened before laying.
assessments.rationale: Hardness at laying versus hardness after a short interval is a direct test, and poultry physiology has measured calcification in the shell gland. Those measurements are scattered and mostly about the domestic fowl. They are sufficient to assess the hen and only a start for birds generally.

assessments.operationalization: For live-bearing selachians, especially smooth-hounds, record whether the embryo remains attached to the uterus by a cord after the yolk is exhausted.
